3.overview:
Ahab's second son reforms exactly as far as it is convenient — the pillar of Baal comes down, his mother's discredited religion, while he clings to Jeroboam's calves, which are state policy and hold the kingdom together. Then Moab stops paying its hundred thousand lambs, and he sends south for help.

Jehoshaphat's answer is the sentence he gave Ahab word for word: I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses. That pledge nearly killed him at Ramoth-gilead and earned him a prophet's rebuke at his own gate, and he had learned enough to refuse a joint fleet — and not enough to refuse a joint army. Seven days into a clever desert route the water runs out, the king of Israel's first mention of God is an accusation, and Jehoshaphat asks for a prophet in the same words and in the same position in the sequence as last time: afterwards.

Elisha answers only for Jehoshaphat's sake, and the promise is water without weather. It arrives at the hour of the sacrifice in Jerusalem, saves one army in the night and destroys the other at sunrise. And then the chapter ends where nobody expects: a boy burning on a city wall, an unexplained wrath, and three victorious armies going home with nothing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — I Am As You Are
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahab's second son takes the northern throne and does what is evil though not like his father and mother, for he put away the pillar of Baal — and clings to Jeroboam's calves (vv. 2-3). Moab has stopped paying its hundred thousand lambs, so he musters Israel and sends south for help; and Jehoshaphat answers I will go. I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses (v. 7). They take the long desert road round Edom, march seven days, and run out of water (vv. 8-9). The king of Israel's first mention of God is an accusation (v. 10) — and Jehoshaphat asks the question he always asks a little too late: is there no prophet of the LORD here, through whom we may inquire of the LORD? (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 7 is verse-for-verse what he said to Ahab in 1 Kings 22:4. He gave that pledge, was nearly killed in the chariot at Ramoth-gilead, was met at his own gate by a prophet asking should you help the wicked? — and here he is saying the same sentence to the same family. He had learned about ships and declined a joint fleet (1 Kgs. 22:49). Nothing transferred to armies.
verseByVerse.examples: And note how Elisha is identified to the kings: not by the Jordan or the bears or the healed spring, but as Elisha the son of Shaphat, who poured water on the hands of Elijah. The man who burned his plough and slaughtered his oxen is known in the army as the one who did the washing.

verseByVerse.quote: In the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, Jehoram the son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned twelve years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, though not like his father and mother, for he put away the pillar of Baal that his father had made. Nevertheless, he clung to the sin of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin; he did not depart from it. Now Mesha king of Moab was a sheep breeder, and he had to deliver to the king of Israel 100,000 lambs and the wool of 100,000 rams. But when Ahab died, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel. So King Jehoram marched out of Samaria at that time and mustered all Israel. And he went and sent word to Jehoshaphat king of Judah: "The king of Moab has rebelled against me. Will you go with me to battle against Moab?" And he said, "I will go. I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses." Then he said, "By which way shall we march?" Jehoram answered, "By the way of the wilderness of Edom." So the king of Israel went with the king of Judah and the king of Edom. And when they had made a circuitous march of seven days, there was no water for the army or for the animals that followed them. Then the king of Israel said, "Alas! The LORD has called these three kings to give them into the hand of Moab." And Jehoshaphat said, "Is there no prophet of the LORD here, through whom we may inquire of the LORD?" Then one of the king of Israel's servants answered, "Elisha the son of Shaphat is here, who poured water on the hands of Elijah." And Jehoshaphat said, "The word of the LORD is with him." So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom went down to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, Jehoram the son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned twelve years.'

'He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, though not like his father and mother, for he put away the pillar of Baal that his father had made.'

'Nevertheless, he clung to the sin of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin; he did not depart from it.'

Here is a reform, and it is the most instructive kind, because it is genuine and it is exactly as deep as it was convenient to go.

He takes down the pillar of Baal. That is a real act; his father put it up and his mother is still alive. But look at what it costs him. Baal was Jezebel's religion, it was humiliated in public on Carmel, its four hundred and fifty prophets are dead, and the country has watched fire fall from heaven. Removing that pillar was popular.

What he keeps is the golden calves at Bethel and Dan, and the writer chooses a strong verb for it: he clung to them. Those were state policy. They were installed to stop Israelites going south to Jerusalem to worship, and they are what holds the northern kingdom together as a separate country. Give those up and the throne is in question.

So he surrendered the sin that had become an embarrassment and held on to the one that was still paying. That is not hypocrisy exactly; it is the ordinary arithmetic of partial repentance, and it happens in Christian lives constantly. The habit everybody can see goes first, and stays gone. The one that is load-bearing is renegotiated.

'Now Mesha king of Moab was a sheep breeder, and he had to deliver to the king of Israel 100,000 lambs and the wool of 100,000 rams.'

'But when Ahab died, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel.'

A hundred thousand lambs a year, and the wool of a hundred thousand rams. That is the scale of what Moab had been handing over the border annually, and it explains both why they stopped and why Israel could not let it go.

'So King Jehoram marched out of Samaria at that time and mustered all Israel.'

'And he went and sent word to Jehoshaphat king of Judah: "The king of Moab has rebelled against me. Will you go with me to battle against Moab?" And he said, "I will go. I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses."'

Stop on that answer, because you have read it before, in exactly those words.

In 1 Kings 22, Ahab asked him to come to Ramoth-gilead and he replied: I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses (1 Kgs. 22:4). It is not a similar sentence. It is the same sentence.

Now recall what that pledge bought him. He went to a war he was never asked to fight, was talked into wearing the royal robes while his ally hid in a private's armour, was chased across a battlefield by thirty-two chariot squadrons who thought he was the king of Israel, and screamed for his life. He got home, and a prophet was waiting at the gate to ask him should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD? (2 Chron. 19:2).

And here he is, some years later, saying the identical words to that man's son.

What makes it worse is that he had learned something. When Ahaziah proposed a joint shipping venture, Jehoshaphat was not willing (1 Kgs. 22:49). He had lost a fleet to one of these alliances and he would not do it again — with ships.

That is how most of us learn. Not in principle but in departments. The lesson is filed under the particular disaster that taught it, and the identical mistake in a different costume walks straight past the guard. Ask yourself where you have been genuinely burned and genuinely careful ever since, and then ask whether the carefulness ever crossed into the next room.

'Then he said, "By which way shall we march?" Jehoram answered, "By the way of the wilderness of Edom."'

Note which question he does ask. The route.

It is a shrewd plan, too — instead of coming at Moab from the north across the Arnon gorge where they will be waiting, swing right round the bottom of the Dead Sea and come up through Edom into their undefended flank, picking up the Edomite king on the way.

'So the king of Israel went with the king of Judah and the king of Edom. And when they had made a circuitous march of seven days, there was no water for the army or for the animals that followed them.'

Seven days in the desert south of the Dead Sea, three armies and their baggage animals, and the wells are dry.

The clever plan has put them somewhere they cannot survive. Nobody asked God about the route either.

'Then the king of Israel said, "Alas! The LORD has called these three kings to give them into the hand of Moab."'

The first time the name of the LORD is spoken in this campaign, it is an accusation.

He has not consulted him, prayed to him, or mentioned him. He has taken down one pillar and kept two calves. And on day seven, with the water gone, he knows exactly who is behind it and says so.

People who never speak to God are often remarkably confident about what he is doing.

'And Jehoshaphat said, "Is there no prophet of the LORD here, through whom we may inquire of the LORD?" Then one of the king of Israel's servants answered, "Elisha the son of Shaphat is here, who poured water on the hands of Elijah."'

There is the other half of the pattern, also word for word. Is there not here another prophet of the LORD of whom we may inquire? (1 Kgs. 22:7).

Same man, same question, same position in the sequence: after the pledge, after the march, after the disaster. He is a good king and he does not forget God; he simply never remembers him first, and this chapter shows what it costs to be a day-seven believer.

Then the way Elisha is identified, which is the loveliest line in the chapter. A staff officer knows who he is, and describes him as the man who poured water on the hands of Elijah.

Not the man who parted the Jordan. Not the man who healed the spring at Jericho. The man who did the washing.

Ten years or more ago a wealthy young farmer slaughtered twelve yoke of oxen, burned the ploughs to cook them, fed his village and walked away to be somebody's servant (1 Kgs. 19:21). That is what he has been known for ever since, in the army, by strangers. It is the only c.v. he has and it was enough to fetch three kings down to his tent.

'And Jehoshaphat said, "The word of the LORD is with him." So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom went down to him.'

They go down to him. Three crowned heads walk out of the camp to a prophet's tent, because the man with the water is the man with the word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — You Shall Not See Wind or Rain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elisha will not be treated as a convenience: what have I to do with you? Go to the prophets of your father and to the prophets of your mother (v. 13). He answers at all only for the sake of the man from Judah — were it not that I have regard for Jehoshaphat the king of Judah, I would neither look at you nor see you (v. 14). Then a musician is called, the hand of the LORD comes on him, and the word is I will make this dry streambed full of pools... you shall not see wind or rain, but that streambed shall be filled with water (vv. 15-17), with a verdict attached: this is a light thing in the sight of the LORD (v. 18). And in the morning, at the hour of the sacrifice, the water comes (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Water without weather. The rain that fills that wadi falls in the Edomite hills, out of sight, on people who will never know what it was for; the army will drink a river and never see a cloud. Elijah at Carmel had to send a man to look seven times and watch the sky go black. This time the answer arrives from a storm nobody in the camp witnesses.
verseByVerse.examples: And the thing that is killing three armies is called a light thing. Not small in itself — small to him. The trouble that has your whole attention is not being weighed on the scale you are weighing it on.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elisha said to the king of Israel, "What have I to do with you? Go to the prophets of your father and to the prophets of your mother." But the king of Israel said to him, "No; it is the LORD who has called these three kings to give them into the hand of Moab." And Elisha said, "As the LORD of hosts lives, before whom I stand, were it not that I have regard for Jehoshaphat the king of Judah, I would neither look at you nor see you. But now bring me a musician." And when the musician played, the hand of the LORD came upon him. And he said, "Thus says the LORD, 'I will make this dry streambed full of pools.' For thus says the LORD, 'You shall not see wind or rain, but that streambed shall be filled with water, so that you shall drink, you, your livestock, and your animals.' This is a light thing in the sight of the LORD. He will also give the Moabites into your hand, and you shall attack every fortified city and every choice city, and shall fell every good tree and stop up all springs of water and ruin every good piece of land with stones." The next morning, about the time of offering the sacrifice, behold, water came from the direction of Edom, till the country was filled with water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Elisha said to the king of Israel, "What have I to do with you? Go to the prophets of your father and to the prophets of your mother." But the king of Israel said to him, "No; it is the LORD who has called these three kings to give them into the hand of Moab."'

It is a hard greeting for a man in trouble and it is entirely deserved.

The prophets of your father are the four hundred who told Ahab to go up to Ramoth-gilead and triumph. The prophets of your mother are the ones who ate at Jezebel's table and died at the Kishon. Elisha is saying: you have a religious establishment, and you have never once come to me until the water ran out; go and ask them.

The prophet declines to be a utility. The word of God is not a service you call out when the arrangements you actually trust have failed.

Notice the king's answer, because he does not defend himself. He repeats his complaint about God. He is standing in front of the one man who can help him and the only thing he can think of to say is that this is God's fault.

'And Elisha said, "As the LORD of hosts lives, before whom I stand, were it not that I have regard for Jehoshaphat the king of Judah, I would neither look at you nor see you."'

The oath is his master's, word for word — as the LORD of hosts lives, before whom I stand, which is what Elijah swore to a frightened Obadiah on a road in the famine (1 Kgs. 18:15). The heir has the family formula.

Then the sentence itself, and it should not be softened. You are getting an answer because of somebody else. Not for your sake. I would not look at you.

Turn that over before moving on, because it is more encouraging than it sounds. An army of thousands of men — Israelites, Edomites, mercenaries, camp followers, most of whom had no more claim on God than their king did — is about to drink because one man in the tent had a standing with God that the rest of them did not.

That is not a curiosity. It is the ground any of us stand on. Nobody is heard on his own showing. The whole of the gospel is that the Father regards the Son, and that those who are found in him are looked at with the regard that belongs to somebody else. Jehoshaphat could not transfer his righteousness to Jehoram, and the arrangement here is only a shadow of a real one; but the shape of it — mercy arriving because of who you are standing next to — is exact.

'But now bring me a musician." And when the musician played, the hand of the LORD came upon him.'

He asks for music before he prophesies, and the writer records it without explaining it.

Do not build a system on one verse. But it is not isolated: David's harp settled Saul when the tormenting spirit came (1 Sam. 16:23), and the temple musicians under David are described as men who prophesied with lyres, with harps, and with cymbals (1 Chron. 25:1). Elisha has just come out of a shouting match with a king who blames God for everything, and before he can hear anything he wants a musician.

Whatever else that means, it means the prophet was a man, and needed quieting.

'And he said, "Thus says the LORD, 'I will make this dry streambed full of pools.'

'For thus says the LORD, 'You shall not see wind or rain, but that streambed shall be filled with water, so that you shall drink, you, your livestock, and your animals.'

Water without weather. That is the promise, and it is stranger than a rainstorm would have been.

Somewhere south and east of them, up in the Edomite hills, it is going to rain — on people who have no idea an army is dying in the valley below, who will get up the next morning and think nothing of it. And the water will run down the dry wadi in the night and be standing in pools by dawn.

The men in the camp will not hear thunder or feel a drop. They will simply wake up beside a river.

Set that beside Carmel, where Elijah put his face between his knees and sent a servant to the ridge seven times until a cloud the size of a hand came up out of the sea. He watched his answer arrive. These men will not see any part of theirs.

Most answered prayer is of this second kind. The thing that saves you was set in motion days earlier, somewhere you have never been, by people you will never meet, and the first you know of it is that it is simply there in the morning.

'This is a light thing in the sight of the LORD. He will also give the Moabites into your hand,'

A light thing. The problem that has three kings on their knees in a tent on day seven is, in the sight of God, a small item, and he mentions it in passing before getting to the main business.

He is not being dismissive. He is giving them a true reading of the scale. What is at the absolute limit of your resources is not being weighed on your scale, and the God who is about to hand them a kingdom mentions the drinking water first only because that is what they came about.

'and you shall attack every fortified city and every choice city, and shall fell every good tree and stop up all springs of water and ruin every good piece of land with stones."'

This verse should not be passed over quietly, because it sits in real tension with the law, and a reader who knows the law will feel it.

Deuteronomy expressly forbids this in a siege: you shall not destroy its trees by wielding an axe against them... Are the trees in the field human, that they should be besieged by you? (Deut. 20:19-20). Fruit trees take a generation to grow and feed people who had no part in the quarrel, and Israel was told to leave them standing.

Here a prophet of the LORD tells them to fell every good tree, block every spring and stone every field.

The honest thing is to say that the tension is there. The best reading is that this is a particular sentence of judgment on Moab, announced by God and not devised by the army, rather than a repeal of a standing law about how Israel is to conduct its ordinary wars; the two texts are doing different jobs. But nobody should pretend the verse is comfortable, and the chapter's ending suggests the writer did not think it was either.

'The next morning, about the time of offering the sacrifice, behold, water came from the direction of Edom, till the country was filled with water.'

About the time of offering the sacrifice. The writer times it by the altar in Jerusalem — the morning lamb, in the other kingdom, over the border.

Elijah did the same thing on Carmel, waiting to pray until the hour of the evening offering (1 Kgs. 18:36). Twice now, the decisive moment in a northern crisis is dated by a clock in a temple these kings do not attend.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–27 — A Boy on the Wall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sun comes up on the flooded valley and the Moabites see water as red as blood and conclude the allied kings have destroyed each other; they break ranks for plunder and are cut to pieces (vv. 22-24). Israel goes through the country stopping springs, felling trees and covering the fields with stones, until only Kir-hareseth is left (v. 25). Mesha tries to cut his way out with seven hundred swordsmen and cannot; and then he took his oldest son who was to reign in his place and offered him for a burnt offering on the wall. And there came great wrath against Israel. And they withdrew from him and returned to their own land (vv. 26-27).
verseByVerse.theology: The water God sent to keep Israel alive is the same water that destroys Moab. One night it is a drink; at sunrise it is a trick of the light that empties a whole army out of its defensive line and onto the swords of men it thought were dead.
verseByVerse.examples: And the ending is left unexplained, deliberately. The writer does not say whose wrath, or why the siege lifted, or what any of it was for. What he does record is that a campaign which began with a pledge given before a prayer ended with a child burning on a city wall and three armies walking home with nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: When all the Moabites heard that the kings had come up to fight against them, all who were able to put on armor, from the youngest to the oldest, were called out and were drawn up at the border. And when they rose early in the morning and the sun shone on the water, the Moabites saw the water opposite them as red as blood. And they said, "This is blood; the kings have surely fought together and struck one another down. Now then, Moab, to the spoil!" But when they came to the camp of Israel, the Israelites rose and struck the Moabites, till they fled before them. And they went forward, striking the Moabites as they went. And they overthrew the cities, and on every good piece of land every man threw a stone until it was covered. They stopped every spring of water and felled all the good trees, till only its stones were left in Kir-hareseth, and the slingers surrounded and attacked it. When the king of Moab saw that the battle was going against him, he took with him 700 swordsmen to break through, opposite the king of Edom, but they could not. Then he took his oldest son who was to reign in his place and offered him for a burnt offering on the wall. And there came great wrath against Israel. And they withdrew from him and returned to their own land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When all the Moabites heard that the kings had come up to fight against them, all who were able to put on armor, from the youngest to the oldest, were called out and were drawn up at the border.'

A general mobilisation, everyone who can carry a shield, drawn up along the frontier. They are ready and they are in position.

'And when they rose early in the morning and the sun shone on the water, the Moabites saw the water opposite them as red as blood.'

'And they said, "This is blood; the kings have surely fought together and struck one another down. Now then, Moab, to the spoil!"'

Low morning sun, red sandstone country, and a valley full of standing water where yesterday there was nothing. The whole basin lights up the colour of blood.

They read it exactly wrong, in the way people always read the evidence when they have already decided what they hope. Three kings in one camp, and everyone knows that alliances of three kings come apart; obviously they have fought each other; obviously the field is full of dead men and unguarded baggage. Now then, Moab, to the spoil.

So the army that was drawn up in a defensive line at the border breaks ranks and runs downhill after plunder.

'But when they came to the camp of Israel, the Israelites rose and struck the Moabites, till they fled before them. And they went forward, striking the Moabites as they went.'

The same water did both things. It kept one army alive in the night and pulled the other out of its position at dawn. God did not need two miracles.

'And they overthrew the cities, and on every good piece of land every man threw a stone until it was covered. They stopped every spring of water and felled all the good trees, till only its stones were left in Kir-hareseth, and the slingers surrounded and attacked it.'

Every man throwing one stone onto a field until the field is gone. It is a slow, deliberate, communal way to ruin farmland, and it takes an army to do it.

'When the king of Moab saw that the battle was going against him, he took with him 700 swordsmen to break through, opposite the king of Edom, but they could not.'

He picks the Edomite sector, which is the sensible choice — Edom is the junior partner, dragged along, with least reason to hold the line. Seven hundred men go at it and the line does not break.

'Then he took his oldest son who was to reign in his place and offered him for a burnt offering on the wall. And there came great wrath against Israel. And they withdrew from him and returned to their own land.'

The last thing he has is his son, so he burns him on the city wall where the besieging army can watch.

Take in what the verse is describing. Not a symbolic act and not a threat: a boy who was going to be king, killed and burned as an offering, in the open, on the ramparts, in front of thousands of men who were close enough to see it. The child had done nothing and had no say. His father is buying a god's attention with him.

Now the sentence the commentators have argued over for centuries. And there came great wrath against Israel.

The Hebrew does not say whose wrath, and the honest thing is to admit it. Three readings are defensible. It may be God's anger — at a campaign nobody asked him about, or at the ruin of a whole country, or at a people who provoked a horror like that and stood watching it. It may be the fury of the Moabites, whose desperation broke over the besiegers and drove them off. Or it may be something nearer to horror in the Israelite ranks — men who had seen enough and would not stay in front of that wall.

The writer does not tell us. He records that the wrath came and the siege lifted and three armies went home, and he offers no explanation at all for a campaign in which God gave them water out of a clear sky and a kingdom into their hand.

They won every engagement and came away with nothing. Moab is not reconquered; the tribute never resumes; and Mesha's own memorial stone, set up in Dibon, records the whole business as his victory.

This book has begun to keep a tally that nobody in it is keeping. Hiel of Bethel buried his eldest son in the foundations of Jericho and his youngest under the gates, to finish a building (1 Kgs. 16:34). Naboth's sons died with him in a field so that a king could have a vegetable garden (2 Kgs. 9:26). Now a boy burns on a wall so that his father can hold a town for another week. Three different religions, three different projects, and the price is always somebody's children.

Which is where the Christian reader has to be careful, because there is a resemblance here and it runs the opposite way from how it first appears. Mesha gave up his firstborn to get something out of a god. That is what pagan sacrifice is: a payment, offered upward, to move a power that is not otherwise interested.

The cross is not that transaction improved. It is that transaction reversed. Nobody gave God a son to buy his favour; God gave his own Son to people who were not asking. God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom. 5:8). The offering came down, not up, and it was not to purchase anything but to pay for everything — and there has not needed to be another one since.

Mesha's son was burned to keep a wall standing for a day. The wall fell eventually. The Son who was given is alive, and what he bought does not come down.

3.theology:
The reform that costs nothing (vv. 2-3). He removes the pillar of Baal — humiliated on Carmel, its prophets dead, its patroness his mother — and clings to the calves, which are the reason the northern kingdom exists as a separate country. The sin that had become an embarrassment goes; the one that is load-bearing is renegotiated. That is the ordinary arithmetic of partial repentance.

Learning in departments (v. 7). The pledge is 1 Kings 22:4 word for word. He had been nearly killed for it, rebuked for it, and had refused Ahaziah's shipping venture on the strength of it (1 Kgs. 22:49). The lesson was filed under ships. Most of us are genuinely careful about the precise disaster that taught us and let the identical mistake walk past in a different costume.

For Jehoshaphat's sake (v. 14). An army drinks because of the standing one man in the tent has with God. Jehoshaphat could not actually transfer anything to Jehoram and the arrangement is only a shadow — but the shape is exact, and it is the ground every Christian stands on. Nobody is heard on his own showing; the Father regards the Son, and those found in him are looked at with a regard that belongs to somebody else.

Water without weather (v. 17). The rain falls in the Edomite hills on people who will never know why, and the army wakes beside a river having neither heard thunder nor felt a drop. Elijah watched his answer come up out of the sea on the seventh look; these men see no part of theirs. Most answered prayer is of the second kind — set going days earlier, somewhere you have never been, by people you will never meet.

A light thing (v. 18). What has three kings on their knees on day seven is mentioned in passing before God gets to the main business. Not dismissive — a true reading of the scale. What is at the absolute limit of your resources is not being weighed on your scale.

The trees (v. 19), honestly. Deuteronomy forbids felling fruit trees in a siege in as many words: are the trees in the field human, that they should be besieged by you? (Deut. 20:19-20). The tension is real. The best reading is that this is a specific announced judgment on Moab rather than a repeal of the standing law for Israel's ordinary wars — but the verse is uncomfortable, and the chapter's ending suggests the writer knew it.

The wrath that is not identified (v. 27). The Hebrew does not say whose. It may be God's — at a campaign nobody consulted him about, or at the ruin of a country; it may be Moabite fury breaking over the besiegers; it may be horror in Israel's own ranks. Scripture leaves it open and so should we. What is not left open is the outcome: every engagement won, and nothing gained.

Sons, and which direction the offering runs (v. 27). Hiel buried two boys in Jericho's foundations and gates to finish a building; Naboth's sons died for a vegetable garden; this one burns to hold a wall for another week. Pagan sacrifice is a payment offered upward to move a power that is not otherwise interested. The cross is not that transaction improved but reversed: God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom. 5:8). It came down, not up, and there has not needed to be another.
3.examples:
Then: An army drew up along its own frontier, ready and in position, saw a valley of standing water turn red in the morning sun, decided the enemy had destroyed itself, broke ranks for the plunder, and ran downhill onto the swords of men it had just concluded were dead.

Now: Three things. First, Jehoshaphat, who is the most useful man in the chapter for ordinary Christians because he is genuinely good and genuinely caught. He never forgets God; he simply never remembers him first, and the cost of being a day-seven believer is a seven-day march into a desert with no water at the end of it. Ask where you have been badly burned and carefully cautious ever since — and then whether the caution ever crossed into the next room. Second, Elisha as the army knew him: the man who poured water on the hands of Elijah. Not the Jordan, not the healed spring — the washing. That was the whole of his reputation and it was enough to bring three kings out of the camp to his tent. Third, water without weather. If you are waiting on something and there is no cloud in the sky, notice that the men in this chapter never saw one either, and woke up beside a river.

And they ate and had some left, according to the word of the LORD.
4.overview:
Four scenes, and every one of them happens in a house or a field rather than on a mountain in front of a nation. Elijah's ministry was public and confrontational; his heir's is domestic, and this chapter is where that becomes plain.

A widow from the prophetic guild is about to lose her sons to a creditor exercising his legal rights, and is asked what is in the house: nothing except a jar of oil. She borrows pots from the neighbours, shuts the door, and pours until there is nowhere left to pour. Then a wealthy woman at Shunem builds the prophet a room with a bed, a table, a chair and a lamp, declines any favour in return — I dwell among my own people — and is given the one thing she had never let herself ask for, and answers do not lie to your servant.

The boy dies on her lap at noon. She lays him on the prophet's bed, says all is well to everyone who asks, rides seventeen miles, refuses the staff and the servant in Elisha's own words, and gets her son back. And the chapter closes in a famine with poison in a communal pot and twenty barley loaves set before a hundred men, with some left over.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Nothing in the House Except
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A widow from the prophetic guild is about to lose her two sons to a creditor — which was entirely lawful — and Elisha begins where God usually begins: what have you in the house? She has nothing in the house except a jar of oil (vv. 1-2). The instruction is to borrow vessels from the neighbours, empty vessels and not too few, shut the door and pour (vv. 3-4). She pours until there is not another, and then the oil stopped flowing (v. 6). And the proceeds are enough to clear the debt and leave her an income: you and your sons can live on the rest (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The thing she called nothing is the thing she is saved by. A flask of anointing oil, the smallest container in the house, listed under except — and God asks for an inventory before he does anything, because he works with what is actually there rather than with what she wishes were there.
verseByVerse.examples: And the oil stops at the last borrowed pot. Not at the limit of God's supply; at the limit of hers. The size of that miracle was settled out in the street, in how many jars a frightened woman was willing to knock on doors and ask for.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the wife of one of the sons of the prophets cried to Elisha, "Your servant my husband is dead, and you know that your servant feared the LORD, but the creditor has come to take my two children to be his slaves." And Elisha said to her, "What shall I do for you? Tell me; what have you in the house?" And she said, "Your servant has nothing in the house except a jar of oil." Then he said, "Go outside, borrow vessels from all your neighbors, empty vessels and not too few. Then go in and shut the door behind yourself and your sons and pour into all these vessels. And when one is full, set it aside." So she went from him and shut the door behind herself and her sons. And as she poured they brought the vessels to her. When the vessels were full, she said to her son, "Bring me another vessel." And he said to her, "There is not another." Then the oil stopped flowing. She came and told the man of God, and he said, "Go, sell the oil and pay your debts, and you and your sons can live on the rest."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the wife of one of the sons of the prophets cried to Elisha, "Your servant my husband is dead, and you know that your servant feared the LORD, but the creditor has come to take my two children to be his slaves."'

She is one of their own. Her husband belonged to the company of prophets — Elisha's own men, the fifty who stood at the Jordan and the ones who sit before him at meals — and he has died and left debt, and she says so on the assumption that Elisha will remember him.

Understand what the creditor is doing, because it matters that he is not a criminal. Debt-slavery was lawful in Israel. A man who could not pay could be taken, or his children could, and the law regulated it rather than forbidding it — service was limited, the seventh year brought release, the Jubilee restored the land (Ex. 21:7; Lev. 25:39-41). Nehemiah found the same thing happening in his own day and was furious about it (Neh. 5:5).

So this is a man exercising his legal rights, and the protections written into the law are not reaching her in time. Her boys are going to be taken this week.

Notice, too, what her husband's godliness has not bought her. You know that your servant feared the LORD — and he died in debt, and his widow is losing her children. The Bible is entirely unembarrassed about this. Fearing God is not a financial instrument, and the families of faithful men have been poor in every century.

'And Elisha said to her, "What shall I do for you? Tell me; what have you in the house?" And she said, "Your servant has nothing in the house except a jar of oil."'

He asks for an inventory before he does anything.

He does that habitually. What is in your hand, Moses? A staff. How many loaves have you? Five. What have you in the house? He begins with what is actually there, and not with what she wishes were there.

Listen to how she words it. Nothing in the house except a jar of oil.

The word for the jar is a small one — a flask, the sort of thing anointing oil is kept in, a few mouthfuls. She files it under nothing and adds it as an exception in the same breath, because in her accounting it is not an asset. It is the last scrapings, and it is about to be the means of her rescue.

'Then he said, "Go outside, borrow vessels from all your neighbors, empty vessels and not too few.'

'Then go in and shut the door behind yourself and your sons and pour into all these vessels. And when one is full, set it aside."'

Two instructions, and each one is doing something.

Borrow vessels from all your neighbors. She has to go out and knock on doors, in a village where everybody knows her husband died owing money and her sons are about to be taken. She has to ask for empty pots and give no reason that will not sound like madness. Faith is very rarely a private feeling; here it is a woman walking up a street carrying other people's jars.

Empty vessels and not too few. That is as close as the chapter comes to telling her the size of what is about to happen, and it leaves the number entirely to her.

Then: shut the door. No crowd, no witnesses, nothing to see. Elijah's great works were public — an altar on a mountain with a nation watching. A very great deal of Elisha's ministry happens behind a closed door in somebody's house, and this is the first of it.

'So she went from him and shut the door behind herself and her sons. And as she poured they brought the vessels to her.'

Picture the room. The boys are running the empty pots to her and carrying the full ones away, and their mother is standing in the middle of it pouring out of a flask that should have been finished after the first one.

And note who is doing the fetching and carrying. The two sons — the ones who were to be taken on Friday — are the workforce of their own rescue. They spend the afternoon lifting jars, and every jar they set down is another few days of their own freedom, and nobody has told them what is happening.

'When the vessels were full, she said to her son, "Bring me another vessel." And he said to her, "There is not another." Then the oil stopped flowing.'

Read those two sentences in the order they are given, because the order is the whole point.

She asks for another. There is not another. Then the oil stopped.

It did not stop because the flask was empty. It stopped because she ran out of room. The supply was limited by her capacity to receive it and by nothing else, and that capacity had been fixed an hour earlier, out in the street, by how many doors she was willing to knock on.

Do not turn that into a formula about how much faith unlocks how much blessing, because the chapter does not say that and other chapters would contradict it. But do let it stand as it is written. There were more pots in that village.

'She came and told the man of God, and he said, "Go, sell the oil and pay your debts, and you and your sons can live on the rest."'

Two things, and the second is the generous one.

Pay your debts — first, and in full. The rescue does not consist of the debt being waived or the creditor being struck down. He is paid what he is owed, and the family walks out of the transaction with nothing hanging over it.

And then: you and your sons can live on the rest. God does not merely get her past Thursday. He leaves her a capital sum to live on, so that the crisis does not simply recur next quarter with the same creditor at the same door.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — I Dwell Among My Own People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A wealthy woman of Shunem notices the prophet passing, feeds him, and persuades her husband to build him a room on the roof with a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp (vv. 8-10). Offered a word in her favour to the king or the army commander, she declines: I dwell among my own people (v. 13). It is Gehazi who names the thing she has not asked for — she has no son, and her husband is old (v. 14) — and Elisha tells her at this season, about this time next year, you shall embrace a son. Her answer is not thanks: no, my lord, O man of God; do not lie to your servant (v. 16). And the following spring it happens (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise is given in the angel's own words. About this time next year is what was said at the door of Abraham's tent about Sarah (Gen. 18:10, 14), in a scene where the woman who overheard it laughed. Elisha is not inventing a formula; he is using one.
verseByVerse.examples: And her reply is the most human sentence in the chapter. It is not unbelief — it is a woman who has stopped permitting herself to hope in that particular place, and would rather go on with nothing than have the wound opened again. Do not lie to your servant is what disappointment sounds like when it has been thorough.

verseByVerse.quote: One day Elisha went on to Shunem, where a wealthy woman lived, who urged him to eat some food. So whenever he passed that way, he would turn in there to eat food. And she said to her husband, "Behold now, I know that this is a holy man of God who is continually passing our way. Let us make a small room on the roof with walls and put there for him a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp, so that whenever he comes to us, he can go in there." One day he came there, and he turned into the chamber and rested there. And he said to Gehazi his servant, "Call this Shunammite." When he had called her, she stood before him. And he said to him, "Say now to her, 'See, you have taken all this trouble for us; what is to be done for you? Would you have a word spoken on your behalf to the king or to the commander of the army?'" She answered, "I dwell among my own people." And he said, "What then is to be done for her?" Gehazi answered, "Well, she has no son, and her husband is old." He said, "Call her." And when he had called her, she stood in the doorway. And he said, "At this season, about this time next year, you shall embrace a son." And she said, "No, my lord, O man of God; do not lie to your servant." But the woman conceived, and she bore a son about that time the following spring, as Elisha had said to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'One day Elisha went on to Shunem, where a wealthy woman lived, who urged him to eat some food. So whenever he passed that way, he would turn in there to eat food.'

The Hebrew calls her a great woman — substantial, of standing, with means. Shunem is in the Jezreel valley, on the road Elisha travels between Carmel and the Jordan.

Every initiative in this scene is hers. She notices him. She presses him to eat, more than once and against some resistance, until the meal becomes a standing arrangement.

'And she said to her husband, "Behold now, I know that this is a holy man of God who is continually passing our way.'

'Let us make a small room on the roof with walls and put there for him a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp, so that whenever he comes to us, he can go in there."'

Before the room, though, take her reason: I know that this is a holy man of God who is continually passing our way.

Nothing had happened. He had performed no sign at her table and made no claim; the word she uses is continually, and it is the giveaway. She had watched a man eat in her house repeatedly over a period of time and drawn a conclusion from it.

That is how the judgment is nearly always made, and it is a better method than the one most people use. She did not assess him by a platform or a reputation or an occasion when he was at his best. She fed him, more than once, and watched.

She works it out, and then she talks her husband into it, and the room gets built.

Look at the furniture, because the list is one of the kindest things in the Old Testament. A bed. A table. A chair. A lamp.

Somewhere to sleep, somewhere to eat, somewhere to sit, and light to see by. That is the entire requirement of a human being who works with his mind, and she has thought it through item by item. She did not put up a shrine or a memorial. She built a man a room he could live in, on the roof, with its own stair, so that he could come and go without troubling the household.

Hospitality of this kind is almost never spontaneous. It is the product of somebody sitting down and thinking concretely about what another person actually needs, and then paying for it.

'One day he came there, and he turned into the chamber and rested there.'

'And he said to Gehazi his servant, "Call this Shunammite." When he had called her, she stood before him.'

'And he said to him, "Say now to her, 'See, you have taken all this trouble for us; what is to be done for you? Would you have a word spoken on your behalf to the king or to the commander of the army?'" She answered, "I dwell among my own people."'

Notice how the conversation is conducted. She is standing in front of him, in her own house, and he does not address her. He turns to Gehazi and says say now to her, and Gehazi relays it, and she answers, and the prophet asks Gehazi what then is to be done for her?

For years she has fed this man and built him a room, and she is being spoken to through a servant.

Some of that is the ordinary formality of the age between a holy man and a woman of the household, and it is not presented as a fault. But keep it in view, because it puts one man permanently between Elisha and the people who come to him, and it is the same man who will shortly try to shove her off his master's feet, and who in the next chapter will run down a road after a foreign general with a lie in his mouth and his master's name on it. Standing in the doorway of somebody else's importance does something to a person.

He offers her the one thing he has that a wealthy woman might want: access. A word in the right ear at court, or with the army. In a country where land disputes and taxes and requisitions were settled by who knew whom, that is a substantial gift.

Her reply is five words in English and repays a moment's thought. I dwell among my own people.

She means: I am not a petitioner. I have family here, and standing here, and I am not in want of a patron at court. Whatever I did for you, I did not do it to be owed something.

It is a refusal of payment, and it is a statement of contentment, and it is the rarest answer anybody gives a powerful man. Note it and remember it, because four chapters from now she will be a refugee with her land confiscated, standing in front of the king she declined to be introduced to (8:1-6).

'And he said, "What then is to be done for her?" Gehazi answered, "Well, she has no son, and her husband is old."'

Gehazi supplies it, and Gehazi is right.

She had said she wanted nothing, and she had told the truth as far as it went, and there was one thing she wanted so much that she had not mentioned it. Her husband is old. There will be no son. The room she built on the roof is on a house that will pass to somebody else's family.

People who say they need nothing are frequently telling the truth about everything except the one thing, and the reason it goes unmentioned is not modesty. It is that saying it out loud costs more than doing without.

'He said, "Call her." And when he had called her, she stood in the doorway.'

She stands in the doorway. Not in the room — at the edge of it, half in and half out, which is exactly where a person stands when they suspect what is coming and are not sure they can bear it.

'And he said, "At this season, about this time next year, you shall embrace a son." And she said, "No, my lord, O man of God; do not lie to your servant."'

The promise is not in his own words. About this time next year is the sentence spoken at the door of a tent in Mamre — I will surely return to you about this time next year, and Sarah your wife shall have a son (Gen. 18:10, 14). The woman inside that tent laughed, and was asked whether anything is too hard for the LORD.

This woman does not laugh. She says something sharper and sadder. Do not lie to your servant.

Hear it properly, because it is not unbelief and it is not rudeness. It is what a person says who has been disappointed so often in one particular place that they have made a settled decision to stop hoping there, and who experiences a fresh promise about it as a cruelty rather than a kindness.

She would genuinely rather have nothing than have that particular door opened again. Anyone who has wanted a child, or a marriage, or sobriety, or a reconciliation for long enough knows the exact feeling: do not do this to me. Do not start me off again.

The man of God does not argue with her, or rebuke her for weak faith, or explain that God is able. He has said what he was given to say, and he lets it stand.

'But the woman conceived, and she bore a son about that time the following spring, as Elisha had said to her.'

One verse, no celebration recorded, and the phrase as Elisha had said to her closing it like a ledger entry.

The writer does not linger, and there is a reason. He needs us to have the boy, and to know exactly how he was got, before the next paragraph takes him away.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–37 — Did I Ask My Lord for a Son?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The boy collapses in the harvest field — oh, my head, my head! — and dies on his mother's lap at noon (vv. 19-20). She lays him on the prophet's bed, shuts the door, tells her husband nothing but all is well, and rides seventeen miles to Carmel (vv. 21-24). She gets past Gehazi, takes hold of Elisha's feet, and asks the two questions that are the whole of her grief: did I ask my lord for a son? Did I not say, do not deceive me? (v. 28). The staff sent ahead in Gehazi's hand does nothing (v. 31). Then Elisha shuts the door on the two of them, prays, and lies on the child mouth to mouth, eyes to eyes, hands to hands, until the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes (vv. 33-35). Pick up your son (v. 36).
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me (v. 27). The man of God says plainly that he does not know what is wrong, in front of his servant and the woman, and does not pretend otherwise for a moment. And Gehazi, whose instinct is to keep a distraught woman off his master, is overruled in five words: leave her alone.
verseByVerse.examples: And her oath in verse 30 is Elisha's own. As the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you is exactly what he said to Elijah three times on the road to the Jordan (2:2, 4, 6). She has been offered a staff and a servant, and she will have the man himself, and she says so in his own words.

verseByVerse.quote: When the child had grown, he went out one day to his father among the reapers. And he said to his father, "Oh, my head, my head!" The father said to his servant, "Carry him to his mother." And when he had lifted him and brought him to his mother, the child sat on her lap till noon, and then he died. And she went up and laid him on the bed of the man of God and shut the door behind him and went out. Then she called to her husband and said, "Send me one of the servants and one of the donkeys, that I may quickly go to the man of God and come back again." And he said, "Why will you go to him today? It is neither new moon nor Sabbath." She said, "All is well." Then she saddled the donkey, and she said to her servant, "Urge the animal on; do not slacken the pace for me unless I tell you." So she set out and came to the man of God at Mount Carmel. When the man of God saw her coming, he said to Gehazi his servant, "Look, there is the Shunammite. Run at once to meet her and say to her, 'Is all well with you? Is all well with your husband? Is all well with the child?'" And she answered, "All is well." And when she came to the mountain to the man of God, she caught hold of his feet. And Gehazi came to push her away. But the man of God said, "Leave her alone, for she is in bitter distress, and the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me." Then she said, "Did I ask my lord for a son? Did I not say, 'Do not deceive me?'" He said to Gehazi, "Tie up your garment and take my staff in your hand and go. If you meet anyone, do not greet him, and if anyone greets you, do not reply. And lay my staff on the face of the child." Then the mother of the child said, "As the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So he arose and followed her. Gehazi went on ahead and laid the staff on the face of the child, but there was no sound or sign of life. Therefore he returned to meet him and told him, "The child has not awakened." When Elisha came into the house, he saw the child lying dead on his bed. So he went in and shut the door behind the two of them and prayed to the LORD. Then he went up and lay on the child, putting his mouth on his mouth, his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. And as he stretched himself upon him, the flesh of the child became warm. Then he got up again and walked once back and forth in the house, and went up and stretched himself upon him. The child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes. Then he summoned Gehazi and said, "Call this Shunammite." So he called her. And when she came to him, he said, "Pick up your son." She came and fell at his feet, bowing to the ground. Then she picked up her son and went out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When the child had grown, he went out one day to his father among the reapers.'

'And he said to his father, "Oh, my head, my head!" The father said to his servant, "Carry him to his mother."'

A boy old enough to walk out to the harvest field to be with the men, in the sun, and something goes wrong in his head.

His father does not go with him. He is in the middle of the harvest, he has no idea this is serious, and he tells a servant to take him home to his mother. That is the ordinary reflex of an ordinary busy man and it is not held against him, and he will spend the rest of his life remembering it.

'And when he had lifted him and brought him to his mother, the child sat on her lap till noon, and then he died.'

She held him until midday, and then he died.

There is no medical detail, no last words, no scene. The writer gives the hours and the lap and one verb, and anyone who has sat like that does not need the rest of it filled in.

'And she went up and laid him on the bed of the man of God and shut the door behind him and went out.'

Now watch this woman, because from here to the end of the scene she does not put a foot wrong.

She carries him up the outside stair to the roof and lays him on the bed she bought, in the room she built, for the man who promised her he would be born. Then she shuts the door and comes back down and tells nobody.

She has not given up and she is not in denial. She has taken the body to the address where the promise came from, and she is going to fetch the man who made it.

'Then she called to her husband and said, "Send me one of the servants and one of the donkeys, that I may quickly go to the man of God and come back again."'

'And he said, "Why will you go to him today? It is neither new moon nor Sabbath." She said, "All is well."'

Her husband's question tells us something in passing about the religion of ordinary people in the northern kingdom: they went to see a prophet on the holy days, at new moon and Sabbath, the way you might go to church. A visit on a working Tuesday needed explaining.

She does not explain. All is well — the word is shalom.

His son is dead on a bed on his own roof, and she says shalom, and rides out. It is not a lie exactly; it is a woman who has decided that the conversation which would follow the truth is a conversation she does not have time for.

'Then she saddled the donkey, and she said to her servant, "Urge the animal on; do not slacken the pace for me unless I tell you."'

Carmel is the best part of seventeen miles across the plain. Her instruction is: do not slow down on my account. She will be shaken half to pieces and she does not care.

'So she set out and came to the man of God at Mount Carmel. When the man of God saw her coming, he said to Gehazi his servant, "Look, there is the Shunammite.'

'Run at once to meet her and say to her, 'Is all well with you? Is all well with your husband? Is all well with the child?'" And she answered, "All is well."'

She has ridden to Carmel, and the place matters. That ridge is where his master stood alone against four hundred and fifty prophets and called fire out of a clear sky, and it is where Elisha now keeps his base. The mother of a dead boy has come to the mountain where God answered.

Three questions, sent out by a servant, and the third one is the question.

Shalom, she says again, to Gehazi, and rides past him. She has come seventeen miles and she is not going to hand this over at the door.

'And when she came to the mountain to the man of God, she caught hold of his feet. And Gehazi came to push her away. But the man of God said, "Leave her alone, for she is in bitter distress, and the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me."'

Two things here, and both should be preached.

The first is Gehazi, who comes forward to push a woman off his master's feet. His instinct is protective and it is entirely wrong, and it is the standing occupational hazard of everybody who works close to a person people need. There is nearly always somebody managing access, deciding who is in a fit state to be seen, keeping the undignified at a distance. Leave her alone is five words and it should be written over the desk of every gatekeeper in every church.

The second is the admission. The LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me.

He does not know. The man who has just been shown the woman coming a mile off does not know why she is coming, and he says so out loud, in front of his servant and in front of her, without a trace of embarrassment and without inventing anything to cover it.

Prophets in this book are not omniscient and never claim to be. They know exactly what they are told and nothing else, and the honesty of a man who will say God has not told me is a large part of why you can trust him when he says God has.

'Then she said, "Did I ask my lord for a son? Did I not say, 'Do not deceive me?'"'

Here is the grief, and it comes out as two questions rather than a request.

Did I ask you for a son? No, she did not. She asked for nothing at all; she said she dwelt among her own people and wanted no favours. The child was a gift she never applied for.

Did I not say, do not deceive me? She had said it, in that doorway, in those words. She had told him at the time that this was exactly what she was afraid of.

And that is the hardest version of this particular sorrow, and a great many people are living in it. Not the thing longed for and never given, but the thing never asked for, given anyway, and then taken back — which leaves you unable even to say that you brought it on yourself by wanting it too much. She had protected herself, carefully and deliberately, and God overruled the protection, and now the wound is exactly where she said it would be.

The chapter does not answer her with an argument. It answers her with a living boy, and no argument would have done.

'He said to Gehazi, "Tie up your garment and take my staff in your hand and go. If you meet anyone, do not greet him, and if anyone greets you, do not reply. And lay my staff on the face of the child."'

Tie up your robe so you can run. Speak to nobody on the road — eastern greetings were long, and this is an instruction about speed.

'Then the mother of the child said, "As the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So he arose and followed her.'

She has been offered a staff and a servant, and she refuses both, and the sentence she uses to refuse them is one Elisha has heard before.

As the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you. That is word for word what he himself said to Elijah, three times, on the road from Gilgal to the Jordan, when the old man kept offering him an honourable place to stop (2:2, 4, 6).

She could not have known that. The writer knew it, and put her sentence in the same words, and the effect is that a woman from Shunem holds the prophet to the standard he set for himself. She will not be handed off to an assistant with a piece of equipment. If he comes, there is hope; if he sends, there is not.

So he arose and followed her. She has taken over the direction of travel.

'Gehazi went on ahead and laid the staff on the face of the child, but there was no sound or sign of life. Therefore he returned to meet him and told him, "The child has not awakened."'

The staff does nothing.

That failure is in the chapter on purpose. Elisha's staff is the nearest thing in these books to a relic, carried by his own servant with his own instructions — and laid on a dead child's face it produces no sound and no movement at all.

The object holds no power at all, and there is none in the office-holder's deputy either. The mother was right and the prophet was, for a moment, wrong.

'When Elisha came into the house, he saw the child lying dead on his bed.'

'So he went in and shut the door behind the two of them and prayed to the LORD.'

The door again, and this time on the two of them — the prophet and the body. No mother, no servant, no audience. And the first thing he does is pray.

The writer does not tell us one word of what he said.

Elijah's prayer over the boy at Zarephath is recorded in full, and it is an accusation — O LORD my God, have you brought calamity even upon the widow with whom I sojourn, by killing her son? (1 Kgs. 17:20). Here we are given the shut door and the fact of the prayer and nothing else. Whatever a man says to God with a dead child on the bed behind him, this writer does not consider it ours to overhear.

'Then he went up and lay on the child, putting his mouth on his mouth, his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. And as he stretched himself upon him, the flesh of the child became warm.'

Mouth to mouth, eyes to eyes, hands to hands. A living man laid out along a dead one, matching himself to him part for part.

His master had done something like it at Zarephath, stretching himself on the widow's son three times and crying out to God (1 Kgs. 17:21). This is that, and more of it — closer, more deliberate, more costly in every way a man can spend himself on another body.

Consider the shape of what he is doing, because it is more than a technique for transferring warmth. To raise the boy he has to make himself the same shape as the boy — get down onto the bed of the dead, take that small body's own posture, put his living mouth where a dead mouth is and his open eyes on closed ones, and stay there.

He cannot do it from the doorway and he cannot do it with a staff. He has to go the whole way down onto the bed.

That is what God did. Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Heb. 2:14). Not a word spoken from a safe distance, not an instrument sent on ahead — the Son laid down alongside us, in our own flesh, matched to us part for part, and went as far down as we had gone.

The flesh of the child became warm. Not alive. Warm.

'Then he got up again and walked once back and forth in the house, and went up and stretched himself upon him. The child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.'

He walks up and down the room once, and then goes back and does it again.

That is a detail no inventor of stories would supply. The man is pacing. Something has happened and it is not enough, and he does not know what else to do, so he walks the length of the house and back and then climbs onto the bed a second time.

And then the boy sneezes seven times and opens his eyes, which is the other detail nobody would have made up. It is the least dignified possible way for a resurrection to begin and it is exactly the kind of thing an eyewitness remembers.

'Then he summoned Gehazi and said, "Call this Shunammite." So he called her. And when she came to him, he said, "Pick up your son."'

Three words. Pick up your son.

The same scene has been played once before and will be played once more. Elijah carried the widow's boy down the stairs and said see, your son lives (1 Kgs. 17:23). And outside a town called Nain, a man stopped a funeral, spoke to a dead body, and he gave him to his mother (Luke 7:15).

Three widowed or childless women, three only sons, and three times a boy handed back. When Hebrews lists what faith has done in the world it puts this line in: women received back their dead by resurrection (Heb. 11:35). This chapter is one of the two it is thinking of.

Measure the three against each other, because the difference is not in the men's sincerity. Elijah stretched himself out three times and pleaded. Elisha prayed, lay on the body twice, and paced the room in between. Jesus touched a plank and said young man, I say to you, arise. The prophets asked. The Son commanded, and death did as it was told.

'She came and fell at his feet, bowing to the ground. Then she picked up her son and went out.'

Not a word from her. She had spoken plenty on the mountain; here she gets down on the floor, and then she picks up her boy and walks out with him.

Whatever she thought about the promise she had begged him not to make, she is not recorded as saying it. She is carrying him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a famine, a hungry man out gathering herbs shreds a lapful of wild gourds into the company's stew not knowing what they were, and the cry goes up: O man of God, there is death in the pot! (vv. 39-40). Flour is thrown in, and there was no harm in the pot (v. 41). Then a man brings the firstfruits — twenty loaves of barley and fresh ears of grain — for a hundred men, and the servant does the arithmetic out loud (vv. 42-43). So he set it before them. And they ate and had some left, according to the word of the LORD (v. 44).
verseByVerse.theology: Neither flour nor salt is a remedy — no more than the salt that healed the spring at Jericho. The sign is arranged so that nobody can credit the method, and the poison in this case got into the common pot through a man who was trying to help and did not know what he had picked. The answer was not to throw out the pot.
verseByVerse.examples: And the last four verses are a rehearsal. Barley loaves, which is the poor man's grain; a servant objecting that the numbers do not work; a crowd fed; and food left over. John alone records that the boy on the hillside had five barley loaves (John 6:9). Twenty loaves to a hundred men here; five to five thousand there, with twelve baskets taken up.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elisha came again to Gilgal when there was a famine in the land. And as the sons of the prophets were sitting before him, he said to his servant, "Set on the large pot, and boil stew for the sons of the prophets." One of them went out into the field to gather herbs, and found a wild vine and gathered from it his lap full of wild gourds, and came and cut them up into the pot of stew, not knowing what they were. And they poured out some for the men to eat. But while they were eating of the stew, they cried out, "O man of God, there is death in the pot!" And they could not eat it. He said, "Then bring flour." And he threw it into the pot and said, "Pour some out for the men, that they may eat." And there was no harm in the pot. A man came from Baal-shalishah, bringing the man of God bread of the firstfruits, twenty loaves of barley and fresh ears of grain in his sack. And Elisha said, "Give to the men, that they may eat." But his servant said, "How can I set this before a hundred men?" So he repeated, "Give them to the men, that they may eat, for thus says the LORD, 'They shall eat and have some left.'" So he set it before them. And they ate and had some left, according to the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Elisha came again to Gilgal when there was a famine in the land. And as the sons of the prophets were sitting before him, he said to his servant, "Set on the large pot, and boil stew for the sons of the prophets."'

A famine, a company of student prophets with nothing, and the head of the school telling his servant to put the big pot on. Whatever else Elisha is, he is running a household that has to be fed.

'One of them went out into the field to gather herbs, and found a wild vine and gathered from it his lap full of wild gourds, and came and cut them up into the pot of stew, not knowing what they were.'

Note the last clause and do not lose it. Not knowing what they were.

He is hungry, there is a famine, and he goes out to find something to put in the pot. He comes back with a lapful of a wild vine — most likely the colocynth, a bitter desert gourd that looks like a small melon and is violently purgative — and shreds the lot into the communal stew, pleased with himself.

No wickedness appears anywhere in this story. A well-meaning man tried to help, was ignorant, and poisoned the whole company's dinner.

'And they poured out some for the men to eat. But while they were eating of the stew, they cried out, "O man of God, there is death in the pot!" And they could not eat it.'

They taste it and they know at once.

Take the sentence out of the kitchen for a moment, because it names something that happens in churches with some regularity. The poison did not come in through an enemy. It came in through a member of the household who was trying to contribute, out of genuine hunger, having picked up something off a wild vine without knowing what it was. That is how most bad teaching enters a congregation.

'He said, "Then bring flour." And he threw it into the pot and said, "Pour some out for the men, that they may eat." And there was no harm in the pot.'

Flour does not neutralise colocynth, any more than salt sweetens a poisoned spring. Elisha's signs are consistently arranged so that the material used could not possibly have done it: a handful of salt at Jericho, a handful of flour here, a stick thrown in the water in the next chapter.

And what he does not do is throw out the pot. The meal is not abandoned and the man who ruined it is not named or shamed — the writer does not tell us who he was. The stew that was death is served out and eaten.

'A man came from Baal-shalishah, bringing the man of God bread of the firstfruits, twenty loaves of barley and fresh ears of grain in his sack. And Elisha said, "Give to the men, that they may eat."'

A small detail carries a good deal. Firstfruits belonged by law to the priests (Num. 18:13) — and this man carries his to a prophet instead, because the priesthood in the northern kingdom is Jeroboam's, staffed with men appointed to serve two golden calves. A believer in the north in a famine walks past the official religion and brings his offering to Elisha.

It is also barley. Barley is the poor crop, the grain of people who cannot afford wheat, and this is a famine year.

'But his servant said, "How can I set this before a hundred men?" So he repeated, "Give them to the men, that they may eat, for thus says the LORD, 'They shall eat and have some left.'"'

Read what Elisha does with it. The loaves were brought to the man of God — they are a gift to him personally, in a famine, from a man who walked a long way with them. His whole response is give to the men, that they may eat.

There is no dividing it, no keeping a share, no thanking the donor first. The food arrives in his hands and is out of them in the same breath.

The servant does the arithmetic out loud, and the arithmetic is correct. Twenty small barley loaves among a hundred men is a mouthful each and not a meal.

Elisha does not argue with the sum. He repeats the instruction and attaches the word of the LORD to it, and adds a detail that cannot be hedged: not merely that it will do, but that they shall eat and have some left.

'So he set it before them. And they ate and had some left, according to the word of the LORD.'

Now hold this beside a hillside in Galilee, because the resemblance is not a coincidence and the Gospels mean it to be noticed.

A crowd with nothing to eat. A servant who points out that the numbers do not work — two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little (John 6:7). Loaves that are specifically, and only in John's account, barley loaves (John 6:9), the poor man's grain, which is the very word this chapter uses. Everyone fed. And food left over, gathered up afterwards so that nothing is lost.

The shape is identical and the scale is not. Elisha had twenty loaves for a hundred men, and there was some left. Jesus had five loaves for five thousand, and there were twelve baskets of fragments picked up off the grass.

The people who ate that bread had this chapter in their Scriptures, and some of them worked it out; it is immediately after the feeding that John records them saying this is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world (John 6:14), and trying to make him king. They had the category right. It was too small.

4.theology:
What have you in the house? (v. 2). God begins with the inventory. What is in your hand, Moses? How many loaves have you? And what she has is filed under nothing except — a small anointing flask she does not count as an asset, which is the thing she is saved by.

Where the oil stopped (v. 6). She asks for another vessel, there is not another, then the oil stopped. It ran out of room, not out of oil. The size of that miracle had been settled an hour earlier in the street, by how many doors a frightened widow was willing to knock on. Do not turn it into a formula; do let it stand as written.

Do not lie to your servant (v. 16). The promise is Genesis 18:10 word for word, the angel's own formula about Sarah. And the answer is not unbelief but self-protection: a woman who has stopped permitting herself to hope in one particular place and would rather have nothing than have the wound opened. Elisha does not rebuke her for it, argue with her, or explain that God is able. He says what he was given to say and lets it stand.

The LORD has hidden it from me (v. 27). The man of God does not know what is wrong and says so, in front of his servant and the woman, inventing nothing to cover the gap. Prophets in these books know precisely what they are told and no more, and the willingness to say God has not told me is most of the reason you can trust a man when he says God has. In the same verse Gehazi moves to push a grieving woman off his master and is stopped in five words: leave her alone.

The staff fails (v. 31). The nearest thing to a relic in these books, carried by the prophet's own servant on the prophet's own instructions, laid on a dead child's face — and there is no sound and no sign of life. The mother, who had refused it in Elisha's own words of loyalty to Elijah (2:2, 4, 6), was right.

Three boys handed back. Elijah stretched himself out three times and pleaded; Elisha prayed, lay on the body twice and paced the room between; Jesus touched a bier and said young man, I say to you, arise. Hebrews has this chapter in view when it says women received back their dead by resurrection (Heb. 11:35). The prophets asked. The Son commanded.

Twenty barley loaves (vv. 42-44). A servant states the arithmetic correctly and is overruled by a word; the men eat and there is some left. John alone records that the loaves on the Galilean hillside were barley (John 6:9), the poor man's grain and this chapter's word. Twenty loaves to a hundred, with some left; five to five thousand, with twelve baskets gathered. The crowd that ate it had this chapter in their Bibles and said this is indeed the Prophet who is to come (John 6:14). The category was right and far too small.
4.examples:
Then: A woman whose son had died on her lap at midday carried him upstairs, laid him on the bed she had bought for the prophet, shut the door, told her husband and then the prophet's servant that all was well, and rode seventeen miles telling the man leading the donkey not to slow down on her account.

Now: Three things. First, do not lie to your servant. If there is a place in your life where you have quietly decided to stop hoping — a child, a marriage, a besetting sin, a person who will not speak to you — you will recognise her instantly, and you should notice that nobody in this chapter treats her as faithless for it. Second, Gehazi with his hand out to push her away. Anyone who works near a person other people need becomes a gatekeeper eventually, deciding who is in a fit state to be seen; leave her alone belongs over that desk. Third, the pot. The poison came into the household through a hungry man who wanted to help and did not know what he had picked, which is how most bad teaching arrives in a church — and the answer was not to throw out the pot or to name the man.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master and in high favor, because by him the LORD had given victory to Syria. He was a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper.<sup>2</sup>Now the Syrians on one of their raids had carried off a little girl from the land of Israel, and she worked in the service of Naaman's wife.<sup>3</sup>She said to her mistress, "Would that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! He would cure him of his leprosy."<sup>4</sup>So Naaman went in and told his lord, "Thus and so spoke the girl from the land of Israel."<sup>5</sup>And the king of Syria said, "Go now, and I will send a letter to the king of Israel."
