'And the two divisions of you, which come on duty in force on the Sabbath and guard the house of the LORD on behalf of the king,'

'shall surround the king, each with his weapons in his hand. And whoever approaches the ranks is to be put to death. Be with the king when he goes out and when he comes in."'

The detail is dull to read and it is the reason the thing works.

He picks the Sabbath, and he picks it because that is changeover day. The shift going off and the shift coming on are both in the temple at once, which means twice the normal number of armed men can be standing in those courts without a single person in Jerusalem thinking it odd.

He is not relying on a miracle. He is using the rota.

There is a kind of faith that thinks planning is a failure of trust. This chapter is one of the places the Bible quietly disagrees. A man who has waited six years for God to keep a promise spends the last week of it working out shift patterns and gate assignments, and the promise is kept through the shift patterns.

'The captains did according to all that Jehoiada the priest commanded, and they each brought his men who were to go off duty on the Sabbath, with those who were to come on duty on the Sabbath, and came to Jehoiada the priest.'

'And the priest gave to the captains the spears and shields that had been King David's, which were in the house of the LORD.'

Stop here, because this is the loveliest verse in the chapter.

Those weapons had been David's. They were the spoil and the ceremonial arms of his own campaigns — when he defeated Hadadezer, David took the shields of gold that were carried by the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem (2 Sam. 8:7) — and they had hung in the house of the LORD as dedicated trophies for a century and a half. Nobody had expected to use them.

They come down off the wall and are put into the hands of the men who will stand round the last living descendant of the man who carried them.

David's own spears, guarding David's last son, in the house David wanted to build, to keep alive the promise David was given.

'And the guards stood, every man with his weapons in his hand, from the south side of the house to the north side of the house, around the altar and the house on behalf of the king.'

A line of armed men right across the width of the temple, from one wall to the other, with the boy behind it.

'Then he brought out the king's son and put the crown on him and gave him the testimony. And they proclaimed him king and anointed him, and they clapped their hands and said, "Long live the king!"'

Two things are put on him, and the second is as important as the first.

The crown, and the testimony — almost certainly a copy of the law, which Deuteronomy requires every king of Israel to write out for himself and keep beside him and read in it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God (Deut. 17:18-20).

Crown and book together. That is what makes a king in Israel and not merely a ruler: authority in one hand and a text over him that he did not write and cannot amend.

Athaliah had the throne for six years and never had that. It is the whole difference between the house of David and the house of Ahab.

Then the sound: hands clapping, and men shouting long live the king at a seven-year-old who six days ago had never been outside.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Athaliah hears the noise and walks into the temple, and sees the thing she believed she had destroyed standing by the pillar with a crown on: and Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, Treason! Treason! (v. 14). Jehoiada has her taken out through the horses' entrance — let her not be put to death in the house of the LORD — and killed there (vv. 15-16). Then a covenant, in two directions: between the LORD and the king and people, that they should be the LORD's people, and also between the king and the people (v. 17). The people pull down the house of Baal in Jerusalem and kill its priest (v. 18), the boy is seated on the throne, the city is quiet — and Jehoash was seven years old when he began to reign (vv. 19-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Treason, from the woman who murdered the royal family in order to take the throne. It is the usurper's word, and she is the only person in the building with no right to use it.
verseByVerse.examples: And the reform goes further than a change of ruler. There was a house of Baal in Jerusalem — Athaliah had built her mother's religion into the capital of Judah — and it comes down in the same week, so that within a few years of each other Baal is put out of both kingdoms. What makes it more than a coup is verse 17: they are bound to God first, and then to one another.

verseByVerse.quote: When Athaliah heard the noise of the guard and of the people, she went into the house of the LORD to the people. And when she looked, there was the king standing by the pillar, according to the custom, and the captains and the trumpeters beside the king, and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing trumpets. And Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, "Treason! Treason!" Then Jehoiada the priest commanded the captains who were set over the army, "Bring her out between the ranks, and put to death with the sword anyone who follows her." For the priest said, "Let her not be put to death in the house of the LORD." So they laid hands on her; and she went through the horses' entrance to the king's house, and there she was put to death. And Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and people, that they should be the LORD's people, and also between the king and the people. Then all the people of the land went to the house of Baal and tore it down; his altars and his images they broke in pieces, and they killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars. And the priest posted watchmen over the house of the LORD. And he took the captains, the Carites, the guards, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of the LORD, marching through the gate of the guards to the king's house. And he took his seat on the throne of the kings. So all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet after Athaliah had been put to death with the sword at the king's house. Jehoash was seven years old when he began to reign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When Athaliah heard the noise of the guard and of the people, she went into the house of the LORD to the people.'

She walks into the temple.

Six years she has ruled this city without setting foot in that building, because it was not her god's house and she had a house of her own for him. And the first time she goes in, it is because of a noise she cannot account for.

'And when she looked, there was the king standing by the pillar, according to the custom, and the captains and the trumpeters beside the king, and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing trumpets. And Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, "Treason! Treason!"'

And when she looked, there was the king.

She had counted the bodies. She had made certain, six years ago, in a room in her own palace, and she had been queen ever since on the strength of it. And there he is by the pillar, in the place where kings of Judah stood, crowned, with the trumpets going and the whole city cheering.

Then she says the one word she has no right to. Treason.

The woman who murdered her own grandchildren to seize a throne that was never hers stands in the temple and accuses everybody else of it. That is not an unusual sound. People who have taken something are frequently the loudest about theft, and they are not being cynical when they say it; they have been in possession long enough to feel robbed.

'Then Jehoiada the priest commanded the captains who were set over the army, "Bring her out between the ranks, and put to death with the sword anyone who follows her." For the priest said, "Let her not be put to death in the house of the LORD."'

In the middle of a coup, with the woman who destroyed the royal family standing in front of him, the priest stops to give an instruction about where she may be killed.

Let her not be put to death in the house of the LORD.

That is restraint of a rare kind. Everything is going his way; the guard is his, the city is his, the king is crowned, and nobody would have said a word if she had been cut down where she stood. And he takes the trouble to have her walked out first, because the house of God is not a place for that, even for her, even now.

Jehu, in the north, killed a temple full of men and turned the building into a latrine, and God gave him four generations. Jehoiada, in the south, will not have one guilty woman executed on holy ground. Both were doing God's work; only one of them was careful.

'So they laid hands on her; and she went through the horses' entrance to the king's house, and there she was put to death.'

She dies at the horses' entrance of the palace.

Her mother died in a gateway in Jezreel with her blood on the wall and the horses trampling over her. The writer does not draw the line, and it may be nothing. But the two women who brought Baal into two kingdoms both died in a gateway among horses, twenty-five miles and a few years apart.

'And Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and people, that they should be the LORD's people, and also between the king and the people.'

Two covenants, and this is what raises the day above a palace coup.

The first is vertical: the LORD, the king and the people, that they should be the LORD's people. That is the Sinai formula being taken up again by a nation that had spent six years under a Baalist queen — we are yours.

The second is horizontal: between the king and the people. The seven-year-old is bound to them and they to him. Judah has just watched what happens when a ruler is accountable to nothing, and the answer is an agreement in both directions before the boy has been on the throne an hour.

'Then all the people of the land went to the house of Baal and tore it down; his altars and his images they broke in pieces, and they killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars. And the priest posted watchmen over the house of the LORD.'

There was a house of Baal in Jerusalem.

Let that land. Athaliah had not merely taken the throne of David; she had built her mother's religion into the capital of Judah, with a temple and altars and images and a named priest, within sight of the house of the LORD. That is what one marriage alliance, made in a spirit of family friendship two generations earlier, had grown into.

It comes down in an afternoon, torn apart by the people of the land — not by the guard and not by decree, but by ordinary Judeans who had evidently been waiting a long time for permission.

Within a few years of each other, Baal has now been put out of both kingdoms: by a soldier in the north, by a congregation in the south.

'And he took the captains, the Carites, the guards, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of the LORD, marching through the gate of the guards to the king's house. And he took his seat on the throne of the kings.'

They walk him down from the temple to the palace under guard, and a child sits down on the throne of David.

'So all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet after Athaliah had been put to death with the sword at the king's house.'

'Jehoash was seven years old when he began to reign.'

End on that sentence, because the writer does.

Seven years old. The entire weight of every promise God ever made about a king from David's line — the throne established forever, the offspring of the woman, the one whose kingdom would have no end — rested that morning on a boy who had spent six of his seven years in a back bedroom of the temple and had never seen the city he was king of.

Nine hundred years later another child of that line was carried out of reach of a king who was killing children, by relatives who moved at night, and kept alive in obscurity until it was safe (Matt. 2:13-16). The pattern is not accidental. Twice the promise came down to one infant and a family willing to hide him, and both times the people trying to put the light out did not know which room to look in.

One honest word before leaving him. This boy will do well for as long as Jehoiada lives, and after the old priest dies he will listen to different men, and he will have Jehoiada's own son stoned to death in the temple court (2 Chron. 24:20-22). The rescue in this chapter was real and God's promise was kept, and the child who was saved grew into a man who needed saving from himself. That is not a flaw in the story. It is why the line had to keep going.

11.theology:
What was at stake (v. 1). The throne established forever (2 Sam. 7:16), the offspring of the woman who would crush the serpent's head (Gen. 3:15), and the lamp the writer named two chapters ago as the only reason Judah still existed (8:19) — all of it ran through the children Athaliah had killed. For six years there was no son of David on David's throne and Jezebel's daughter ruled in Jerusalem.

How the promise was actually kept (vv. 2-3). No army, no angel, no sign. A woman with the nerve to walk into the room while it was happening; the presence of mind to take the wet nurse as well, without whom a one-year-old would have been dead in three days; a priest with a spare bedroom; and six years of a handful of people saying nothing. God keeps his word through means, and the means are usually somebody's courage and somebody else's competence.

The rota (vv. 5-9). Jehoiada picks the Sabbath because both shifts are present and the courts can be full of soldiers without anyone thinking it strange. There is a piety that treats planning as a failure of trust; a man who had waited six years for God to keep a promise spent the last week of it on gate assignments, and the promise came through the gate assignments.

David's weapons (v. 10). Spoil from David's own wars, dedicated in the house of the LORD (cf. 2 Sam. 8:7) and hanging there unused for a century and a half, taken down and put into the hands of the men guarding David's last descendant.

Crown and testimony (v. 12). He is given the law along with the crown, as Deuteronomy requires of a king (Deut. 17:18-20) — authority in one hand and over him a text he did not write and cannot amend. Athaliah held the throne for six years and never had that, and it is the whole difference between the house of David and the house of Ahab.

Not in the house of the LORD (v. 15). Everything is going Jehoiada's way and nobody would have objected, and he stops the execution long enough to have her walked outside. Jehu killed a temple full of men and made the building a latrine; Jehoiada will not have one guilty woman put to death on holy ground. Both were doing God's work and only one was careful.

Two covenants (v. 17). Vertical first — the LORD, the king and the people, that they should be the LORD's people — and then horizontal, between the king and the people. That is what lifts the day above a palace coup, and it is the answer of a nation that has just watched what a ruler accountable to nothing does.
11.examples:
Then: A woman walked into the room where her family's children were being killed, took one of them out, and remembered to take the wet nurse too — and then a priest, his wife, and a nurse kept a boy alive in a back bedroom of the temple for six years without one of them ever mentioning it.

Now: Three things. First, the shape of the rescue. If you are waiting for God to keep a promise, notice that in the largest such moment in the Old Testament he used a brave sister-in-law, a nurse, a spare room and a duty roster, and that from inside those six years it must have looked exactly like nothing happening. Second, Jehoiada's planning. The man had a divine promise, a rightful king and a usurper on the throne, and he spent his last week on shift patterns; treating careful preparation as a failure of faith is a piety this chapter does not share. Third, Athaliah's cry. Treason was shouted by the one person in the building with no right to the word — and she almost certainly meant it, because six years of possession is long enough to feel robbed of something you stole.

Now therefore take no more money from your donors, but hand it over for the repair of the house."<sup>8</sup>So the priests agreed that they should take no more money from the people, and that they should not repair the house.<sup>9</sup>Then Jehoiada the priest took a chest and bored a hole in the lid of it and set it beside the altar on the right side as one entered the house of the LORD. And the priests who guarded the threshold put in it all the money that was brought into the house of the LORD.<sup>10</sup>And whenever they saw that there was much money in the chest, the king's secretary and the high priest came up and they bagged and counted the money that was found in the house of the LORD.<sup>11</sup>Then they would give the money that was weighed out into the hands of the workmen who had the oversight of the house of the LORD. And they paid it out to the carpenters and the builders who worked on the house of the LORD,<sup>12</sup>and to the masons and the stonecutters, as well as to buy timber and quarried stone for making repairs on the house of the LORD, and for any outlay for the repairs of the house.<sup>13</sup>But there were not made for the house of the LORD basins of silver, snuffers, bowls, trumpets, or any vessels of gold, or of silver, from the money that was brought into the house of the LORD,<sup>14</sup>for that was given to the workmen who were repairing the house of the LORD with it.<sup>15</sup>And they did not ask for an accounting from the men into whose hand they delivered the money to pay out to the workmen, for they dealt honestly.<sup>16</sup>The money from the guilt offerings and the money from the sin offerings was not brought into the house of the LORD; it belonged to the priests.<sup>17</sup>At that time Hazael king of Syria went up and fought against Gath and took it. But when Hazael set his face to go up against Jerusalem,<sup>18</sup>Jehoash king of Judah took all the sacred gifts that Jehoshaphat and Jehoram and Ahaziah his fathers, the kings of Judah, had dedicated, and his own sacred gifts, and all the gold that was found in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and of the king's house, and sent these to Hazael king of Syria. Then Hazael went away from Jerusalem.<sup>19</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Joash and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?<sup>20</sup>His servants arose and made a conspiracy and struck down Joash in the house of Millo, on the way that goes down to Silla.<sup>21</sup>It was Jozacar the son of Shimeath and Jehozabad the son of Shomer, his servants, who struck him down, so that he died. And they buried him with his fathers in the city of David, and Amaziah his son reigned in his place.
12.overview:
The boy from the temple bedroom reigns forty years and does what is right — and the writer attaches a reason: because Jehoiada the priest instructed him. Everything in the chapter runs off that clause.

The temple repair fund is the test case. Money comes in from three streams, the priests collect it and are to do the work, and twenty-three years later nothing has been mended. Nobody is accused of theft, and the writer does not accuse them either; the money simply went where money goes when no one is answerable for a stated purpose. The remedy is a chest with a hole bored in the lid, standing beside the altar where givers put money in themselves, opened and counted by two officials from two institutions together — and no audit at all on the foremen, because they had proved honest. The fabric is repaired before a single silver basin is made, and the priests keep their income.

Then Hazael turns toward Jerusalem, and the king who repaired the house strips it — four generations of dedicated gifts, his own included — and sends it all to Damascus, without consulting anybody. There is no prophet in this chapter. And his own servants kill him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Because Jehoiada the Priest Instructed Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehoash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all his days, because Jehoiada the priest instructed him (v. 2) — with the usual exception, that the high places remained (v. 3). He orders the temple repaired out of the money brought in, and leaves the priests to collect it and do the work (vv. 4-5). But by the twenty-third year of King Jehoash, the priests had made no repairs on the house (v. 6). Summoned and asked why, they agree to a settlement that costs them the income and the responsibility together: they should take no more money from the people, and... should not repair the house (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: The verse that governs the reign is verse 2, and it is a causal clause. He did right because somebody instructed him. Chronicles records what happened when that somebody was buried: he listened to the princes of Judah instead, the house of God was abandoned, and he had Jehoiada's own son stoned to death in the temple court (2 Chron. 24:17-22) — a murder the Lord Jesus was still naming eight centuries later (Matt. 23:35).
verseByVerse.examples: And twenty-three years is the number to sit with. The king was seven when he came to the throne and thirty when he asked the question; he had lived in that building as a child. Nobody is accused of stealing. The money simply came in, and went where money goes when nobody has been made responsible for a particular purpose, and the roof went unmended for a generation.

verseByVerse.quote: In the seventh year of Jehu, Jehoash began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Zibiah of Beersheba. And Jehoash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all his days, because Jehoiada the priest instructed him. Nevertheless, the high places were not taken away; the people continued to sacrifice and make offerings on the high places. Jehoash said to the priests, "All the money of the holy things that is brought into the house of the LORD, the money for which each man is assessed—the money from the assessment of persons—and the money that a man's heart prompts him to bring into the house of the LORD, let the priests take, each from his donor, and let them repair the house wherever any need of repairs is discovered." But by the twenty-third year of King Jehoash, the priests had made no repairs on the house. Therefore King Jehoash summoned Jehoiada the priest and the other priests and said to them, "Why are you not repairing the house? Now therefore take no more money from your donors, but hand it over for the repair of the house." So the priests agreed that they should take no more money from the people, and that they should not repair the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the seventh year of Jehu, Jehoash began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Zibiah of Beersheba.'

Forty years. The boy from the bedroom in the temple gets the second-longest reign in Judah's history.

'And Jehoash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all his days, because Jehoiada the priest instructed him.'

Everything about this man is in the last four words.

He did what was right — the writer says so without qualification — because Jehoiada the priest instructed him. Not because he sought God, or because his heart was whole, or because he loved the law. Because a particular man taught him.

That man had saved his life, hidden him for six years, crowned him at seven, put the book of the law in his hands, and stood beside him ever since. He was the uncle who married the aunt who carried him out of the massacre, and he was the only father the king had ever had.

Chronicles tells us what happened when he died, and a reader of Kings needs it, because Kings does not say. After the death of Jehoiada the princes of Judah came and paid homage to the king. Then the king listened to them. They abandoned the house of the LORD and served Asherim and idols; prophets were sent and not heard; and when Jehoiada's own son Zechariah stood up in the court and told them why they were failing, they conspired against him, and by command of the king they stoned him with stones in the court of the house of the LORD (2 Chron. 24:17-22).

The boy Jehoiada hid had Jehoiada's son killed on the temple pavement.

The Lord Jesus was still naming it eight hundred years later, at the end of the bitterest thing he ever said to the religious leaders of his own day: from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar (Matt. 23:35; Luke 11:51).

So take verse 2 at face value and take it seriously as a warning. A man can be genuinely good on borrowed convictions for forty years. The instruction was real, the reforms in this chapter are real, and none of it was his. The test of whether a thing has become yours is what survives the burial of the person who taught it to you.

'Nevertheless, the high places were not taken away; the people continued to sacrifice and make offerings on the high places.'

The standing exception in Judah, and it appears here as it appears for almost every good king. He could reform the temple. He could not change what a village did on its own hill.

'Jehoash said to the priests, "All the money of the holy things that is brought into the house of the LORD, the money for which each man is assessed—the money from the assessment of persons—and the money that a man's heart prompts him to bring into the house of the LORD,'

'let the priests take, each from his donor, and let them repair the house wherever any need of repairs is discovered."'

The plan is sensible and it is the plan almost every institution starts with. Three streams of income — the fixed assessment, the valuation money, and freewill gifts — all of it received by the priests, and the priests to see the repairs done.

One body collects, holds and spends, and nobody is given a specific job.

'But by the twenty-third year of King Jehoash, the priests had made no repairs on the house.'

Twenty-three years.

He was seven when he was crowned; he is thirty now. That is a working lifetime by the standards of the age, and in all of it not one repair has been made to a building that had been standing for a century and a half and had been looted at least twice.

Notice what the verse does not say. It does not say the priests stole the money. It does not accuse anybody of dishonesty, then or later, and neither should we — the writer is not shy about naming corruption when he sees it.

What he records is that money came in for a stated purpose and the purpose was not carried out, for a generation. That is not usually theft. It is what happens when income arrives without anybody being personally answerable for a specific outcome: it gets absorbed. Salaries are paid, the ordinary running of the place is met, next year's repairs are next year's problem, and twenty-three years go past.

Every church treasurer and every charity board in the world knows this verse from the inside.

'Therefore King Jehoash summoned Jehoiada the priest and the other priests and said to them, "Why are you not repairing the house? Now therefore take no more money from your donors, but hand it over for the repair of the house."'

He summons the man who raised him, along with the rest of them, and asks the question directly. There is no accusation in it — just why are you not repairing the house? — and then a change of arrangements.

'So the priests agreed that they should take no more money from the people, and that they should not repair the house.'

Read the settlement carefully, because it is generous on both sides and slightly sad.

They give up the collection, and they give up the responsibility with it. No more money through their hands, and no more expectation that they will do the work.

It is the right outcome, and it is an admission. The men whose job it was said, in effect: we are not going to do this, so take it off us. Which is at least honest, and is a great deal better than twenty-three more years of intending to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–16 — A Chest and a Hole in the Lid
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The solution is a piece of joinery: Jehoiada the priest took a chest and bored a hole in the lid of it and set it beside the altar, and donors put their money in themselves as they came in (v. 9). When it filled, the king's secretary and the high priest came up together, bagged and counted it (v. 10), and paid it straight to the carpenters, builders, masons and stonecutters and for timber and quarried stone (vv. 11-12). No silver basins or gold vessels were made until the fabric was done (vv. 13-14). And no accounts were demanded of the foremen, for they dealt honestly (v. 15), while the guilt and sin offering money still went to the priests as their living (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: The fix is structural rather than moral. Nobody preaches at anybody; a box is built with a hole in it, put where the givers can reach it, and opened only by two officials from two different institutions standing together. Good systems are not a substitute for honest men, but they are a great kindness to them.
verseByVerse.examples: And verse 15 keeps it from tipping into suspicion of everyone. The foremen paying the workmen were not audited at all, because they had been shown to be trustworthy. Controls went exactly where the failure had been and nowhere else, and the priests' own income was left untouched. This is a reform, not a purge.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jehoiada the priest took a chest and bored a hole in the lid of it and set it beside the altar on the right side as one entered the house of the LORD. And the priests who guarded the threshold put in it all the money that was brought into the house of the LORD. And whenever they saw that there was much money in the chest, the king's secretary and the high priest came up and they bagged and counted the money that was found in the house of the LORD. Then they would give the money that was weighed out into the hands of the workmen who had the oversight of the house of the LORD. And they paid it out to the carpenters and the builders who worked on the house of the LORD, and to the masons and the stonecutters, as well as to buy timber and quarried stone for making repairs on the house of the LORD, and for any outlay for the repairs of the house. But there were not made for the house of the LORD basins of silver, snuffers, bowls, trumpets, or any vessels of gold, or of silver, from the money that was brought into the house of the LORD, for that was given to the workmen who were repairing the house of the LORD with it. And they did not ask for an accounting from the men into whose hand they delivered the money to pay out to the workmen, for they dealt honestly. The money from the guilt offerings and the money from the sin offerings was not brought into the house of the LORD; it belonged to the priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Jehoiada the priest took a chest and bored a hole in the lid of it and set it beside the altar on the right side as one entered the house of the LORD. And the priests who guarded the threshold put in it all the money that was brought into the house of the LORD.'

The solution to twenty-three years of failure is a box with a hole drilled in the lid.

Look at where it stands. Beside the altar, on the right as you come in — the first thing a worshipper passes. The money no longer goes to a priest who receives it and holds it. It goes through a slot, into a locked chest, in public, where the giver can see it go.

Nobody has been rebuked. No sermon has been preached about stewardship. Jehoiada has made it structurally impossible for the problem to recur, and the whole cost of the reform is one chest and an afternoon with a drill.

'And whenever they saw that there was much money in the chest, the king's secretary and the high priest came up and they bagged and counted the money that was found in the house of the LORD.'

Two men from two institutions, together.

The king's secretary represents the crown; the high priest represents the temple. Neither can open that box alone and neither counts alone, and each is a witness on the other. It is dual control, and it was invented for exactly the reason it is always invented: because a single honest man is one accusation away from ruin, and a single dishonest one is a temptation that need never have been offered.

Good systems do not make men honest. They protect honest men and they remove opportunities from the rest, and it is not cynical to build them. It is a kindness.

'Then they would give the money that was weighed out into the hands of the workmen who had the oversight of the house of the LORD. And they paid it out to the carpenters and the builders who worked on the house of the LORD,'

'and to the masons and the stonecutters, as well as to buy timber and quarried stone for making repairs on the house of the LORD, and for any outlay for the repairs of the house.'

Carpenters, builders, masons, stonecutters, timber, quarried stone. The writer lists the trades and the materials, because that is what the money was for and this time that is where it went.

'But there were not made for the house of the LORD basins of silver, snuffers, bowls, trumpets, or any vessels of gold, or of silver, from the money that was brought into the house of the LORD,'

'for that was given to the workmen who were repairing the house of the LORD with it.'

A discipline about priorities, and it went against the grain.

Silver basins and gold bowls and trumpets are visible. They are the things a donor can look at, and the things a king is remembered for. Rafters and quarried stone are not. And the rule they held to was that nothing went on the furnishings until the fabric was sound.

Any congregation that has ever had to choose between a new sound system and the drains will recognise the decision, and this is the one time in Judah's history somebody made it the right way round.

'And they did not ask for an accounting from the men into whose hand they delivered the money to pay out to the workmen, for they dealt honestly.'

Here the chapter refuses to become what it could easily have become.

Having installed dual control at the chest, they impose no audit at all on the foremen paying the wages — for they dealt honestly. Those men had been tested and found reliable, and they were left alone.

That is the balance, and it should be stated plainly, because institutions almost always get it wrong in one direction or the other. Controls went precisely where the failure had been, and nowhere else. A system that treats everybody as a suspect is not more righteous than one that treats nobody as a suspect; it is simply a different way of not thinking.

'The money from the guilt offerings and the money from the sin offerings was not brought into the house of the LORD; it belonged to the priests.'

The priests keep their living.

The reform took the building fund out of their hands and left their income exactly where the law had put it (Lev. 7:7; Num. 18:9). Nobody was punished, nobody was replaced, and the men who had failed for twenty-three years went on serving with their salaries intact.

It is a reform and not a purge, and in a book this full of purges the difference stands out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–21 — He Sent These to Hazael
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hazael takes Gath and turns toward Jerusalem, and Joash buys him off with all the sacred gifts that Jehoshaphat and Jehoram and Ahaziah his fathers... had dedicated, and his own sacred gifts, and all the gold that was found in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and of the king's house (v. 18). Then Hazael went away from Jerusalem. And the reign ends in a conspiracy of his own household: two servants strike him down in the house of Millo, and he is buried in the city of David (vv. 20-21).
verseByVerse.theology: He spent the middle of his life restoring that building and the end of it emptying the building he restored. The fabric was mended and the contents went to Damascus — his own dedicated gifts among them, and three generations of his fathers' offerings with them.
verseByVerse.examples: There is no prophet in this chapter and no word from the LORD in it anywhere. The king who had done what was right all the days somebody was instructing him consults no one, asks nothing, and pays. Chronicles supplies what Kings withholds: the servants killed him because of the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest (2 Chron. 24:25).

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Hazael king of Syria went up and fought against Gath and took it. But when Hazael set his face to go up against Jerusalem, Jehoash king of Judah took all the sacred gifts that Jehoshaphat and Jehoram and Ahaziah his fathers, the kings of Judah, had dedicated, and his own sacred gifts, and all the gold that was found in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and of the king's house, and sent these to Hazael king of Syria. Then Hazael went away from Jerusalem. Now the rest of the acts of Joash and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? His servants arose and made a conspiracy and struck down Joash in the house of Millo, on the way that goes down to Silla. It was Jozacar the son of Shimeath and Jehozabad the son of Shomer, his servants, who struck him down, so that he died. And they buried him with his fathers in the city of David, and Amaziah his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'At that time Hazael king of Syria went up and fought against Gath and took it. But when Hazael set his face to go up against Jerusalem,'

The man Elisha wept over is now at the gates of Judah.

He has taken Gath, on the coastal plain, which puts him on the wrong side of Judah's western defences with the road to Jerusalem open. And then, the writer says, he set his face to go up.

'Jehoash king of Judah took all the sacred gifts that Jehoshaphat and Jehoram and Ahaziah his fathers, the kings of Judah, had dedicated, and his own sacred gifts, and all the gold that was found in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and of the king's house, and sent these to Hazael king of Syria. Then Hazael went away from Jerusalem.'

Read the inventory, because the writer has laid it out to be read.

The dedicated gifts of Jehoshaphat. The dedicated gifts of Jehoram. The dedicated gifts of Ahaziah. And his own sacred gifts. And all the gold in the temple treasury and the palace treasury.

Four generations of things given to God, gathered up and sent to Damascus in a convoy.

Set that beside the rest of the chapter. This is the man who spent the middle of his life organising the repair of that building — the chest by the altar, the carpenters and the masons, the discipline of putting the fabric before the furnishings. He mended the house and then emptied it.

Something else is missing from this chapter. There is no prophet in it anywhere. Nobody is consulted, no word of the LORD comes, nothing is asked. Hezekiah, in the same city facing a worse army, will take a letter up to the temple and spread it out before God. Joash counts what is in the treasury and pays.

It worked, in the sense that Hazael went away. That is the sort of success that is available to anybody with enough gold, and it is available exactly once.

'Now the rest of the acts of Joash and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?'

'His servants arose and made a conspiracy and struck down Joash in the house of Millo, on the way that goes down to Silla.'

'It was Jozacar the son of Shimeath and Jehozabad the son of Shomer, his servants, who struck him down, so that he died. And they buried him with his fathers in the city of David, and Amaziah his son reigned in his place.'

His own household kills him.

Kings names the two men and their fathers and the place, and offers no motive at all. Chronicles supplies it, and it is the sentence this whole chapter has been walking towards: his servants conspired against him because of the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest (2 Chron. 24:25).

So the reign closes as it opened, with a priest's family and a king in the same room. Jehoiada's wife carried him out of a massacre when he was one year old. Jehoiada taught him for forty years and every good thing recorded here came from it. And when Jehoiada was dead, Joash had his son stoned in the court of the house he had spent twenty years repairing, and two of his own servants killed him in his bed for it.

He was buried in the city of David — though Chronicles adds one more detail, that they did not put him in the tombs of the kings.

12.theology:
Borrowed convictions (v. 2). He did right because a particular man instructed him — the man who had hidden him, crowned him and put the law in his hands. Chronicles records what followed the funeral: he listened to the princes instead, the house of God was abandoned, and he had Jehoiada's own son Zechariah stoned in the temple court (2 Chron. 24:17-22) — a murder the Lord Jesus was still naming eight centuries later (Matt. 23:35). A man may be genuinely good for forty years on somebody else's convictions, and the test of whether a thing has become yours is what survives the burial of the person who taught it.

What actually went wrong (v. 6). No theft is alleged, and the writer is not shy about naming corruption elsewhere. Money arrived for a stated purpose with nobody personally answerable for it, and was absorbed — salaries, running costs, next year's problem — for twenty-three years. That is the ordinary failure of institutions and not usually a moral one, which is exactly why preaching does not fix it.

A structural remedy (vv. 9-10). No rebuke and no sermon: a box, a hole, a position beside the altar where the giver can watch his money go in, and two men from two different institutions to open it. Good systems do not make anyone honest. They protect the honest and remove opportunities from the rest, and building them is a kindness rather than a cynicism.

And the limit of it (v. 15). The foremen paying the wages were not audited at all, for they dealt honestly. Controls went precisely where the failure had been and nowhere else, and the priests' own livelihood was left untouched (v. 16). A system that suspects everybody is not more righteous than one that suspects nobody; it is another way of not thinking. This is a reform, not a purge.

Fabric before furnishings (vv. 13-14). No silver basins, no gold vessels, no trumpets until the building was sound. The visible items are the ones donors look at and kings are remembered for; rafters and quarried stone are not. It is the one time in Judah's history that choice was made the right way round.

The house mended and emptied (vv. 17-18). Four generations of dedicated gifts, his own among them, sent to Damascus to buy off Hazael. And there is no prophet anywhere in this chapter and no word from God sought. Hezekiah will take a threatening letter up to the temple and spread it out; Joash counts the treasury and pays. It worked, in the way that always works for anybody with enough gold, and works once.
12.examples:
Then: For twenty-three years the money for the temple repairs came in and the repairs were not done, and nobody had stolen anything — until a priest drilled a hole in the lid of a box, set it where every worshipper walked past, and had it opened by two men who did not work for the same master.

Now: Three things. First, verse 2. If you can trace your convictions to one person — a parent, a minister, a friend who has always been the reason you keep going — ask what would be left the year after their funeral. Joash's forty good years were real and none of them were his. Second, the chest. Money given for a purpose, with nobody personally answerable for that purpose, gets absorbed; that is not wickedness and no amount of preaching cures it, and the fix is a box with a hole in it and two signatures. Third, the balance in verse 15. Put the controls where the failure was and nowhere else. Treating everyone as a suspect is not integrity, and it costs you the people who were never the problem.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>In the twenty-third year of Joash the son of Ahaziah, king of Judah, Jehoahaz the son of Jehu began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned seventeen years.<sup>2</sup>He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and followed the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin; he did not depart from them.<sup>3</sup>And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he gave them continually into the hand of Hazael king of Syria and into the hand of Ben-hadad the son of Hazael.<sup>4</sup>Then Jehoahaz sought the favor of the LORD, and the LORD listened to him, for he saw the oppression of Israel, how the king of Syria oppressed them.<sup>5</sup>(Therefore the LORD gave Israel a savior, so that they escaped from the hand of the Syrians, and the people of Israel lived in their homes as formerly.<sup>6</sup>Nevertheless, they did not depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, which he made Israel to sin, but walked in them; and the Asherah also remained in Samaria.)<sup>7</sup>For there was not left to Jehoahaz an army of more than fifty horsemen and ten chariots and ten thousand footmen, for the king of Syria had destroyed them and made them like the dust at threshing.<sup>8</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jehoahaz and all that he did, and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>9</sup>So Jehoahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in Samaria, and Joash his son reigned in his place.<sup>10</sup>In the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned sixteen years.<sup>11</sup>He also did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not depart from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin, but he walked in them.<sup>12</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Joash and all that he did, and the might with which he fought against Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>13</sup>So Joash slept with his fathers, and Jeroboam sat on his throne. And Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel.<sup>14</sup>Now when Elisha had fallen sick with the illness of which he was to die, Joash king of Israel went down to him and wept before him, crying, "My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!"<sup>15</sup>And Elisha said to him, "Take a bow and arrows." So he took a bow and arrows.<sup>16</sup>Then he said to the king of Israel, "Draw the bow," and he drew it. And Elisha laid his hands on the king's hands.<sup>17</sup>And he said, "Open the window eastward," and he opened it. Then Elisha said, "Shoot," and he shot. And he said, "The LORD's arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Syria! For you shall fight the Syrians in Aphek until you have made an end of them."<sup>18</sup>And he said, "Take the arrows," and he took them. And he said to the king of Israel, "Strike the ground with them." And he struck three times and stopped.<sup>19</sup>Then the man of God was angry with him and said, "You should have struck five or six times; then you would have struck down Syria until you had made an end of it, but now you will strike down Syria only three times."<sup>20</sup>So Elisha died, and they buried him. Now bands of Moabites used to invade the land in the spring of the year.<sup>21</sup>And as a man was being buried, behold, a marauding band was seen and the man was thrown into the grave of Elisha, and as soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived and stood on his feet.<sup>22</sup>Now Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz.<sup>23</sup>But the LORD was gracious to them and had compassion on them, and he turned toward them, because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and would not destroy them, nor has he cast them from his presence until now.<sup>24</sup>When Hazael king of Syria died, Ben-hadad his son became king in his place.<sup>25</sup>Then Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz took again from Ben-hadad the son of Hazael the cities that he had taken from Jehoahaz his father in war. Three times Joash defeated him and recovered the cities of Israel.
13.overview:
Jehu's dynasty runs on for two more generations and neither of them touches the golden calves. Under Jehoahaz the kingdom is ground down to fifty horsemen and ten chariots — against the two thousand Ahab once put in the field — and the king prays under the pressure and is heard, and nothing changes afterwards. The Asherah is still standing in Samaria when the deliverance comes.

Then Elisha falls ill, and the king of Israel comes down and weeps over him with the words Elisha himself shouted at the Jordan half a century earlier: my father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen! The dying prophet lays his hands on the king's hands over a drawn bow, calls the shot east toward Syria, and then tells him to strike the ground with the arrows. He strikes three times and stops, and is told he has just fixed the number of his own victories.

Elisha dies and is buried without ceremony, and the last miracle of his ministry happens to a stranger tipped into his tomb by a funeral party running from raiders. And the writer explains why there is still a northern kingdom at all: not for anything in it, but because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — with two words at the end that are a warning, until now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Like the Dust at Threshing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehu's son Jehoahaz reigns seventeen years, keeps the calves, and is handed continually into the hand of Hazael (vv. 1-3). Then a sentence nobody expects of him: Jehoahaz sought the favor of the LORD, and the LORD listened to him, for he saw the oppression of Israel (v. 4). A deliverer is given, unnamed (v. 5) — nevertheless, they did not depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam (v. 6). And the state of the army is given as a number: fifty horsemen, ten chariots, ten thousand foot, for the king of Syria had destroyed them and made them like the dust at threshing (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Measure that army against the one this kingdom used to field. Ahab put two thousand chariots into the line at Qarqar; his great-grandson has ten. Elisha wept in a room in Damascus because he had been shown what Hazael would do, and this verse is the arithmetic of it.
verseByVerse.examples: And a bad king prayed, and God listened. The writer does not dress it up — Jehoahaz did evil, kept Jeroboam's calves, left the Asherah standing in Samaria, and after the deliverance changed nothing at all. God heard him anyway, for he saw the oppression of Israel. The mercy was aimed at the suffering of a people, not at the merit of the man who asked.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twenty-third year of Joash the son of Ahaziah, king of Judah, Jehoahaz the son of Jehu began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned seventeen years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and followed the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin; he did not depart from them. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he gave them continually into the hand of Hazael king of Syria and into the hand of Ben-hadad the son of Hazael. Then Jehoahaz sought the favor of the LORD, and the LORD listened to him, for he saw the oppression of Israel, how the king of Syria oppressed them. (Therefore the LORD gave Israel a savior, so that they escaped from the hand of the Syrians, and the people of Israel lived in their homes as formerly. Nevertheless, they did not depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, which he made Israel to sin, but walked in them; and the Asherah also remained in Samaria.) For there was not left to Jehoahaz an army of more than fifty horsemen and ten chariots and ten thousand footmen, for the king of Syria had destroyed them and made them like the dust at threshing. Now the rest of the acts of Jehoahaz and all that he did, and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? So Jehoahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in Samaria, and Joash his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the twenty-third year of Joash the son of Ahaziah, king of Judah, Jehoahaz the son of Jehu began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned seventeen years.'

'He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and followed the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin; he did not depart from them.'

Jehu's son, and the formula is his father's. The calves are still at Bethel and Dan, exactly as they were when Jehu decided not to touch them, and the reason they are still there is that the man who pulled down the house of Baal would not.

'And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he gave them continually into the hand of Hazael king of Syria and into the hand of Ben-hadad the son of Hazael.'

Continually. Not one campaign but a whole reign of them, father and son, seventeen years of being handed over.

'Then Jehoahaz sought the favor of the LORD, and the LORD listened to him, for he saw the oppression of Israel, how the king of Syria oppressed them.'

This verse ought to stop anybody who has decided their own prayers are disqualified.

Here is a king the writer has just described in the harshest formula he has, who keeps the golden calves, who leaves an Asherah standing in the capital, and who — as verse 6 will tell us — does not change one thing afterwards. He seeks the LORD's favour because he is being crushed, and God listens.

The reason given is not the king's sincerity. For he saw the oppression of Israel. The mercy is aimed at the suffering of a people, and the man doing the asking is simply the one who happened to ask.

'(Therefore the LORD gave Israel a savior, so that they escaped from the hand of the Syrians, and the people of Israel lived in their homes as formerly.'

A saviour, and the writer does not name him.

He may mean Joash or Jeroboam the second, who recover territory in the next chapters; he may mean pressure from Assyria on Damascus that took the weight off Israel without anybody in Samaria knowing why. The text leaves it open, and the openness is part of the point: the deliverance came, and the people who were delivered could not have told you the mechanism.

Most rescues look like that from underneath. The people of Israel lived in their homes as formerly — which is not a spectacle. It is the ordinary life of ordinary families, given back.

'Nevertheless, they did not depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, which he made Israel to sin, but walked in them; and the Asherah also remained in Samaria.)'

There is the sad half of it, in one word. Nevertheless.

They prayed under pressure, they were heard, they were delivered, and they went back to exactly what they had been doing. Relief is not repentance. A great many people have mistaken the one for the other in their own lives, and the tell is what is still standing six months later: the Asherah also remained in Samaria.

'For there was not left to Jehoahaz an army of more than fifty horsemen and ten chariots and ten thousand footmen, for the king of Syria had destroyed them and made them like the dust at threshing.'

Fifty horsemen. Ten chariots.

Set that against what this kingdom used to be. Assyrian records of the battle of Qarqar credit Ahab of Israel with two thousand chariots — one of the largest chariot forces in the region. His great-grandson has ten.

Like the dust at threshing — the fine chaff that blows off the floor and is not gathered. Elisha stood in a room in Damascus and cried because he had been shown what Hazael would do to this country, and this verse is that grief converted into a muster roll.

'Now the rest of the acts of Jehoahaz and all that he did, and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?'

'So Jehoahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in Samaria, and Joash his son reigned in his place.'

And his might. The formula is used of every king, and there is something bleak about applying it to a man with ten chariots.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–19 — You Should Have Struck Five or Six Times
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehoahaz's son Joash reigns sixteen years and also does evil (vv. 10-13). Then Elisha falls ill, and the king goes down and weeps over him: my father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen! (v. 14). The dying prophet has him take a bow, lays his own hands on the king's hands, has the east window opened, and calls the shot the LORD's arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Syria (vv. 15-17). Then: strike the ground with them — and he strikes three times and stops. Then the man of God was angry with him and said, You should have struck five or six times; then you would have struck down Syria until you had made an end of it, but now you will strike down Syria only three times (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 14 is the sentence Elisha himself shouted at the Jordan when the whirlwind took his master (2:12), and it comes back word for word over his own deathbed. The same line opens and closes the ministry. What makes it strange is the mouth it comes out of: a king the writer has called evil four verses earlier, weeping and calling him father and saying that the real defence of the country is leaving the room.
verseByVerse.examples: He was never told how many times to strike, and readers often feel the anger is unfair. But he had just been told the arrow meant the end of Syria, and he had the prophet's hands on his own, and he stopped. It was an invitation, not a rite, and he treated it as something to get through. He had wept a minute earlier. Verse 25 gives him exactly three victories.

verseByVerse.quote: In the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned sixteen years. He also did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not depart from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin, but he walked in them. Now the rest of the acts of Joash and all that he did, and the might with which he fought against Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? So Joash slept with his fathers, and Jeroboam sat on his throne. And Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel. Now when Elisha had fallen sick with the illness of which he was to die, Joash king of Israel went down to him and wept before him, crying, "My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!" And Elisha said to him, "Take a bow and arrows." So he took a bow and arrows. Then he said to the king of Israel, "Draw the bow," and he drew it. And Elisha laid his hands on the king's hands. And he said, "Open the window eastward," and he opened it. Then Elisha said, "Shoot," and he shot. And he said, "The LORD's arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Syria! For you shall fight the Syrians in Aphek until you have made an end of them." And he said, "Take the arrows," and he took them. And he said to the king of Israel, "Strike the ground with them." And he struck three times and stopped. Then the man of God was angry with him and said, "You should have struck five or six times; then you would have struck down Syria until you had made an end of it, but now you will strike down Syria only three times."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned sixteen years.'

'He also did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not depart from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin, but he walked in them.'

The third generation of Jehu's house, and the third identical verdict. Hold on to it, because in four verses this man is going to do something that does not fit it at all.

'Now the rest of the acts of Joash and all that he did, and the might with which he fought against Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?'

'So Joash slept with his fathers, and Jeroboam sat on his throne. And Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel.'

The writer closes his file and then reopens it, because there is one scene left that belongs to this reign and he is not willing to leave it out.

'Now when Elisha had fallen sick with the illness of which he was to die, Joash king of Israel went down to him and wept before him, crying, "My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!"'

Stop here. You have read this sentence before, word for word.

A young man stood on the far bank of the Jordan and watched horses and chariots of fire come between him and the only father he had, and shouted after him into the wind: my father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen! (2:12). Then he tore his own clothes in two and picked up the cloak.

Some fifty years later a king of Israel stands over that man's deathbed and says the identical thing.

The same line opens the ministry and closes it. Elisha said it about Elijah; Joash says it about Elisha; and what it means both times is that the real defence of this country has never been its cavalry. Israel has ten chariots left, and the king weeping in that room knows perfectly well that what is dying in the bed is worth more than all of them.

Look whose mouth it comes out of. Four verses ago the writer said this man did evil and walked in the sins of Jeroboam. He is not a good king and he is not going to become one. He is also weeping over a dying prophet, calling him father, and grasping the one thing about his kingdom that his great-grandfather Jehu never grasped.

People are not tidy. A man can see something true, and feel it to the point of tears, and go home unchanged, and the Bible reports both halves without embarrassment.

'And Elisha said to him, "Take a bow and arrows." So he took a bow and arrows.'

'Then he said to the king of Israel, "Draw the bow," and he drew it. And Elisha laid his hands on the king's hands.'

A dying man puts his hands over a king's hands on a bowstring.

He has not the strength to draw it himself. What he can do is lay his hands on top of the hands that can, and the picture is exact: the power was never in the prophet's arm, and the king's arm is not going to do anything on its own either.

'And he said, "Open the window eastward," and he opened it. Then Elisha said, "Shoot," and he shot. And he said, "The LORD's arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Syria! For you shall fight the Syrians in Aphek until you have made an end of them."'

East, out of the window, over the Jordan and toward Gilead and Damascus — the territory Hazael has taken and the direction the trouble comes from.

The promise is not modest. Until you have made an end of them.

'And he said, "Take the arrows," and he took them. And he said to the king of Israel, "Strike the ground with them." And he struck three times and stopped.'

'Then the man of God was angry with him and said, "You should have struck five or six times; then you would have struck down Syria until you had made an end of it, but now you will strike down Syria only three times."'

This exchange troubles readers, and the trouble should be faced rather than talked around. He was never told how many times to strike. How is he at fault for stopping?

Take what he did know. He had just been told, thirty seconds earlier, that the arrow in his hand meant victory over Syria until you have made an end of them. He had felt the prophet's hands close over his own. He was holding a fistful of arrows and had been told to strike the ground with them, by a dying man whose every word in fifty years had come true.

He hit the floor three times and stopped, and waited to be told what came next.

It was an invitation and he treated it as a formality — a thing to be performed correctly and got through, rather than an opening he was being handed. The measure of the answer was left to him, and he took a small one.

The reader of this book has seen that before. A widow was told to borrow empty vessels, and not too few, and the oil flowed until she ran out of jars and then stopped — not because the supply failed but because her capacity to receive it had been fixed out in the street an hour earlier (4:6). God has more than once let the size of what he gives be settled by the earnestness of the asking.

None of which makes God stingy. Joash was given three real victories he had done nothing to deserve, by a prophet on his deathbed, in a kingdom with ten chariots. He simply had five or six within reach and put the arrows down.

Notice the emotional distance travelled in four verses. He came into that room weeping. By the time he is holding the arrows he is going through the motions. Feeling is not the same as faith, and it does not last as long.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–25 — Because of His Covenant With Abraham
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elisha dies and is buried, and in the spring a burial party dumps a body in his tomb because raiders are coming — and as soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived and stood on his feet (vv. 20-21). Hazael goes on oppressing Israel; and then the sentence that explains why there is still an Israel: but the LORD was gracious to them and had compassion on them, and he turned toward them, because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and would not destroy them, nor has he cast them from his presence until now (v. 23). Hazael dies; and Joash takes back the lost cities three times (vv. 24-25).
verseByVerse.theology: The last thing Elisha does happens after he is dead. Elijah went up in a whirlwind and left a cloak; Elisha stayed in the ground and one more miracle came out of it. Nothing here licenses a theology of relics — the writer draws no lesson and nobody afterwards goes near that tomb. What it says is that the power at work in that man was never his own and did not stop when his heart did.
verseByVerse.examples: And verse 23 is the north's version of the lamp. Judah survives for the sake of David his servant (8:19); Israel survives because of a covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Two kingdoms, both undeserving, both carried on promises made to men who had been dead for centuries. The chill is in the last two words: until now.

verseByVerse.quote: So Elisha died, and they buried him. Now bands of Moabites used to invade the land in the spring of the year. And as a man was being buried, behold, a marauding band was seen and the man was thrown into the grave of Elisha, and as soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived and stood on his feet. Now Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz. But the LORD was gracious to them and had compassion on them, and he turned toward them, because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and would not destroy them, nor has he cast them from his presence until now. When Hazael king of Syria died, Ben-hadad his son became king in his place. Then Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz took again from Ben-hadad the son of Hazael the cities that he had taken from Jehoahaz his father in war. Three times Joash defeated him and recovered the cities of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Elisha died, and they buried him. Now bands of Moabites used to invade the land in the spring of the year.'

Four words for the end of a fifty-year ministry: so Elisha died, and they buried him.

His master went up in a whirlwind with horses of fire and was never buried at all. Elisha, who asked for a double portion and got it, dies in a bed of an ordinary illness and is put in a tomb like anybody else. There is no drama in it whatever, and the writer moves straight on to a note about seasonal raiding.

'And as a man was being buried, behold, a marauding band was seen and the man was thrown into the grave of Elisha, and as soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived and stood on his feet.'

Picture the scene, because it is almost comic and entirely undignified.

A funeral party is out with a body when somebody spots raiders on the horizon. There is no time to finish; there is a tomb standing open nearby; they tip the corpse in and run.

The dead man hits the bones of Elisha and stands up.

The last miracle of Elisha's ministry happens after his own funeral, to a man nobody has named, in front of witnesses who were running away at the time and were not looking for anything of the kind.

Be careful here, and note what the passage does not do. It draws no lesson. Nobody afterwards goes near that tomb, no shrine is built, and the bones are never mentioned again in Scripture. There is no warrant here for relics, and it would be a poor use of the verse to find one.

What it does say should be kept. The power that worked through that man for fifty years was never his, and it did not belong to his lungs or his hands or his voice, and it did not stop when his heart did. He had asked for a double portion of Elijah's spirit and received it, and there was still enough of it in a grave to raise a stranger.

There is a hint in it that the rest of Scripture will make explicit. A dead man touched what was left of a servant of God and stood on his feet. One day a great many dead men will hear the voice of the Son of God and come out (John 5:28-29), and the graves of his people will not be the end of them either.

'Now Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz.'

'But the LORD was gracious to them and had compassion on them, and he turned toward them, because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and would not destroy them, nor has he cast them from his presence until now.'

Here is the northern kingdom's version of the lamp, and the reader should set the two verses side by side.

Of Judah, five chapters ago: yet the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever (8:19).

Of Israel, here: the LORD was gracious to them and had compassion on them... because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Two kingdoms, neither of them deserving anything, both still standing — and in each case the reason given is a promise made to a man who had been dead for centuries. Judah is carried by David. Israel, which has no David and no temple and no lamp, is carried by Abraham.

Mark what the verse says God did. He was gracious, he had compassion, and he turned toward them — which is the language of a face, and of somebody choosing to look at people who had given him no reason to.

Then the last two words, which are the coldest in the chapter. Until now.

The writer is composing this after the end, and he knows how it finishes. He is telling us that God had not yet cast them out at the point his account has reached, and that is not the same as saying he never would. Four chapters from now an Assyrian army will take Samaria and carry that kingdom off the map, and this verse is quietly telling us that the only thing holding it up in the meantime was an old promise, and that patience is not the same as impunity.

'When Hazael king of Syria died, Ben-hadad his son became king in his place.'

'Then Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz took again from Ben-hadad the son of Hazael the cities that he had taken from Jehoahaz his father in war. Three times Joash defeated him and recovered the cities of Israel.'

Three times.

The writer does not comment and does not need to. A dying prophet told a king to strike the ground with a handful of arrows and he struck three times and stopped, and was told that he had just fixed the number of his own victories.

He got every one of them. Three real defeats of Syria, three sets of towns recovered, more than his father saw in seventeen years — and the man who told him he could have had it all is in a grave that has already produced one more miracle than the king ever will.

13.theology:
A bad king prays and is heard (vv. 4-6). Jehoahaz keeps the calves, leaves the Asherah standing, changes nothing after the rescue — and God listens, and the stated reason is not the man's sincerity but he saw the oppression of Israel. The mercy was aimed at a suffering people; the king was simply the one who asked. And verse 6 supplies the sad half: relief is not repentance, and the tell is what is still standing six months later.

The bookend (v. 14). My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen! is word for word what Elisha cried at the Jordan when the whirlwind took Elijah (2:12). The same sentence opens and closes the ministry, and both times it means that the real defence of the country was never its cavalry — which is a pointed thing to say in a kingdom with ten chariots left. And it is said by a king the writer has just called evil, in tears. People are not tidy; a man can see something true, feel it to the point of weeping, and go home unchanged.

The arrows (vv. 18-19). He was never told how many times to strike, and the anger looks unfair until you count what he did know: that the arrow meant the end of Syria, that the prophet's hands had just closed over his, and that he was holding a fistful of arrows. It was an invitation and he treated it as a formality to be performed correctly and got through. The measure was left to him and he took a small one — as the widow's oil ran until she ran out of borrowed jars and then stopped (4:6). And note the distance travelled in four verses: he came in weeping and was going through the motions by the end of the visit. Feeling is not faith and does not last as long.

After the funeral (vv. 20-21). Elijah went up in a whirlwind and was never buried; Elisha died of an illness and was put in a tomb, and his last miracle happened to an unnamed corpse tipped in by a burial party running from raiders. The passage draws no lesson, builds no shrine, and never mentions the bones again — there is no warrant here for relics. What it says is that the power at work in that man was never his own and did not stop when his heart did. And it leans forward: one day a great many dead will hear the voice of the Son of God and come out (John 5:28-29).

The north's lamp (v. 23). Judah stands for the sake of David his servant (8:19); Israel stands because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Two undeserving kingdoms, each carried by a promise made to a man dead for centuries. And he turned toward them is the language of a face. Then the last two words: until now. Patience is not impunity, and Samaria falls in chapter 17.
13.examples:
Then: A burial party carrying a body saw raiders on the skyline, tipped the corpse into the nearest open tomb and ran — and the dead man touched what was left of Elisha and stood up on his feet.

Now: Three things. First, verse 4. If you have concluded that your prayers are disqualified by the state of your life, look at who is praying here and what he does afterwards, and at the reason God gives for listening. Second, the arrows. Joash was not disobedient; he was perfunctory. He performed the action correctly, stopped early, and waited to be told what came next, and it cost him a kingdom's worth of victory. Ask where you are doing exactly what you were told and nothing more — in prayer, most likely. Third, the four verses between his tears and his three taps on the floor. He meant the weeping. It simply did not survive the next few minutes, and the Bible reports both halves of him without surprise.
