14.overview:
Two kingdoms, and one verse in the middle of the first that is worth the whole chapter. Amaziah executes the men who murdered his father and then declines to touch their children according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, and the writer quotes Deuteronomy 24:16 in full. In a book that has shown us seventy heads in baskets and a queen destroying her own grandchildren, a king reads a text and stops.

Then he beats Edom, and the victory undoes him. He challenges Israel for no reason and is answered with a fable about a thistle proposing marriage to a cedar and being trodden flat by an animal that was not even fighting it — and with advice that is entirely sound: your heart has lifted you up. Be content with your glory, and stay at home. He will not listen, and Jerusalem loses two hundred yards of wall and the contents of the temple.

In the north, Jeroboam the second reigns forty-one years and restores the borders to where Solomon had them — and gets seven verses, a bad verdict, and an explanation that credits none of it to him: God saw that the affliction of Israel was very bitter and there was nobody to help. The prophet who announced it was Jonah the son of Amittai.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — According to What Is Written
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Amaziah does what is right yet not like David his father, and the high places stay (vv. 3-4). He executes the servants who murdered his father — and then does something no king in this book has done: he did not put to death the children of the murderers, according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, where the LORD commanded, Fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. But each one shall die for his own sin (vv. 5-6). Then a victory: ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, and Sela taken by storm (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Consider what the surrounding chapters have accustomed us to. Seventy of Ahab's sons beheaded and sent in baskets; forty-two Judean travellers killed at a cistern; a queen destroying her own grandchildren. Wiping out a rival's family was not an atrocity in that world, it was procedure — and here a king with every political reason to finish the job stops because of a sentence in a book.
verseByVerse.examples: And the writer quotes the sentence in full rather than referring to it, which he rarely does. Deuteronomy 24:16 stood in Israel's law for centuries before anybody is recorded as obeying it against his own interest. A written word, consulted and allowed to overrule a decision already made, is the rarest thing in these two books.

verseByVerse.quote: In the second year of Joash the son of Joahaz, king of Israel, Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, began to reign. He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jehoaddin of Jerusalem. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, yet not like David his father. He did in all things as Joash his father had done. But the high places were not removed; the people still sacrificed and made offerings on the high places. And as soon as the royal power was firmly in his hand, he struck down his servants who had struck down the king his father. But he did not put to death the children of the murderers, according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, where the LORD commanded, "Fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. But each one shall die for his own sin." He struck down ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt and took Sela by storm, and called it Joktheel, which is its name to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the second year of Joash the son of Joahaz, king of Israel, Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, began to reign.'

'He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jehoaddin of Jerusalem.'

'And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, yet not like David his father. He did in all things as Joash his father had done.'

A qualified verdict, and the qualification is a comparison in two directions. Not like David; exactly like his father Joash — which the reader of the last two chapters knows means good for a while, on somebody else's convictions, and finished badly.

'But the high places were not removed; the people still sacrificed and made offerings on the high places.'

'And as soon as the royal power was firmly in his hand, he struck down his servants who had struck down the king his father.'

His father was murdered in his bed by two of the household staff. He waits until the throne is secure and then executes them, which is justice and is also what any king in the region would have done.

'But he did not put to death the children of the murderers, according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, where the LORD commanded, "Fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. But each one shall die for his own sin."'

Here is the best verse in the chapter, and it is easy to read past because nothing happens in it.

What did not happen is the point. The children of those two men were not killed.

Set that against everything this book has shown us. Jehu had seventy of Ahab's sons beheaded and the heads sent to him in baskets, and forty-two Judean travellers killed at a cistern. Athaliah destroyed her own grandchildren. Baasha wiped out the house of Jeroboam and Zimri wiped out the house of Baasha, and in each case the writer notes that not one male was left. Eliminating a dead enemy's sons was not an atrocity in that world; it was housekeeping, and any adviser would have urged it — a murdered king's assassins leave sons who grow up.

Amaziah does not do it, and the writer tells us exactly why: according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses.

Then he quotes it, at length, which he almost never does. Fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. But each one shall die for his own sin (Deut. 24:16).

That law had been in Israel's books for something like six hundred years. This is the first time in either of these two books that a king is recorded as reading it, applying it to a decision he had every political reason to make the other way, and letting it stop him.

A written word, consulted at cost, and obeyed against interest. It is the rarest event in the whole history of these kingdoms, and it takes one verse.

'He struck down ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt and took Sela by storm, and called it Joktheel, which is its name to this day.'

A real victory in the rift valley south of the Dead Sea, and the capture of a fortress in the Edomite highlands, which he renames.

Keep the victory in view, because it is about to be the ruin of him. Nothing in this chapter goes wrong until something goes right.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Flushed with Edom, Amaziah challenges the king of Israel — come, let us look one another in the face (v. 8) — and gets back a fable: a thistle on Lebanon proposing a marriage alliance to a cedar, and a wild animal walking past and treading the thistle flat (v. 9). The advice attached is sound and almost kind: you have indeed struck down Edom, and your heart has lifted you up. Be content with your glory, and stay at home (v. 10). He will not listen. Judah is broken at Beth-shemesh, the king is captured, four hundred cubits of Jerusalem's wall comes down, and the temple and the treasury are emptied into Samaria (vv. 11-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The fable is contemptuous and it is accurate. Jehoash is not pretending to be a good man and the counsel he gives is better than anything in Amaziah's own court: one victory over Edom has convinced a small king that he is a large one, and the cure prescribed is to stay at home and enjoy what he has.
verseByVerse.examples: And the wall is the part to feel. Two hundred yards of Jerusalem's defences pulled down from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate — not stormed but demolished at leisure, by a brother kingdom, because a king could not leave well alone. It stayed down for the best part of a century.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amaziah sent messengers to Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, "Come, let us look one another in the face." And Jehoash king of Israel sent word to Amaziah king of Judah, "A thistle on Lebanon sent to a cedar on Lebanon, saying, 'Give your daughter to my son for a wife,' and a wild beast of Lebanon passed by and trampled down the thistle. You have indeed struck down Edom, and your heart has lifted you up. Be content with your glory, and stay at home, for why should you provoke trouble so that you fall, you and Judah with you?" But Amaziah would not listen. So Jehoash king of Israel went up, and he and Amaziah king of Judah faced one another in battle at Beth-shemesh, which belongs to Judah. And Judah was defeated by Israel, and every man fled to his home. And Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Jehoash, son of Ahaziah, at Beth-shemesh, and came to Jerusalem and broke down the wall of Jerusalem for four hundred cubits, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate. And he seized all the gold and silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the king's house, also hostages, and he returned to Samaria. Now the rest of the acts of Jehoash that he did, and his might, and how he fought with Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? And Jehoash slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel, and Jeroboam his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Amaziah sent messengers to Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, "Come, let us look one another in the face."'

It is a challenge, and there is no need for it. Judah and Israel are not at war. He has just beaten Edom and he wants to find out how far the feeling goes.

'And Jehoash king of Israel sent word to Amaziah king of Judah, "A thistle on Lebanon sent to a cedar on Lebanon, saying, 'Give your daughter to my son for a wife,' and a wild beast of Lebanon passed by and trampled down the thistle.'

The reply is a fable, and it is beautifully cruel.

A thistle — a weed at ankle height — sends a formal marriage proposal to a cedar of Lebanon, the tallest and most valuable tree in the ancient world, as though they were houses of equal standing. And while the message is being delivered, an animal walks past and treads the thistle into the ground without noticing it was there.

The insult is not merely that Judah is small. It is that the thistle is destroyed by something that was not even fighting it.

'You have indeed struck down Edom, and your heart has lifted you up. Be content with your glory, and stay at home, for why should you provoke trouble so that you fall, you and Judah with you?"'

Then, having been thoroughly rude, he gives him genuinely good advice.

You have indeed struck down Edom — the victory is granted, without sarcasm. And your heart has lifted you up — the diagnosis, and it is correct. Be content with your glory, and stay at home.

Nobody in Jerusalem said anything so useful to that king. It came from a man the writer has called evil, wrapped in a joke at his expense, which is very often the packaging that true things arrive in.

Notice the mechanism it describes, because it is one of the commonest ways a life comes apart. Not failure. A success, sincerely earned, which quietly resets a man's estimate of himself, so that the next thing he attempts is measured against the new estimate rather than against the facts.

'But Amaziah would not listen. So Jehoash king of Israel went up, and he and Amaziah king of Judah faced one another in battle at Beth-shemesh, which belongs to Judah.'

'And Judah was defeated by Israel, and every man fled to his home.'

Note where it is fought. Beth-shemesh belongs to Judah — he issued the challenge and the battle happened on his own ground, which is what usually comes of provoking somebody larger.

'And Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Jehoash, son of Ahaziah, at Beth-shemesh, and came to Jerusalem and broke down the wall of Jerusalem for four hundred cubits, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate.'

Four hundred cubits is about two hundred yards.

He does not storm the city; there is no need, since he has the king. He walks in and demolishes the north wall between two named gates, at leisure, and leaves it lying open.

That is a considered act. Killing Amaziah would have solved nothing; leaving Jerusalem with a two-hundred-yard hole in its defences leaves Judah unable to threaten anybody for a generation. The breach was still a live problem when Uzziah and later Hezekiah came to build.

'And he seized all the gold and silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the king's house, also hostages, and he returned to Samaria.'

The temple is emptied again.

Count the times in these chapters. Joash spent twenty years repairing that building and then stripped it to buy off Hazael. Now what is left goes north to Samaria, taken by a fellow Israelite, because a king of Judah wanted to see how a war would go. Ahaz will do it again in two chapters.

'Now the rest of the acts of Jehoash that he did, and his might, and how he fought with Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?'

'And Jehoash slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel, and Jeroboam his son reigned in his place.'

The man who wept at Elisha's bedside and struck the ground three times dies in his bed, having beaten Syria three times and Judah once.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Amaziah outlives his conqueror by fifteen years and is then killed by a conspiracy at Lachish (vv. 17-20); his sixteen-year-old son Azariah is made king (v. 21). And then the north gets its most successful reign: Jeroboam the second, forty-one years, who did what was evil and yet restored the border of Israel from Lebo-hamath as far as the Sea of the Arabah, according to the word of the LORD, the God of Israel, which he spoke by his servant Jonah the son of Amittai, the prophet, who was from Gath-hepher (vv. 23-25). The reason is given and it is not merit: the LORD saw that the affliction of Israel was very bitter... and there was none to help Israel (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: That is the Jonah — the same name, the same father, the same town (cf. Jon. 1:1). Before he was the prophet who ran to Tarshish he was a court prophet of national expansion, whose word to Israel was that the borders would come back. Set that beside a commission to go and preach to Nineveh so that Nineveh might be spared, and his reluctance stops being a curiosity.
verseByVerse.examples: And a wicked king is used to save a people God pitied. Forty-one years of recovered territory and returning prosperity — and Amos and Hosea preach in this reign, which tells you what the country was like underneath. God had not said he would blot out the name of Israel; not yet.

verseByVerse.quote: Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, lived fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel. Now the rest of the deeds of Amaziah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish. But they sent after him to Lachish and put him to death there. And they brought him on horses; and he was buried in Jerusalem with his fathers in the city of David. And all the people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king instead of his father Amaziah. He built Elath and restored it to Judah, after the king slept with his fathers. In the fifteenth year of Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel, began to reign in Samaria, and he reigned forty-one years. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not depart from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin. He restored the border of Israel from Lebo-hamath as far as the Sea of the Arabah, according to the word of the LORD, the God of Israel, which he spoke by his servant Jonah the son of Amittai, the prophet, who was from Gath-hepher. For the LORD saw that the affliction of Israel was very bitter, for there was none left, bond or free, and there was none to help Israel. But the LORD had not said that he would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven, so he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash. Now the rest of the acts of Jeroboam and all that he did, and his might, how he fought, and how he restored Damascus and Hamath to Judah in Israel, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? And Jeroboam slept with his fathers, the kings of Israel, and Zechariah his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, lived fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel.'

'Now the rest of the deeds of Amaziah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?'

'And they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish. But they sent after him to Lachish and put him to death there.'

Fifteen years of reigning over a capital with a hole in its wall, in a kingdom that had been humiliated because of him, and then his own people come for him.

He runs thirty miles to Lachish and they send after him. His father was murdered by servants in his own house and he executed them for it and spared their children by the law of Moses, and now the same thing happens to him.

'And they brought him on horses; and he was buried in Jerusalem with his fathers in the city of David.'

'And all the people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king instead of his father Amaziah.'

'He built Elath and restored it to Judah, after the king slept with his fathers.'

Another boy king — sixteen — put on the throne by all the people of Judah after an assassination. He will reign fifty-two years, and the next chapter will tell us how it ended.

'In the fifteenth year of Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel, began to reign in Samaria, and he reigned forty-one years.'

'And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not depart from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin.'

Forty-one years, and the writer gives him seven verses.

By every measure the world uses this is the most successful reign in the history of the northern kingdom. The borders go back out to where they were under Solomon; the economy recovers; Samaria becomes wealthy. And the historian's entire verdict is the standing formula about the calves, exactly as he gave it to Omri, who founded the capital, and for the same reason.

'He restored the border of Israel from Lebo-hamath as far as the Sea of the Arabah, according to the word of the LORD, the God of Israel, which he spoke by his servant Jonah the son of Amittai, the prophet, who was from Gath-hepher.'

Stop on that name, because it is one of the most illuminating verses in the Old Testament and almost nobody notices it.

Jonah the son of Amittai, the prophet, who was from Gath-hepher.

That is the Jonah. The book that bears his name opens now the word of the LORD came to Jonah the son of Amittai (Jon. 1:1) — the same name, the same father, and this verse even supplies his home town, a village in Galilee a few miles from Nazareth.

Look at what his ministry was before the whale. He was the prophet who told Jeroboam the second that Israel's lost borders would be restored — the man whose word to his nation was national recovery, delivered in a reign of expansion and prosperity, and vindicated on the map.

Now set beside that a commission to go to Nineveh, the capital of the empire that will eventually destroy his country, and preach so that it might repent and be spared.

His reluctance stops being a puzzle. He was not merely frightened, and he tells us himself what the real trouble was: I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster (Jon. 4:2). He did not want Assyria forgiven. And he had spent his career as the prophet of Israel's borders.

'For the LORD saw that the affliction of Israel was very bitter, for there was none left, bond or free, and there was none to help Israel.'

'But the LORD had not said that he would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven, so he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash.'

Two verses of explanation, and neither of them mentions anything good about the king.

The reason is pity. The LORD saw that the affliction of Israel was very bitter, and there was nobody to help them, and so he helped them — through a man who did evil in his sight and kept the calves at Bethel for forty-one years.

This is now the third time in a few chapters that the writer has said something like it. Jehoahaz prayed and was heard because God saw the oppression of Israel. Israel was not destroyed because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And here a wicked king's greatest achievement is credited to God's compassion for people who had earned nothing.

Note the careful clause: the LORD had not said that he would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven. Not yet. It is the same shadow as the until now at the end of the last chapter, and this prosperity is the last of it.

One more thing belongs here, because Kings does not say it and the reader should know. Amos and Hosea both prophesied in this reign, and what they describe underneath the boom is a country selling the needy for a pair of sandals, storing violence in its palaces, and lying on beds of ivory. The most prosperous forty-one years the northern kingdom ever had were also the years in which its prophets could not find an honest man in the market.

'Now the rest of the acts of Jeroboam and all that he did, and his might, how he fought, and how he restored Damascus and Hamath to Judah in Israel, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?'

'And Jeroboam slept with his fathers, the kings of Israel, and Zechariah his son reigned in his place.'

Zechariah his son, who is the fourth generation from Jehu, and whose reign will last six months.

14.theology:
A written word obeyed against interest (v. 6). Executing an assassin's sons was standard practice and any adviser would have urged it. Amaziah does not, and the reason given is a text — quoted in full, which this writer almost never does. Deuteronomy 24:16 had stood in Israel's books for six centuries; this is the first time in either of these books that a king is recorded consulting the law and letting it overrule a decision he had every reason to make the other way.

How a life comes apart (v. 10). Not by failure. By a success, sincerely earned, that quietly resets a man's estimate of himself, so that the next thing he attempts is measured against the new estimate instead of the facts. You have indeed struck down Edom, and your heart has lifted you up — said by a wicked king, inside an insult, and truer than anything Amaziah's own court told him. True things frequently arrive in that packaging.

Jonah before Nineveh (v. 25). Same name, same father, and this verse even gives the village (cf. Jon. 1:1). Before he ran to Tarshish he was the prophet of Israel's borders, whose word to his own nation was recovery and who was vindicated on the map. Then he was sent to preach to the capital of the empire that would destroy his country, so that it might be spared — and told God exactly what his objection was: I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful... and relenting from disaster (Jon. 4:2).

Saved on the ground of pity (vv. 26-27). Nothing good is said about Jeroboam anywhere. God acted because the affliction of Israel was very bitter and there was none to help. That is the third time in a few chapters — Jehoahaz heard because God saw the oppression (13:4), Israel spared for the covenant with Abraham (13:23), and now this. And the qualifying clause is ominous: he had not said he would blot out the name of Israel. Not yet.

What Kings does not say about those forty-one years. Amos and Hosea preached in this reign. Underneath the recovered borders and the returning money they describe a country selling the needy for a pair of sandals and lying on beds of ivory. The most prosperous stretch in the northern kingdom's history was the one its prophets found most rotten.
14.examples:
Then: A king with the throne newly secure, the men who murdered his father freshly executed, and every political reason to finish their families as well, opened a book instead and left the children alive.

Now: Two things. First, verse 6 is what obedience actually looks like when it costs something: not a feeling, but a written sentence consulted at the exact moment it is inconvenient, and allowed to reverse a decision already made. Ask when you last let a text do that. Second, the thistle. Amaziah was not ruined by defeat but by his one genuine success, and the counsel he ignored came from somebody he had every reason to despise. If the most accurate thing anyone has said about you lately came wrapped in an insult from a person you do not respect, that is not a reason to discount it.

15.overview:
Judah's longest reign and Israel's fastest collapse, side by side. Uzziah holds the throne in Jerusalem for fifty-two years, and the only event this writer records from all of them is that the LORD touched the king and he finished his life a leper in a separate house with his son governing for him. Chronicles supplies the reason Kings withholds: he grew strong, and when he was strong he grew proud, and went into the temple to burn incense.

In the north, five kings in twenty-four verses and four of them murdered. Zechariah lasts six months — and the writer stops in brackets to note that God's promise to Jehu of four generations has just been fulfilled and used up in the same breath. Shallum lasts a month. Menahem rips open the pregnant women of an Israelite town for closing its gate to him, which is the precise atrocity Elisha wept over when it was foretold of a foreign enemy. Then Assyria arrives, and is paid a thousand talents raised from sixty thousand men.

And under Pekah the first deportation happens: Galilee, Naphtali and Gilead emptied and carried off. The chapter ends in Judah with a good king, a new gate, and one sentence about a border war — in those days the LORD began to send Syria and Israel against Judah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Leper to the Day of His Death
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Azariah — Uzziah in Isaiah and Chronicles — comes to the throne at sixteen and reigns fifty-two years, longer than anyone in either kingdom, doing what is right with the high places still standing (vv. 1-4). And then one sentence disposes of the whole reign: the LORD touched the king, so that he was a leper to the day of his death, and he lived in a separate house. And Jotham the king's son was over the household, governing the people of the land (v. 5). He is buried with his fathers and his son succeeds (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Kings gives the fact and withholds the reason. Chronicles supplies it: he grew strong, and when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction, went into the temple to burn incense himself, was confronted by eighty priests, and the leprosy broke out on his forehead while he stood there with the censer in his hand (2 Chron. 26:16-21).
verseByVerse.examples: And the year he died is one of the great dates in the Bible, though this chapter does not say so. In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up (Isa. 6:1). The year Judah lost the longest reign it ever had is the year a young man in Jerusalem saw the throne that does not change hands.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Azariah the son of Amaziah, king of Judah, began to reign. He was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jecoliah of Jerusalem. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that his father Amaziah had done. Nevertheless, the high places were not taken away. The people still sacrificed and made offerings on the high places. And the LORD touched the king, so that he was a leper to the day of his death, and he lived in a separate house. And Jotham the king's son was over the household, governing the people of the land. Now the rest of the acts of Azariah, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And Azariah slept with his fathers, and they buried him with his fathers in the city of David, and Jotham his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Azariah the son of Amaziah, king of Judah, began to reign.'

'He was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jecoliah of Jerusalem.'

Fifty-two years, which is the longest reign in the history of either kingdom.

He is called Azariah here and Uzziah in Isaiah, Amos, Hosea and Chronicles; both names belonged to him. And the fifty-two years were, by every earthly measure, magnificent. Chronicles records the army, the towers, the cisterns, the engineers, the fortifications, the trade — his fame spread far, for he was marvelously helped, till he was strong (2 Chron. 26:15).

'And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that his father Amaziah had done.'

'Nevertheless, the high places were not taken away. The people still sacrificed and made offerings on the high places.'

'And the LORD touched the king, so that he was a leper to the day of his death, and he lived in a separate house. And Jotham the king's son was over the household, governing the people of the land.'

Fifty-two years of reign, and this is the only event in them the writer records.

The LORD touched the king. He does not say why, and a reader of Kings alone is left with a bare and unexplained affliction.

Chronicles gives the reason, and it belongs here. When he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction. He went into the temple to burn incense on the altar of incense, which was the work of the priests and not of kings; Azariah the priest and eighty others followed him in and told him to his face that it was not for him to do; he was angry, with the censer in his hand — and while he was raging at them the leprosy broke out on his forehead, and they hurried him out, and he himself hastened to go out, because the LORD had struck him (2 Chron. 26:16-21).

So the man with the longest reign and the greatest achievements finished it in a separate house — excluded from the temple he had walked into uninvited, excluded from the city, with his son running the country for him.

Chronicles states the mechanism in one clause, and it should be carried away: when he was strong, he grew proud. Not when he was weak, and not when he was failing. The dangerous season was the one that looked like the reward for the earlier faithfulness.

'Now the rest of the acts of Azariah, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?'

'And Azariah slept with his fathers, and they buried him with his fathers in the city of David, and Jotham his son reigned in his place.'

The year of that funeral is one of the most important dates in the Old Testament, and this chapter does not tell us so.

A nation had known one king for fifty-two years. Everybody alive under the age of fifty had never known another. And in the year the throne finally emptied, a young man in Jerusalem was given a look at a different one: in the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple (Isa. 6:1).

The throne that had seemed permanent was vacant, and Isaiah was shown the one that is not.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The north comes apart in twenty-four verses. Zechariah reigns six months and is struck down in public (vv. 8-10) — this was the promise of the LORD that he gave to Jehu, Your sons shall sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation. And so it came to pass (v. 12). Shallum lasts one month (vv. 13-15). Menahem takes the throne and sacks an Israelite town that would not open to him, and he ripped open all the women in it who were pregnant (v. 16); he buys off Assyria with a thousand talents raised from sixty thousand men (vv. 19-20). His son Pekahiah gets two years and is murdered in the citadel (vv. 23-25). Pekah gets twenty and loses Galilee: Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came and captured... all the land of Naphtali, and he carried the people captive to Assyria (v. 29). Then Hoshea murders him (vv. 30-31).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 12 is the quiet horror of the section. God's reward to Jehu is fulfilled and used up in the same sentence — four generations exactly, no more, and the fourth is a six-month king assassinated in front of the people. A promise kept to the letter is not necessarily a promise you would want.
verseByVerse.examples: And what Menahem does at Tiphsah is precisely what Elisha wept over in Damascus, when he was shown that Hazael would rip open their pregnant women (8:12). The atrocity the prophet could not speak of without crying is now being done to Israelite towns by an Israelite king.

verseByVerse.quote: In the thirty-eighth year of Azariah king of Judah, Zechariah the son of Jeroboam reigned over Israel in Samaria six months. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as his fathers had done. He did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin. Shallum the son of Jabesh conspired against him and struck him down at Ibleam and put him to death and reigned in his place. Now the rest of the deeds of Zechariah, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. (This was the promise of the LORD that he gave to Jehu, "Your sons shall sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation." And so it came to pass.) Shallum the son of Jabesh began to reign in the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah king of Judah, and he reigned one month in Samaria. Then Menahem the son of Gadi came up from Tirzah and came to Samaria, and he struck down Shallum the son of Jabesh in Samaria and put him to death and reigned in his place. Now the rest of the deeds of Shallum, and the conspiracy that he made, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. At that time Menahem sacked Tiphsah and all who were in it and its territory from Tirzah on, because they did not open it to him. Therefore he sacked it, and he ripped open all the women in it who were pregnant. In the thirty-ninth year of Azariah king of Judah, Menahem the son of Gadi began to reign over Israel, and he reigned ten years in Samaria. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not depart all his days from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin. Pul the king of Assyria came against the land, and Menahem gave Pul a thousand talents of silver, that he might help him to confirm his hold on the royal power. Menahem exacted the money from Israel, that is, from all the wealthy men, fifty shekels of silver from every man, to give to the king of Assyria. So the king of Assyria turned back and did not stay there in the land. Now the rest of the deeds of Menahem and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? And Menahem slept with his fathers, and Pekahiah his son reigned in his place. In the fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah, Pekahiah the son of Menahem began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned two years. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin. And Pekah the son of Remaliah, his captain, conspired against him with fifty men of the people of Gilead, and struck him down in Samaria, in the citadel of the king's house with Argob and Arieh; he put him to death and reigned in his place. Now the rest of the deeds of Pekahiah and all that he did, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. In the fifty-second year of Azariah king of Judah, Pekah the son of Remaliah began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned twenty years. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin. In the days of Pekah king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came and captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and he carried the people captive to Assyria. Then Hoshea the son of Elah made a conspiracy against Pekah the son of Remaliah and struck him down and put him to death and reigned in his place, in the twentieth year of Jotham the son of Uzziah. Now the rest of the acts of Pekah and all that he did, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the thirty-eighth year of Azariah king of Judah, Zechariah the son of Jeroboam reigned over Israel in Samaria six months.'

'And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as his fathers had done. He did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin.'

'Shallum the son of Jabesh conspired against him and struck him down at Ibleam and put him to death and reigned in his place.'

Six months, and killed in public.

Read the next twenty verses as a single collapsing structure rather than as a list. Five kings will take the throne of Israel in this chapter. Four of them will be murdered, and three of the murderers will take the crown off the body.

'Now the rest of the deeds of Zechariah, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.'

'(This was the promise of the LORD that he gave to Jehu, "Your sons shall sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation." And so it came to pass.)'

The writer puts it in brackets, which is his way of asking you to stop.

God had told Jehu, after the purge, your sons of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel (10:30). Jehoahaz, Joash, Jeroboam, and now Zechariah — count them, and Zechariah is the fourth.

The promise is kept exactly, and it is used up in the same sentence in which it is fulfilled. The reward ran to the generation specified and stopped there, and the fourth generation got six months and a public assassination.

A word from God kept to the letter is not always a word you would have wanted. Jehu was given four generations because he did what was right in God's eyes in the matter of Ahab's house, and four generations is what he got, and not one day of it was security.

'Shallum the son of Jabesh began to reign in the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah king of Judah, and he reigned one month in Samaria.'

'Then Menahem the son of Gadi came up from Tirzah and came to Samaria, and he struck down Shallum the son of Jabesh in Samaria and put him to death and reigned in his place.'

One month. The man who murdered a king to take a throne held it for four weeks and was murdered on it.

'Now the rest of the deeds of Shallum, and the conspiracy that he made, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.'

'At that time Menahem sacked Tiphsah and all who were in it and its territory from Tirzah on, because they did not open it to him. Therefore he sacked it, and he ripped open all the women in it who were pregnant.'

This is an Israelite king, doing this to an Israelite town, because it would not open its gates to him.

The reader of this book has met that exact sentence before, in a room in Damascus, with a prophet crying. Elisha stared at Hazael until the man was squirming and then wept, and when he was asked why, he said: because I know the evil that you will do to the people of Israel... you will kill their young men with the sword and dash in pieces their little ones and rip open their pregnant women (8:12).

That was the atrocity the prophet could not speak of without breaking down, and it was foretold of a foreign enemy. Here it is being done to Israelites, in Israel, by the king of Israel, over a gate.

The nation has stopped needing Syria.

'In the thirty-ninth year of Azariah king of Judah, Menahem the son of Gadi began to reign over Israel, and he reigned ten years in Samaria.'

'And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not depart all his days from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin.'

'Pul the king of Assyria came against the land, and Menahem gave Pul a thousand talents of silver, that he might help him to confirm his hold on the royal power.'

Here is Assyria, for the first time in this book, and everything from now on runs toward it.

Pul is Tiglath-pileser the third, who took the throne in Nineveh and turned a regional power into an empire with a professional standing army and a policy of mass deportation. He is the beginning of the end for both kingdoms, and he arrives in a subordinate clause.

Consider what Menahem buys with a thousand talents. Not the safety of his people. That he might help him to confirm his hold on the royal power — he is a usurper with a weak claim, and he is paying an emperor to guarantee his own throne.

'Menahem exacted the money from Israel, that is, from all the wealthy men, fifty shekels of silver from every man, to give to the king of Assyria. So the king of Assyria turned back and did not stay there in the land.'

Do the arithmetic the verse invites. A thousand talents is three million shekels; at fifty shekels a head, that is sixty thousand men.

Sixty thousand propertied Israelites were each assessed the price of a slave so that a usurper could pay a foreign emperor to keep him on the throne. And it worked, in the sense that the Assyrians went home, and the country now knew that Samaria would pay.

'Now the rest of the deeds of Menahem and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?'

'And Menahem slept with his fathers, and Pekahiah his son reigned in his place.'

'In the fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah, Pekahiah the son of Menahem began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned two years.'

'And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin.'

'And Pekah the son of Remaliah, his captain, conspired against him with fifty men of the people of Gilead, and struck him down in Samaria, in the citadel of the king's house with Argob and Arieh; he put him to death and reigned in his place.'

His own captain, with fifty men, inside the palace.

'Now the rest of the deeds of Pekahiah and all that he did, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.'

'In the fifty-second year of Azariah king of Judah, Pekah the son of Remaliah began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned twenty years.'

'And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin.'

'In the days of Pekah king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came and captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and he carried the people captive to Assyria.'

This is the first deportation, and it should be marked.

Assyria's method was not merely conquest but removal: take a population off its land, scatter it across the empire, and settle strangers in its place, so that there is no nation left to rebel. Here it begins, and the writer names the towns one after another the way a man reads a casualty list.

Look at which territory goes first. Gilead — Elijah's country, and the Transjordan Hazael had already stripped. And Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali, the whole north.

Now hold that beside a promise made in Jerusalem at almost exactly this moment, because the two belong together and the New Testament puts them together.

Isaiah, prophesying in these years, said this about the very districts that had just been carried away: in the former time he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the latter time he has made glorious the way of the sea, the land beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light (Isa. 9:1-2).

Matthew quotes it, in full, at the exact point where Jesus leaves Nazareth and settles at Capernaum in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali, and begins to preach (Matt. 4:13-16).

The first piece of the promised land to be emptied by an empire is the first piece to see the Messiah. Eight hundred years of contempt — deported, resettled, mixed, despised by Jerusalem as Galilee of the nations — and the light comes up there first, and stays there for most of three years.

'Then Hoshea the son of Elah made a conspiracy against Pekah the son of Remaliah and struck him down and put him to death and reigned in his place, in the twentieth year of Jotham the son of Uzziah.'

'Now the rest of the acts of Pekah and all that he did, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.'

The fourth murder in the chapter, and the last king of Israel takes the throne. Hoshea has nine years of his own and the account of them will end with Samaria gone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–38 — In Those Days the LORD Began to Send
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jotham reigns sixteen years in Jerusalem and does what is right, with the standing exception — nevertheless, the high places were not removed — and builds the upper gate of the house of the LORD (vv. 32-36). Then a single sentence that sets up everything that follows: in those days the LORD began to send Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah against Judah (v. 37). And Ahaz his son reigns in his place (v. 38).
verseByVerse.theology: Note who is doing the sending. Not in those days Syria and Israel attacked Judah, but the LORD began to send them. The two kings marching on Jerusalem are described as dispatched, and the writer says it in passing as though it needed no defence.
verseByVerse.examples: And the word began is the one to feel. This is the opening of the pressure that will run through the next ten chapters and end with both capitals gone. It starts as a border problem in the reign of a good king who built a gate.

verseByVerse.quote: In the second year of Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, Jotham the son of Uzziah, king of Judah, began to reign. He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jerusha the daughter of Zadok. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that his father Uzziah had done. Nevertheless, the high places were not removed. The people still sacrificed and made offerings on the high places. He built the upper gate of the house of the LORD. Now the rest of the acts of Jotham and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? In those days the LORD began to send Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah against Judah. Jotham slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father, and Ahaz his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the second year of Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, Jotham the son of Uzziah, king of Judah, began to reign.'

'He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jerusha the daughter of Zadok.'

'And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that his father Uzziah had done.'

He had been running the country already for years while his father lived in a separate house, so he comes to the throne experienced, and he is a good king by the measure of this book.

'Nevertheless, the high places were not removed. The people still sacrificed and made offerings on the high places. He built the upper gate of the house of the LORD.'

The same exception, and one modest achievement recorded: he built a gate.

There is something quietly moving about the summary of a decent reign. Sixteen years, nothing scandalous, one gate, and the high places left exactly where his father and grandfather left them. Most good men's lives read like that in the ledger, and the writer is not sneering.

'Now the rest of the acts of Jotham and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?'

'In those days the LORD began to send Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah against Judah.'

Read who is doing the sending.

Not in those days Syria and Israel attacked Judah, which is what happened. The LORD began to send them. Two hostile kings marching on Jerusalem are described as dispatched, and the writer puts it in as a piece of ordinary information requiring no defence.

It is the same claim he has made all through these books about arrows drawn at random, armies routed by a sound, and empires arriving on schedule. The politics of the region are not a separate department from the will of God.

The word to feel is began.

Nothing much happens in Jotham's reign. There is a border war starting, of the kind the region had seen a hundred times, in the last years of a competent and unremarkable king. That is what the end of a kingdom looks like when it begins: not a catastrophe but a nuisance on the frontier, filed at the bottom of a good man's obituary.

It runs from here to the last chapter of the book. Rezin and Pekah will besiege Jerusalem in the next chapter and Ahaz will write to Assyria for help, and Assyria will come, and will never leave, and in seven chapters Samaria will be gone and in twenty-five years Judah will be a vassal state on the edge of an empire it invited in.

'Jotham slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father, and Ahaz his son reigned in his place.'

15.theology:
When he was strong (v. 5). Kings gives the affliction and no reason; Chronicles gives the reason, and it is one clause worth carrying: when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction (2 Chron. 26:16). The dangerous season was not weakness or failure but the one that looked like the reward for earlier faithfulness. And the year that reign ended is the year Isaiah was shown a throne that does not empty (Isa. 6:1).

Fulfilled and exhausted (v. 12). Your sons shall sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation. And so it came to pass. Count them and Zechariah is the fourth, and he gets six months and a public assassination. The promise was kept exactly to the generation named and stopped there. A word from God honoured to the letter is not always a word anyone would have wanted.

The horror comes home (v. 16). Elisha stared at Hazael until he squirmed and then wept, and gave as his reason that this man would rip open their pregnant women (8:12). Here an Israelite king does it to an Israelite town for refusing to open a gate. The nation has stopped needing an enemy.

What the money bought (v. 19). Assyria enters the book in a subordinate clause. Menahem's thousand talents are not spent on his people's safety but that he might help him to confirm his hold on the royal power — a usurper paying an emperor to guarantee his own throne, with sixty thousand propertied men assessed fifty shekels each to fund it.

The first to be carried off, the first to see the light (v. 29). Galilee, Naphtali and Gilead are emptied and deported. Isaiah, prophesying in these very years, said of those districts that after the contempt the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light (Isa. 9:1-2) — and Matthew quotes it in full at the moment Jesus settles at Capernaum in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali and begins to preach (Matt. 4:13-16). The first piece of the land an empire emptied is the first piece the Messiah lived in.

The LORD began to send (v. 37). Not Syria attacked Judah. Two hostile kings are described as dispatched, and the writer offers no defence of the claim because he has been making it all along — about arrows drawn at random and armies routed by a noise. And began is the word to feel: the end of a kingdom starts as a border nuisance at the bottom of a decent man's obituary.
15.examples:
Then: Five men held the throne of Israel inside one chapter — six months, one month, ten years, two years, twenty years — and four of them were murdered, three by the man who took the crown off the body.

Now: Two things. First, Uzziah. Fifty-two years, an army, towers, cisterns, engineers and international fame — and the wheels came off in the season of strength, not the season of struggle, over a religious act he was not entitled to perform and could not be told he was not entitled to perform. The prosperity that follows years of faithfulness is the part to watch. Second, verse 37. If you are looking for the moment something in your life began to go wrong, it is rarely the crisis; it is the small recurring difficulty that everybody, including you, filed as normal for that stage of life.

16.text: <sup>1</sup>In the seventeenth year of Pekah the son of Remaliah, Ahaz the son of Jotham, king of Judah, began to reign.<sup>2</sup>Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. And he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD his God, as his father David had done,<sup>3</sup>but he walked in the way of the kings of Israel. He even burned his son as an offering, according to the despicable practices of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel.<sup>4</sup>And he sacrificed and made offerings on the high places and on the hills and under every green tree.<sup>5</sup>Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, came up to wage war on Jerusalem, and they besieged Ahaz but could not conquer him.<sup>6</sup>At that time Rezin the king of Syria recovered Elath for Syria and drove the men of Judah from Elath, and the Edomites came to Elath, where they dwell to this day.<sup>7</sup>So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, saying, "I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me from the hand of the king of Syria and from the hand of the king of Israel, who are attacking me."<sup>8</sup>Ahaz also took the silver and gold that was found in the house of the LORD and in the treasures of the king's house and sent a present to the king of Assyria.<sup>9</sup>And the king of Assyria listened to him. The king of Assyria marched up against Damascus and took it, carrying its people captive to Kir, and he killed Rezin.<sup>10</sup>When King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, he saw the altar that was at Damascus. And King Ahaz sent to Uriah the priest a model of the altar, and its pattern, exact in all its details.<sup>11</sup>And Uriah the priest built the altar; in accordance with all that King Ahaz had sent from Damascus, so Uriah the priest made it, before King Ahaz arrived from Damascus.<sup>12</sup>And when the king came from Damascus, the king viewed the altar. Then the king drew near to the altar and went up on it<sup>13</sup>and burned his burnt offering and his grain offering and poured his drink offering and threw the blood of his peace offerings on the altar.<sup>14</sup>And the bronze altar that was before the LORD he removed from the front of the house, from the place between his altar and the house of the LORD, and put it on the north side of his altar.<sup>15</sup>And King Ahaz commanded Uriah the priest, saying, "On the great altar burn the morning burnt offering and the evening grain offering and the king's burnt offering and his grain offering, with the burnt offering of all the people of the land, and their grain offering and their drink offering. And throw on it all the blood of the burnt offering and all the blood of the sacrifice, but the bronze altar shall be for me to inquire by."<sup>16</sup>Uriah the priest did all this, as King Ahaz commanded.<sup>17</sup>And King Ahaz cut off the frames of the stands and removed the basin from them, and he took down the sea from off the bronze oxen that were under it and put it on a stone pedestal.<sup>18</sup>And the covered way for the Sabbath that had been built inside the house and the outer entrance for the king he caused to go around the house of the LORD, because of the king of Assyria.<sup>19</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Ahaz that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?<sup>20</sup>And Ahaz slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.
16.overview:
Ahaz fails the comparison with David flatly, with no nevertheless attached, and the writer states the worst of it in his third verse: he even burned his son as an offering — the practice for which the nations before Israel had been driven out of that land.

Syria and Israel besiege Jerusalem, and this is the crisis of Isaiah 7, which Kings does not mention. Isaiah met this king out inspecting the water supply, told him the two kings were two smouldering stumps of firebrands, warned him that if you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all, and offered him any sign he liked, in heaven or in the depths. Ahaz refused it with a Bible verse, having already decided to write to Assyria — and was given the sign anyway: the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.

He writes to Nineveh signing himself your servant and your son, empties the temple to pay for it, and gets exactly the deliverance Isaiah had promised him for nothing. Then he visits Damascus, admires the altar, sends home the pattern, and the high priest has a copy built and standing before the king gets home. Solomon's bronze altar is moved off the centre-line to the north side and kept for the king to consult privately. And the last five words of the chapter are and Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — I Am Your Servant and Your Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahaz does not do what is right as his father David had done, walks in the way of the kings of Israel, and even burned his son as an offering, according to the despicable practices of the nations whom the LORD drove out (vv. 2-3). Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel besiege Jerusalem and cannot take it (v. 5). So Ahaz writes to Assyria: I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me — and strips the temple and the palace to pay for it (vv. 7-8). Tiglath-pileser obliges, takes Damascus, deports its people and kills Rezin (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the crisis of Isaiah 7, and Kings does not mention the prophet at all. Isaiah met this king at the conduit of the upper pool with his son beside him, told him the two kings were two smouldering stumps of firebrands, and said if you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all. He offered him any sign he cared to name, in heaven or in the depths. Ahaz refused it with a piece of piety — I will not put the LORD to the test — having already decided to write to Nineveh.
verseByVerse.examples: And the sign was given anyway, over the top of his refusal: behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel (Isa. 7:14). The greatest promise in the prophets was handed to the worst king in David's line so far, in a week when he had burned his own son and was drafting a letter offering himself to an emperor as a servant and a son.

verseByVerse.quote: In the seventeenth year of Pekah the son of Remaliah, Ahaz the son of Jotham, king of Judah, began to reign. Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. And he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD his God, as his father David had done, but he walked in the way of the kings of Israel. He even burned his son as an offering, according to the despicable practices of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel. And he sacrificed and made offerings on the high places and on the hills and under every green tree. Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, came up to wage war on Jerusalem, and they besieged Ahaz but could not conquer him. At that time Rezin the king of Syria recovered Elath for Syria and drove the men of Judah from Elath, and the Edomites came to Elath, where they dwell to this day. So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, saying, "I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me from the hand of the king of Syria and from the hand of the king of Israel, who are attacking me." Ahaz also took the silver and gold that was found in the house of the LORD and in the treasures of the king's house and sent a present to the king of Assyria. And the king of Assyria listened to him. The king of Assyria marched up against Damascus and took it, carrying its people captive to Kir, and he killed Rezin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the seventeenth year of Pekah the son of Remaliah, Ahaz the son of Jotham, king of Judah, began to reign.'

'Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. And he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD his God, as his father David had done,'

The comparison is with David rather than with his own father, which is how Judah's kings are always measured, and he fails it flatly. There is no nevertheless and no qualification.

'but he walked in the way of the kings of Israel. He even burned his son as an offering, according to the despicable practices of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel.'

Read that sentence and do not move on quickly.

A son of David, on David's throne, in Jerusalem, burned his own child as a sacrifice.

The reader of these books has seen it once before, on a city wall, when the king of Moab took his eldest son and offered him as a burnt offering in front of a besieging army (3:27), and it was presented as the last act of a pagan in despair. Here it is done by the king of the covenant people.

The writer names the precedent exactly: according to the despicable practices of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel. Those nations were expelled from that land for doing this. The law had said so in advance — you shall not give any of your children to offer them to Molech (Lev. 18:21) — and the reason given for the expulsion of the Canaanites was that the land had vomited them out for it.

Judah is now doing the thing that emptied the country for them.

'And he sacrificed and made offerings on the high places and on the hills and under every green tree.'

Every previous good king left the high places standing and the writer noted it as a failure. Ahaz does not leave them alone; he uses them.

'Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, came up to wage war on Jerusalem, and they besieged Ahaz but could not conquer him.'

Here is the crisis, and it is one of the most important moments in the Old Testament, and this chapter tells it in a sentence.

Syria and Israel have made an alliance against Assyria and want Judah in it. Judah will not come, so they march on Jerusalem intending to remove Ahaz and put their own man on the throne. The city holds, but the king is twenty-something, surrounded, and terrified.

Isaiah tells us what happened next, and the reader of Kings has to be told, because it is the greatest thing that ever happened to this king and the writer here does not mention it.

God sent Isaiah out to meet him. He found him at the end of the conduit of the upper pool — out inspecting the water supply, which is what a man does when he is preparing for a siege — and told him to take his son along (Isa. 7:3).

The message was: do not be afraid of these two. They are two smouldering stumps of firebrands — burnt-out sticks, all smoke and no fire; within sixty-five years Ephraim will not be a people at all. And then the sentence that hangs over the whole reign: if you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all (Isa. 7:9).

Then God did something he almost never does. He offered the king a sign — any sign, of his own choosing: ask a sign of the LORD your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven (Isa. 7:11). Name it, and it will be done.

Ahaz refused, and refused with a piece of Scripture: I will not ask, and I will not put the LORD to the test (Isa. 7:12).

It sounds like reverence and it is nothing of the kind. He had already made up his mind. The letter to Assyria was as good as written, and a sign from God would only have complicated a decision he had taken. Piety used to avoid an obligation is not piety, and Isaiah's answer begins hear then, O house of David! Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?

Then the sign was given anyway, over the top of the refusal.

Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel (Isa. 7:14).

Stand still in front of that for a moment.

The single most famous promise in the prophets, the verse Matthew reaches for in his first chapter to explain who has just been born in Bethlehem (Matt. 1:22-23), was given to this man. In this week. To a king who had burned his own son in a fire, who was refusing the help of God with a Bible verse, and whose next act would be to offer himself to a foreign emperor as a servant and a son.

God with us — announced to a man who had gone to considerable trouble to be without him.

'At that time Rezin the king of Syria recovered Elath for Syria and drove the men of Judah from Elath, and the Edomites came to Elath, where they dwell to this day.'

The port on the Red Sea is lost, and it stays lost.

'So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, saying, "I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me from the hand of the king of Syria and from the hand of the king of Israel, who are attacking me."'

There is the letter, and every word of it is a surrender.

I am your servant and your son. That is the formal language of vassalage — a client king acknowledging an overlord. Judah has never been anybody's vassal. A descendant of David, whose throne was promised by God to stand forever, writes to Nineveh and signs himself as a subject.

Set the sentence beside verse 3. He calls himself the son of the king of Assyria, having put his own son in a fire. He is a man with a great deal to offer and nothing he will not give away, and the one thing he was offered free — a sign of his own choosing, from God — he turned down as too presumptuous to accept.

'Ahaz also took the silver and gold that was found in the house of the LORD and in the treasures of the king's house and sent a present to the king of Assyria.'

The temple is emptied again. That is the fourth time in a few chapters — Joash to Hazael, Jehoash of Israel carrying it off after Beth-shemesh, and now this.

'And the king of Assyria listened to him. The king of Assyria marched up against Damascus and took it, carrying its people captive to Kir, and he killed Rezin.'

It worked.

Damascus falls, its population is deported, Rezin is executed, and the coalition that was besieging Jerusalem is finished. Ahaz got exactly what he paid for, and Isaiah had told him beforehand that those two kings were burnt-out sticks who would come to nothing on their own.

The rescue he bought was a rescue he had already been promised for nothing. And what he actually purchased, along with it, was an empire's permanent interest in the road to Egypt, which runs past Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — A Model of the Altar, Exact in All Its Details
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahaz goes to Damascus to pay homage to his new master, sees the altar there, and sends home a model of the altar, and its pattern, exact in all its details (v. 10). And Uriah the priest built the altar; in accordance with all that King Ahaz had sent from Damascus, so Uriah the priest made it, before King Ahaz arrived (v. 11). The king inspects it and offers on it (vv. 12-13). Solomon's bronze altar is shifted off the centre-line to the north side (v. 14), the new altar takes all the public sacrifices, and the old one is kept back for the king's private use: the bronze altar shall be for me to inquire by (v. 15). Uriah the priest did all this, as King Ahaz commanded (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: The speed is the accusation. The pattern arrives from Damascus and the high priest of Israel has the thing built and standing before the king is home, so that there is something to show him when he walks in. Not one word of hesitation is recorded, then or afterwards.
verseByVerse.examples: And notice that the bronze altar is not destroyed. Solomon's altar, the one Solomon knelt in front of with his hands spread to heaven, is simply moved out of the middle and left standing at the side. That is almost always how it goes. The old thing is not denied, argued with, or removed; the new thing is placed in the centre and the old one keeps its place on the north wall, available, and not used for anything that matters.

verseByVerse.quote: When King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, he saw the altar that was at Damascus. And King Ahaz sent to Uriah the priest a model of the altar, and its pattern, exact in all its details. And Uriah the priest built the altar; in accordance with all that King Ahaz had sent from Damascus, so Uriah the priest made it, before King Ahaz arrived from Damascus. And when the king came from Damascus, the king viewed the altar. Then the king drew near to the altar and went up on it and burned his burnt offering and his grain offering and poured his drink offering and threw the blood of his peace offerings on the altar. And the bronze altar that was before the LORD he removed from the front of the house, from the place between his altar and the house of the LORD, and put it on the north side of his altar. And King Ahaz commanded Uriah the priest, saying, "On the great altar burn the morning burnt offering and the evening grain offering and the king's burnt offering and his grain offering, with the burnt offering of all the people of the land, and their grain offering and their drink offering. And throw on it all the blood of the burnt offering and all the blood of the sacrifice, but the bronze altar shall be for me to inquire by." Uriah the priest did all this, as King Ahaz commanded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, he saw the altar that was at Damascus. And King Ahaz sent to Uriah the priest a model of the altar, and its pattern, exact in all its details.'

He goes north to pay his respects to his new master in a city that has just been destroyed and emptied, and while he is there he admires the local altar.

Note the care he takes. A model, and the pattern, and exact in all its details. He has it measured and drawn and sent to Jerusalem by courier, and he does it before he leaves.

That word pattern has a history in the Old Testament. God showed Moses the pattern of the tabernacle on the mountain and told him to make everything after it (Ex. 25:9, 40); David gave Solomon the plan of the temple, which he had received in writing from the hand of the LORD (1 Chron. 28:19). Israel's furniture had always been made to a pattern, and the pattern had always come down.

This one came from Damascus.

'And Uriah the priest built the altar; in accordance with all that King Ahaz had sent from Damascus, so Uriah the priest made it, before King Ahaz arrived from Damascus.'

The high priest is the villain of this paragraph, and the writer convicts him with a timetable.

Before King Ahaz arrived. The instructions came by messenger; the king was still travelling; and Uriah had the altar designed, built and standing in the courtyard of the house of the LORD before his master got home, so that there would be something to show him at the gate.

Nobody made him hurry. There is no threat in the letter, no deadline recorded, no soldiers at his door. He was not asked to be quick and he was quick, which is the tell.

Not one word from him is recorded, here or anywhere. Isaiah names a Uriah as one of his own reliable witnesses (Isa. 8:2), which is very probably this man — so he was well-regarded and trusted by the prophet, and when the pattern of a Syrian altar came through the door he built it without a syllable of protest.

'And when the king came from Damascus, the king viewed the altar. Then the king drew near to the altar and went up on it'

'and burned his burnt offering and his grain offering and poured his drink offering and threw the blood of his peace offerings on the altar.'

He inspects it, approves it, and then conducts the service himself — burnt offering, grain offering, drink offering, blood of the peace offerings, the full round, on an altar copied from a conquered pagan capital, by a king who is not a priest.

His great-grandfather Uzziah was struck with leprosy in that courtyard for taking a censer. Nothing happens to Ahaz at all.

'And the bronze altar that was before the LORD he removed from the front of the house, from the place between his altar and the house of the LORD, and put it on the north side of his altar.'

Here is the sentence to take away from the chapter.

The bronze altar is Solomon's — the altar of the dedication, the one Solomon stood in front of and then knelt before with his hands spread out to heaven while fire came down and the glory filled the house. It has stood in the middle of that courtyard for two hundred and fifty years.

Ahaz does not smash it. He does not burn it, melt it down, or denounce it. He moves it to the north side, out of the middle, and puts his own altar where it used to stand.

That is almost always how it happens. Very few people in a church or a life ever repudiate the old thing. It is not argued with and not thrown out; it is quietly shifted off the centre-line, left standing where everybody can see it is still there, and something else is put in the middle where the traffic goes.

Note also the writer's phrasing. He calls the new one his altar — Ahaz's — twice in two verses, and the old one the bronze altar that was before the LORD. He is not confused about whose is whose.

'And King Ahaz commanded Uriah the priest, saying, "On the great altar burn the morning burnt offering and the evening grain offering and the king's burnt offering and his grain offering, with the burnt offering of all the people of the land, and their grain offering and their drink offering. And throw on it all the blood of the burnt offering and all the blood of the sacrifice, but the bronze altar shall be for me to inquire by."'

Everything moves across. The morning offering, the evening offering, the king's own, and the offerings of the whole population, with all the blood — the entire public worship of Judah is transferred to a copy of a Syrian altar, by royal memorandum.

Then the last clause, which is stranger than all the rest: but the bronze altar shall be for me to inquire by.

He keeps Solomon's altar for himself, as an instrument for seeking guidance — for divination of some kind. So the old altar is not discarded after all; it is demoted from the place where God is worshipped by a nation to a private device the king uses when he wants to know something.

That is the exact fate of God in a great many lives. Not denied, and not removed from the premises — relocated to the north side, and retained for consultation.

'Uriah the priest did all this, as King Ahaz commanded.'

Seven words, and they are the epitaph of a priesthood.

He did all this. Everything on the list, exactly as instructed, with no note of an objection anywhere in the record. The office existed to guard precisely this, and the man holding it did the paperwork.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–20 — Because of the King of Assyria
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The dismantling continues: King Ahaz cut off the frames of the stands and removed the basin from them, and he took down the sea from off the bronze oxen that were under it and put it on a stone pedestal (v. 17). And the covered way for the Sabbath and the king's own outer entrance to the temple are rerouted — because of the king of Assyria (v. 18). Then the formula, and one last clause: and Hezekiah his son reigned in his place (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything Solomon made is being cut up for the metal or rearranged for a foreigner's convenience, and the writer gives the reason in five words at the end of verse 18. Not because of a theological conviction, or a reform, or a vision. Because of the king of Assyria. Once you have written I am your servant and your son to somebody, the furniture starts moving on its own.
verseByVerse.examples: And the last five words of the chapter are the turn. This king emptied the temple, replaced its altar with a copy of a pagan one, cut up its furnishings and burned his own child; and his son is Hezekiah, of whom the writer will say that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah, before or after.

verseByVerse.quote: And King Ahaz cut off the frames of the stands and removed the basin from them, and he took down the sea from off the bronze oxen that were under it and put it on a stone pedestal. And the covered way for the Sabbath that had been built inside the house and the outer entrance for the king he caused to go around the house of the LORD, because of the king of Assyria. Now the rest of the acts of Ahaz that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And Ahaz slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And King Ahaz cut off the frames of the stands and removed the basin from them, and he took down the sea from off the bronze oxen that were under it and put it on a stone pedestal.'

Now he starts cutting up the furniture.

The stands and their basins and the great bronze sea on its twelve oxen were made by Hiram of Tyre for Solomon, and the writer of 1 Kings spent the best part of a chapter describing them — the lions and oxen and cherubim on the panels, the wheels, the lily-work on the rim, the sea holding two thousand baths of water on the backs of twelve bronze bulls facing out to the four quarters.

Ahaz cuts the decorated panels off the stands, takes the sea off the oxen, and sets it on a stone block.
