He is stripping metal, almost certainly for tribute, and doing it a piece at a time from the least noticeable end. It is not desecration in a rage. It is a slow disassembly by a man who needs the bronze and has stopped feeling anything about where it came from.

'And the covered way for the Sabbath that had been built inside the house and the outer entrance for the king he caused to go around the house of the LORD, because of the king of Assyria.'

There is the reason, given at the end, in five words.

Because of the king of Assyria.

He rerouted the Sabbath colonnade and moved his own entrance to the temple — the ceremonial way a king of Judah went in to worship — to suit the sensibilities or the demands of a foreign emperor who was not even present.

This is what the letter in verse 7 actually cost. I am your servant and your son was written once, in an emergency, and paid for once out of the treasury. And now the building is being rearranged around a man in Nineveh, years later, without anybody asking.

You do not get to choose how far a surrender goes after you have made it. Ahaz bought a rescue from two burnt-out sticks and is still paying for it in architecture.

'Now the rest of the acts of Ahaz that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?'

'And Ahaz slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.'

He dies in his bed and is buried in the city of David, which is more than he deserved and rather less than the writer of Chronicles allows him — there, they do not bring him into the tombs of the kings (2 Chron. 28:27).

Then the last five words, which change everything.

And Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.

The man who burned one son in a fire had another, and that other son is the king of whom this writer will shortly say that he trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel, so that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah after him, nor among those who were before him (18:5) — who will smash the high places his father used, break down the pillars, and take a threatening letter from the next Assyrian emperor up to the very house his father had rearranged, and spread it out before God.

Nothing in this chapter would let you predict that. A boy grew up in the palace of Ahaz, watching an altar from Damascus take the middle of the courtyard and a brother go into a fire, and he turned out to be the best king Judah ever had.

That is a thing to remember about anybody's children, and about anybody's parents.

16.theology:
Immanuel was given to this man (vv. 5-7; Isa. 7). The single most famous promise in the prophets, the verse Matthew quotes to explain the birth at Bethlehem (Matt. 1:22-23), was spoken to a king who had burned his own child, who refused God's offer of a sign of his own choosing by quoting Scripture at him — I will not put the LORD to the test — and whose letter to Assyria was already drafted. Piety used to avoid an obligation is not piety, and Isaiah said so to his face. God gave the sign over the top of the refusal. God with us, announced to a man taking considerable trouble to be without him.

He burned his son (v. 3), and signed himself a son (v. 7). The one practice named as the reason the previous inhabitants were expelled (Lev. 18:21), done by a king of Judah — and then I am your servant and your son to Tiglath-pileser, which is the formal language of vassalage. He gave away his child, his treasury and his kingdom's independence, and the one thing offered him free he declined as too presumptuous to accept.

The pattern (v. 10). God showed Moses the pattern on the mountain (Ex. 25:9, 40) and David gave Solomon the plan he had received in writing from the hand of the LORD (1 Chron. 28:19). Israel's furniture was always made to a pattern, and the pattern always came down. This one came from Damascus.

Uriah's speed (v. 11). The writer convicts the high priest with a timetable: he had it built before King Ahaz arrived. Nobody threatened him and no deadline is recorded; he was not asked to hurry and he hurried, which is the tell. Not one word of objection from him appears anywhere — and Isaiah had counted a Uriah among his own reliable witnesses (Isa. 8:2).

Moved, not destroyed (v. 14). Solomon's bronze altar — the altar of the dedication, where fire fell and the glory filled the house — is not smashed, denounced or melted down. It is shifted off the centre-line to the north side and the new one put where it stood. That is how it nearly always happens: the old thing is not repudiated but relocated, left visibly present, while something else takes the middle where the traffic goes. And it is kept for me to inquire by (v. 15) — demoted from the worship of a nation to a private instrument for getting information. That is the exact fate of God in a great many lives: not denied, not removed, relocated and retained for consultation.

Because of the king of Assyria (v. 18). Years after the emergency, the Sabbath colonnade and the king's own entrance to the temple are rerouted to suit a man in Nineveh who is not present. Nobody chooses how far a surrender goes once it has been made.
16.examples:
Then: A high priest received a drawing of a pagan altar by courier from a king who was still on the road home, and had it built and standing in the courtyard of the house of the LORD before his master arrived — without being threatened, without a deadline, and without a recorded word of objection.

Now: Three things. First, verse 14. Almost nobody throws the old altar out. It gets moved to the north side and left standing, so that it can be pointed to, while the thing that actually governs the week takes the middle of the courtyard. Ask what is on your centre-line, not what is still on the premises. Second, verse 15, which is worse: the LORD kept on to inquire by — consulted for information when it suits, and not worshipped. Third, Ahaz's piety in Isaiah 7. He turned down help from God by quoting a Bible verse about not testing him, because accepting would have complicated a decision he had already made. That sentence can be used honestly, and it can be used as cover, and the difference is whether you have already decided.

17.text: <sup>1</sup>In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea the son of Elah began to reign in Samaria over Israel, and he reigned nine years.<sup>2</sup>And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, yet not as the kings of Israel who were before him.<sup>3</sup>Against him came up Shalmaneser king of Assyria. And Hoshea became his vassal and paid him tribute.<sup>4</sup>But the king of Assyria found treachery in Hoshea, for he had sent messengers to So, king of Egypt, and offered no tribute to the king of Assyria, as he had done year by year. Therefore the king of Assyria shut him up and bound him in prison.<sup>5</sup>Then the king of Assyria invaded all the land and came to Samaria, and for three years he besieged it.<sup>6</sup>In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria captured Samaria, and he carried the Israelites away to Assyria and placed them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.<sup>7</sup>And this occurred because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them up out of the land of Egypt from under the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and had feared other gods<sup>8</sup>and walked in the customs of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel, and in the customs that the kings of Israel had practiced.<sup>9</sup>And the people of Israel did secretly against the LORD their God things that were not right. They built for themselves high places in all their towns, from watchtower to fortified city.<sup>10</sup>They set up for themselves pillars and Asherim on every high hill and under every green tree,<sup>11</sup>and there they made offerings on all the high places, as the nations did whom the LORD carried away before them. And they did wicked things, provoking the LORD to anger,<sup>12</sup>and they served idols, of which the LORD had said to them, "You shall not do this."<sup>13</sup>Yet the LORD warned Israel and Judah by every prophet and every seer, saying, "Turn from your evil ways and keep my commandments and my statutes, in accordance with all the Law that I commanded your fathers, and that I sent to you by my servants the prophets."<sup>14</sup>But they would not listen, but were stubborn, as their fathers had been, who did not believe in the LORD their God.<sup>15</sup>They despised his statutes and his covenant that he made with their fathers and the warnings that he gave them. They went after false idols and became false, and they followed the nations that were around them, concerning whom the LORD had commanded them that they should not do like them.<sup>16</sup>And they abandoned all the commandments of the LORD their God, and made for themselves metal images of two calves; and they made an Asherah and worshiped all the host of heaven and served Baal.<sup>17</sup>And they burned their sons and their daughters as offerings and used divination and omens and sold themselves to do evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger.<sup>18</sup>Therefore the LORD was very angry with Israel and removed them out of his sight. None was left but the tribe of Judah only.<sup>19</sup>Judah also did not keep the commandments of the LORD their God, but walked in the customs that Israel had introduced.<sup>20</sup>And the LORD rejected all the descendants of Israel and afflicted them and gave them into the hand of plunderers, until he had cast them out of his sight.<sup>21</sup>When he had torn Israel from the house of David, they made Jeroboam the son of Nebat king. And Jeroboam drove Israel from following the LORD and made them commit great sin.<sup>22</sup>The people of Israel walked in all the sins that Jeroboam did. They did not depart from them,<sup>23</sup>until the LORD removed Israel out of his sight, as he had spoken by all his servants the prophets. So Israel was exiled from their own land to Assyria until this day.<sup>24</sup>And the king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the people of Israel. And they took possession of Samaria and lived in its cities.<sup>25</sup>And at the beginning of their dwelling there, they did not fear the LORD. Therefore the LORD sent lions among them, which killed some of them.<sup>26</sup>So the king of Assyria was told, "The nations that you have carried away and placed in the cities of Samaria do not know the law of the god of the land. Therefore he has sent lions among them, and behold, they are killing them, because they do not know the law of the god of the land."<sup>27</sup>Then the king of Assyria commanded, "Send there one of the priests whom you carried away from there, and let him go and dwell there and teach them the law of the god of the land."<sup>28</sup>So one of the priests whom they had carried away from Samaria came and lived in Bethel and taught them how they should fear the LORD.<sup>29</sup>But every nation still made gods of its own and put them in the shrines of the high places that the Samaritans had made, every nation in the cities in which they lived.<sup>30</sup>The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth, the men of Cuth made Nergal, the men of Hamath made Ashima,<sup>31</sup>and the Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak; and the Sepharvites burned their children in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.<sup>32</sup>They also feared the LORD and appointed from among themselves all sorts of people as priests of the high places, who sacrificed for them in the shrines of the high places.<sup>33</sup>So they feared the LORD but also served their own gods, after the manner of the nations from among whom they had been carried away.<sup>34</sup>To this day they do according to the former manner. They do not fear the LORD, and they do not follow the statutes or the rules or the law or the commandment that the LORD commanded the children of Jacob, whom he named Israel.<sup>35</sup>The LORD made a covenant with them and commanded them, "You shall not fear other gods or bow yourselves to them or serve them or sacrifice to them,<sup>36</sup>but you shall fear the LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt with great power and with an outstretched arm. You shall bow yourselves to him, and to him you shall sacrifice.<sup>37</sup>And the statutes and the rules and the law and the commandment that he wrote for you, you shall always be careful to do. You shall not fear other gods,<sup>38</sup>and you shall not forget the covenant that I have made with you. You shall not fear other gods,<sup>39</sup>but you shall fear the LORD your God, and he will deliver you out of the hand of all your enemies."<sup>40</sup>However, they would not listen, but they did according to their former manner.<sup>41</sup>So these nations feared the LORD and also served their carved images. Their children did likewise, and their children's children—as their fathers did, so they do to this day.
17.overview:
Samaria holds out three years and falls, and ten tribes are taken five hundred miles east and scattered so thoroughly that they never reassemble. The king it happens under is the least bad king Israel ever had — which is the writer's way of saying that what was being settled had been accumulating for two centuries and was never a verdict on whoever was on the throne.

Then the historian stops. In two long books he has almost never explained himself; here he puts the narrative down and preaches for seventeen verses. The charge is measured against the exodus, the practices are the ones the previous tenants were evicted for, and against it all stands verse 13: the LORD warned Israel and Judah by every prophet and every seer — two hundred years of men who said the same short sentence and were mocked, hunted and imprisoned for it. The verdict underneath is unbelief, and the sharpest line is verse 15: they went after false idols and became false. And in the middle of the indictment, one sentence turns on the reader: Judah also.

The land is refilled with five deported populations who conclude that they must learn the procedures of the local god, and are sent a priest of the calf cult to teach them, at Bethel. What they settle into is the arrangement the previous tenants were removed for: they feared the LORD but also served their own gods, and their children after them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — For Three Years He Besieged It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hoshea reigns nine years and does evil yet not as the kings of Israel who were before him (v. 2). He becomes an Assyrian vassal, then stops paying and opens negotiations with Egypt, and is arrested (vv. 3-4). Shalmaneser invades, and Samaria holds out for three years (v. 5). Then: in the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria captured Samaria, and he carried the Israelites away to Assyria and placed them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The last king of Israel is the least bad of them, and the writer says so. The end did not come in the worst reign — not under Ahab, not under Jeroboam, not in the chapter with five kings and four murders. It came under a man who was an improvement, because what was being settled had been accumulating for two hundred years and was never about the individual at the top.
verseByVerse.examples: And with one verse a kingdom disappears. Ten of the twelve tribes, two centuries of history, a capital, an army, a state religion and a population — taken off the map and resettled across an empire, and they do not come back. Assyrian records of the campaign put the number deported from Samaria at twenty-seven thousand.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea the son of Elah began to reign in Samaria over Israel, and he reigned nine years. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, yet not as the kings of Israel who were before him. Against him came up Shalmaneser king of Assyria. And Hoshea became his vassal and paid him tribute. But the king of Assyria found treachery in Hoshea, for he had sent messengers to So, king of Egypt, and offered no tribute to the king of Assyria, as he had done year by year. Therefore the king of Assyria shut him up and bound him in prison. Then the king of Assyria invaded all the land and came to Samaria, and for three years he besieged it. In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria captured Samaria, and he carried the Israelites away to Assyria and placed them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea the son of Elah began to reign in Samaria over Israel, and he reigned nine years.'

'And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, yet not as the kings of Israel who were before him.'

Stop on the second half of that verse, because it is not what anybody expects at this point.

The last king of Israel was the least bad of them.

Nineteen kings, nine dynasties, a chapter with five kings and four murders in it, a king who set up a temple to Baal in the capital and a queen who had prophets killed by policy — and the reign in which the kingdom is destroyed belongs to a man the writer explicitly grades above his predecessors.

Take the point, because it governs how the rest of the chapter should be read. The end did not come because Hoshea was uniquely wicked. What was being settled had been accumulating for two centuries, and it was never a verdict on whoever happened to be on the throne when the bill was presented.

People generally expect judgment to fall at the worst moment, on the worst person. It usually falls later than that, on somebody who is doing rather better than average, because it was never about him.

'Against him came up Shalmaneser king of Assyria. And Hoshea became his vassal and paid him tribute.'

'But the king of Assyria found treachery in Hoshea, for he had sent messengers to So, king of Egypt, and offered no tribute to the king of Assyria, as he had done year by year. Therefore the king of Assyria shut him up and bound him in prison.'

He stops paying and writes to Egypt.

It is precisely the manoeuvre Ahaz performed in the last chapter, in the other direction — a small king trying to find a large one who will solve his problem for him. Ahaz wrote to Assyria to get free of Syria and Israel; Hoshea writes to Egypt to get free of Assyria; and the prophets of these years spent their breath saying that neither would work. Isaiah called Egypt a broken reed of a staff, which will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it (Isa. 36:6).

Nothing comes from Egypt. What comes is the Assyrian army, and the king is in prison before the siege begins, so that the city holds out for three years without a king in it at all.

'Then the king of Assyria invaded all the land and came to Samaria, and for three years he besieged it.'

Three years.

Omri chose that hill well — Samaria sits on an isolated summit with steep sides, and it took the greatest military power in the world three years to get into it. The reader has seen what a siege does to that city already, in the chapter with the donkey's head and the two women on the wall, and that one lasted months.

Nobody should picture this as a quick collapse. It was three years of the thing the covenant had warned about in detail, in a walled town with no king.

'In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria captured Samaria, and he carried the Israelites away to Assyria and placed them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.'

One verse, and a nation is gone.

Read the place names slowly, because the point of them is the distance. Halah and the Habor are in upper Mesopotamia, five hundred miles away. The cities of the Medes are further still, out east towards modern Iran. This was Assyrian policy and it was designed with care: do not merely conquer a people, take them off their land and scatter them in small groups across the empire so far apart that they cannot combine, cannot go home, and within two generations cannot remember. Then move strangers in behind them.

Ten of the twelve tribes of Israel went out of that gate. The kingdom that began when Jeroboam gathered the northern tribes at Shechem and said behold your gods, O Israel lasted two hundred and eight years, and this is the end of it. Sargon's own inscription claims twenty-seven thousand two hundred and ninety people deported from Samaria.

They do not come back. The writer will say so at the end of his sermon in the flattest words available: so Israel was exiled from their own land to Assyria until this day (v. 23).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Here the historian stops. And this occurred because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them up out of the land of Egypt (v. 7) — and for seventeen verses he sets out the case: high places from watchtower to fortified city, pillars and Asherim on every hill, the two calves, the host of heaven, Baal, divination, and children burned (vv. 9-17). Against it stands verse 13: yet the LORD warned Israel and Judah by every prophet and every seer, with the same message every time. But they would not listen, but were stubborn (v. 14). Then judgment — and, in the middle of it, a sentence aimed at the reader: Judah also did not keep the commandments of the LORD their God (v. 19). It closes where the kingdom began, with Jeroboam and the calves (vv. 21-23).
verseByVerse.theology: In two long books this writer has almost never explained himself. He records reigns, quotes oracles, notes fulfilments, and lets the pattern do the arguing. This is the one place he puts the narrative down and tells you what the whole thing has been about, and it is the longest continuous piece of interpretation in either book.
verseByVerse.examples: And verse 15 is the sentence to carry away: they went after false idols and became false. The Hebrew word in both halves is the same — hevel, vapour, breath, the word Ecclesiastes uses for everything under the sun. They pursued emptiness and turned into it. Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Ps. 115:8).

verseByVerse.quote: And this occurred because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them up out of the land of Egypt from under the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and had feared other gods and walked in the customs of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel, and in the customs that the kings of Israel had practiced. And the people of Israel did secretly against the LORD their God things that were not right. They built for themselves high places in all their towns, from watchtower to fortified city. They set up for themselves pillars and Asherim on every high hill and under every green tree, and there they made offerings on all the high places, as the nations did whom the LORD carried away before them. And they did wicked things, provoking the LORD to anger, and they served idols, of which the LORD had said to them, "You shall not do this." Yet the LORD warned Israel and Judah by every prophet and every seer, saying, "Turn from your evil ways and keep my commandments and my statutes, in accordance with all the Law that I commanded your fathers, and that I sent to you by my servants the prophets." But they would not listen, but were stubborn, as their fathers had been, who did not believe in the LORD their God. They despised his statutes and his covenant that he made with their fathers and the warnings that he gave them. They went after false idols and became false, and they followed the nations that were around them, concerning whom the LORD had commanded them that they should not do like them. And they abandoned all the commandments of the LORD their God, and made for themselves metal images of two calves; and they made an Asherah and worshiped all the host of heaven and served Baal. And they burned their sons and their daughters as offerings and used divination and omens and sold themselves to do evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger. Therefore the LORD was very angry with Israel and removed them out of his sight. None was left but the tribe of Judah only. Judah also did not keep the commandments of the LORD their God, but walked in the customs that Israel had introduced. And the LORD rejected all the descendants of Israel and afflicted them and gave them into the hand of plunderers, until he had cast them out of his sight. When he had torn Israel from the house of David, they made Jeroboam the son of Nebat king. And Jeroboam drove Israel from following the LORD and made them commit great sin. The people of Israel walked in all the sins that Jeroboam did. They did not depart from them, until the LORD removed Israel out of his sight, as he had spoken by all his servants the prophets. So Israel was exiled from their own land to Assyria until this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And this occurred because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them up out of the land of Egypt from under the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and had feared other gods'

Here the historian stops writing history.

Understand how unusual this is. Across two long books he has recorded reign after reign with almost no comment — a formula, a verdict, a note about the high places, a reference to another set of records. He quotes prophets and reports fulfilments and lets the pattern make the argument. He hardly ever explains.

Now, at the moment the northern kingdom disappears, he puts the narrative down and preaches for seventeen verses. This is the longest piece of continuous interpretation in Kings and it is the place where the writer tells you what the whole thing has been about.

Look at how he begins the indictment. Not with the calves and not with Baal. With the exodus.

The LORD their God, who had brought them up out of the land of Egypt from under the hand of Pharaoh.

The sin is measured against the rescue. That is the shape of every commandment God ever gave this people — the Ten Commandments themselves open I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, and only then you shall have no other gods before me (Ex. 20:2-3). The claim was never abstract authority. It was the claim of a rescuer on the rescued.

'and walked in the customs of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel, and in the customs that the kings of Israel had practiced.'

They took up the practices of the people who had been evicted from that land for those practices.

That is the charge the writer keeps returning to, and it has a terrible logic. The land was not given to Israel because Israel was better; it was taken from the Canaanites because of what they did in it, and Israel was told plainly that the same land would not tolerate the same behaviour from them either. They did it anyway, and the land did what it had done before.

'And the people of Israel did secretly against the LORD their God things that were not right. They built for themselves high places in all their towns, from watchtower to fortified city.'

From watchtower to fortified city is an idiom for the whole range of settlement — from a lookout hut in a field with two men in it to the largest walled town. It means everywhere. There was not a place in the country too small to have one.

And the word behind secretly suggests things covered over, done quietly. Some of this was public and state-sponsored — the calves were royal policy — and a great deal of it was not. It was ordinary people, in ordinary villages, building small shrines nobody was going to write down. A national apostasy is very rarely a decision announced from a palace. It is a slow accumulation of private arrangements.

'They set up for themselves pillars and Asherim on every high hill and under every green tree,'

On every high hill and under every green tree is a stock phrase, and the prophets use it constantly (Deut. 12:2; Jer. 2:20; 3:6). It describes where Canaanite fertility religion was conducted: on the summits, because height was thought to be nearness, and under the big evergreens, because a tree that stayed green through the dry season was itself the promise the religion was selling.

And it means the worship was in the landscape rather than in a building. You could avoid a temple. You could not avoid the hills and the trees. A man walking to his own field passed three of them, and his children grew up thinking that was what a hill was for.

'and there they made offerings on all the high places, as the nations did whom the LORD carried away before them. And they did wicked things, provoking the LORD to anger,'

And note the phrase attached: provoking the LORD to anger. It is the standing formula of these two books — Jeroboam provoked him, Baasha provoked him, Ahab provoked him more than all who were before him — and it says something the modern reader is often uneasy with, so it is better said plainly.

God is not indifferent to this. The Bible never presents idolatry as a harmless preference or a category error to be corrected with better information. It presents it as an injury done to somebody, by people who owed him everything, and it describes his response in the language of a wounded party rather than of an administrator. The alternative to a God who can be provoked is not a kinder God. It is one who does not care what you do.

'and they served idols, of which the LORD had said to them, "You shall not do this."'

Four words, quoted as if that ought to have been enough. You shall not do this.

'Yet the LORD warned Israel and Judah by every prophet and every seer, saying, "Turn from your evil ways and keep my commandments and my statutes, in accordance with all the Law that I commanded your fathers, and that I sent to you by my servants the prophets."'

This is the mercy inside the indictment, and it deserves a moment.

By every prophet and every seer. The reader of these two books has met them. Ahijah tearing his cloak into twelve pieces for Jeroboam and warning him at the start. The unnamed man of God who cried against the altar at Bethel on the day it was built. Jehu the son of Hanani. Micaiah in a cell on bread and water. Elijah in the throne room, on Carmel, in the vineyard. Elisha for fifty years in Samaria itself, advising kings who were trying to kill him. Jonah. And in the last generation of that kingdom, Amos and Hosea walking its markets.

Two hundred years of them, and the message never varied: turn from your evil ways.

The exile is not God losing patience. It is the end of two centuries of being told, by an unbroken succession of men who were mocked, hunted, imprisoned and killed for saying the same short sentence. Nobody in Samaria could say they had not heard.

'But they would not listen, but were stubborn, as their fathers had been, who did not believe in the LORD their God.'

Now the root, and the writer names it twice.

Stubborn is literally they hardened their neck — the picture is a plough ox that will not bend its head to take the yoke. It is not ignorance and it is not confusion. It is a refusal to put the neck down.

Underneath the stubbornness: who did not believe in the LORD their God. That is the bottom of it. Behind two centuries of high places and pillars and calves is a settled failure to take God at his word — and it is inherited, as their fathers had been, handed down like a family trade.

'They despised his statutes and his covenant that he made with their fathers and the warnings that he gave them. They went after false idols and became false, and they followed the nations that were around them, concerning whom the LORD had commanded them that they should not do like them.'

Here is a sentence that nearly disappears in English, and it carries the whole diagnosis.

They went after false idols and became false.

The Hebrew uses the same word twice. It is hevel — vapour, breath, a puff of air, the thing that is there for a moment and then is not. It is the word Ecclesiastes repeats thirty-eight times for everything under the sun. They went after emptiness, and they turned into emptiness.

That is not a play on words. It is a law of the soul, and the Bible states it in several places. Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Ps. 115:8) — the idols have mouths that do not speak and eyes that do not see, and so, in the end, do their worshippers. Paul puts it as a downward sequence: they exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images, and became futile in their thinking (Rom. 1:21-23).

Nobody is left unchanged by what he gives himself to. Worship is not an opinion held about an object; it is a process that shapes the worshipper into the likeness of the thing worshipped. Give yourself to something with no substance in it and you will not merely be disappointed. You will get thinner.

That is also the hope on the other side of it, and Paul says so: beholding the glory of the Lord, we are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Cor. 3:18). The mechanism does not change. Only the object does.

'And they abandoned all the commandments of the LORD their God, and made for themselves metal images of two calves; and they made an Asherah and worshiped all the host of heaven and served Baal.'

Watch the list accumulate. Two calves — Jeroboam's, and they were meant to be the LORD under a different image. Then an Asherah, which is a different god. Then the host of heaven, which is astrology. Then Baal.

And all the host of heaven should be named for what it was: the sun, moon and stars, and the reading of them. Deuteronomy had warned about it specifically — beware lest you look up and see the host of heaven and be drawn away and bow down to them, things God allotted to all the peoples under the whole heaven (Deut. 4:19). They were given the sky to look at and began to consult it.

Nothing was ever discarded. Each new thing was added to the last, so that by the end the religion of Israel was everything at once, which is another way of saying it was nothing in particular.

'And they burned their sons and their daughters as offerings and used divination and omens and sold themselves to do evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger.'

It ends where it always ends. Children in the fire.

The reader has watched this arrive by stages across two books — a Moabite king doing it on a wall in desperation, then Ahaz doing it in Jerusalem, and now a whole population, sons and daughters both, as a normal religious practice.

Note the phrase sold themselves to do evil. That is not a general expression. It was said of exactly one man before this: there was none who sold himself to do what was evil in the sight of the LORD like Ahab (1 Kgs. 21:20, 25).

The whole nation has grown into the shape of its worst king.

'Therefore the LORD was very angry with Israel and removed them out of his sight. None was left but the tribe of Judah only.'

Take the phrase the writer chooses for the exile, because he uses it three times in six verses and it is not the obvious one.

Removed them out of his sight (v. 18). Cast them out of his sight (v. 20). Removed Israel out of his sight (v. 23).

Not destroyed them, and not punished them. He put them where he would not be looking at them.

Set that against the blessing the priests had been pronouncing over these people since Sinai: the LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace (Num. 6:24-26). Everything Israel had was in the fact that God was looking at them. The worst thing that could be said of a nation is what is said here in four words.

And it is what they had asked for. Two centuries of preferring gods with no eyes ended in the God with eyes turning his away.

'Judah also did not keep the commandments of the LORD their God, but walked in the customs that Israel had introduced.'

There is the turn, and it is aimed straight at the reader.

He has spent twelve verses building an airtight case against the north, and the sentence a man in Jerusalem is waiting for is the one that begins but Judah. Instead he gets Judah also.

This book was written for people in the south, and quite possibly for people already in Babylon looking back. The writer will not let them read the fall of Samaria as news from abroad, or as a morality tale about somebody else's ancestors. He puts the same charge on them in one line, in the middle of the indictment, and moves on without softening it.

'And the LORD rejected all the descendants of Israel and afflicted them and gave them into the hand of plunderers, until he had cast them out of his sight.'

All the descendants of Israel — not the ten tribes only. The reader in Judah is inside that sentence.

'When he had torn Israel from the house of David, they made Jeroboam the son of Nebat king. And Jeroboam drove Israel from following the LORD and made them commit great sin.'

'The people of Israel walked in all the sins that Jeroboam did. They did not depart from them,'

'until the LORD removed Israel out of his sight, as he had spoken by all his servants the prophets. So Israel was exiled from their own land to Assyria until this day.'

The sermon ends where the kingdom started.

Two centuries ago a competent man was handed ten tribes by God through a prophet, and was afraid that if his people kept going up to Jerusalem to worship he would lose them. So he made two calves and put one at each end of his country and said behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt (1 Kgs. 12:28). It was a political solution to a religious problem, and it worked perfectly.

Every single king of Israel after him is measured by it. The formula the reader has now seen nineteen times — he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin — is the writer's way of saying that nothing ever changed at the foundation, whatever changed on top of it. Jehu tore down the house of Baal and left the calves. So did everybody else.

Then as he had spoken by all his servants the prophets. It happened exactly as it had been said it would, by men nobody listened to, over two hundred years.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–41 — They Feared the LORD but Also Served Their Own Gods
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The empire refills the land with people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim (v. 24). Lions kill some of them, and the report goes to the king that the settlers do not know the law of the god of the land — so a deported Israelite priest is sent back to Bethel to teach them (vv. 25-28). It makes no difference: every nation goes on making its own gods and setting them in the old shrines, and the Sepharvites go on burning their children (vv. 29-31). So they feared the LORD but also served their own gods (v. 33). The covenant is restated — you shall not fear other gods, four times over (vv. 35-39) — and the chapter ends where it began: as their fathers did, so they do to this day (v. 41).
verseByVerse.theology: The arrangement the new population settles into is exactly the one the old population was deported for. They add the God of the land to the gods they brought, keep both, and pass it to their children. That is what Elijah stood on Carmel and called limping between two opinions, and it is now a settled national religion with its own clergy.
verseByVerse.examples: And the irony of verse 28 is complete. The priest sent to teach true religion is a priest of the calf cult that caused the exile, and he is stationed at Bethel, which is where the calf stood. The empire asked for an expert in the local god and got one.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the people of Israel. And they took possession of Samaria and lived in its cities. And at the beginning of their dwelling there, they did not fear the LORD. Therefore the LORD sent lions among them, which killed some of them. So the king of Assyria was told, "The nations that you have carried away and placed in the cities of Samaria do not know the law of the god of the land. Therefore he has sent lions among them, and behold, they are killing them, because they do not know the law of the god of the land." Then the king of Assyria commanded, "Send there one of the priests whom you carried away from there, and let him go and dwell there and teach them the law of the god of the land." So one of the priests whom they had carried away from Samaria came and lived in Bethel and taught them how they should fear the LORD. But every nation still made gods of its own and put them in the shrines of the high places that the Samaritans had made, every nation in the cities in which they lived. The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth, the men of Cuth made Nergal, the men of Hamath made Ashima, and the Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak; and the Sepharvites burned their children in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim. They also feared the LORD and appointed from among themselves all sorts of people as priests of the high places, who sacrificed for them in the shrines of the high places. So they feared the LORD but also served their own gods, after the manner of the nations from among whom they had been carried away. To this day they do according to the former manner. They do not fear the LORD, and they do not follow the statutes or the rules or the law or the commandment that the LORD commanded the children of Jacob, whom he named Israel. The LORD made a covenant with them and commanded them, "You shall not fear other gods or bow yourselves to them or serve them or sacrifice to them, but you shall fear the LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt with great power and with an outstretched arm. You shall bow yourselves to him, and to him you shall sacrifice. And the statutes and the rules and the law and the commandment that he wrote for you, you shall always be careful to do. You shall not fear other gods, and you shall not forget the covenant that I have made with you. You shall not fear other gods, but you shall fear the LORD your God, and he will deliver you out of the hand of all your enemies." However, they would not listen, but they did according to their former manner. So these nations feared the LORD and also served their carved images. Their children did likewise, and their children's children—as their fathers did, so they do to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the people of Israel. And they took possession of Samaria and lived in its cities.'

The other half of the policy. Take a people off their land, and move other people onto it — five different populations from five different places, deported from their own homes for the same reason, mixed together so that none of them has a nation to reassemble.

'And at the beginning of their dwelling there, they did not fear the LORD. Therefore the LORD sent lions among them, which killed some of them.'

The lions are the one point in this whole section where God does something, and it should not be read only as a threat.

Here is a population that has just been deported from five different countries, dumped in a ruined province, and left to get on with it. Nobody has told them anything. And the God of that land does the one thing that will make a people of that age ask a religious question — and they ask it immediately, and correctly identify that they need to know something they do not know, and send for a teacher.

It is a rough mercy and it is a real one. God did not leave the new tenants of his land in ignorance of him; he made himself impossible to ignore within a year of their arrival. What they did with it is the rest of the chapter.

'So the king of Assyria was told, "The nations that you have carried away and placed in the cities of Samaria do not know the law of the god of the land. Therefore he has sent lions among them, and behold, they are killing them, because they do not know the law of the god of the land."'

Read the report to the emperor, because it is a perfect statement of the religion of the ancient world.

The god of the land. Every territory has one; each has his own procedures; move into his country and you must learn the local requirements or there will be trouble. It is exactly what the Syrian staff officers assumed when they decided the LORD was a god of the hills but not of the valleys (1 Kgs. 20:23), and it is the assumption Naaman was still working with when he asked for two mule loads of Israelite soil to take home.

These settlers are not irreligious. They are extremely religious, in the way everybody in that world was religious, and they have correctly identified that something is wrong and are trying to fix it.

What they have not grasped is that the God of that land is not the god of that land.

'Then the king of Assyria commanded, "Send there one of the priests whom you carried away from there, and let him go and dwell there and teach them the law of the god of the land."'

'So one of the priests whom they had carried away from Samaria came and lived in Bethel and taught them how they should fear the LORD.'

The irony here is complete, and the writer does not point at it once.

An emperor asks for an expert in the local religion, and the man who is sent back is a priest of the northern kingdom — which is to say a priest of the calf cult, the very religion this chapter has just spent seventeen verses identifying as the reason the country was emptied. Jeroboam did not use Levites; he appointed priests from among all the people, who were not of the Levites (1 Kgs. 12:31).

He is stationed at Bethel. Of all the towns in Samaria, he is sent to live at the one where the calf stood, to teach a new population how they should fear the LORD.

Nothing about that arrangement could have produced anything good, and the next verse says what it produced.

'But every nation still made gods of its own and put them in the shrines of the high places that the Samaritans had made, every nation in the cities in which they lived.'

And there, in verse 29, is the first time the word Samaritans appears in the Bible.

It arrives as a piece of neutral description — the people of Samaria, whoever they now are — and the reader who knows the Gospels should mark the page, because the whole freight the word carries by the first century is being loaded onto it in this paragraph.

The high places were already built. The new arrivals did not have to construct anything; they simply put their own gods into the shrines the previous tenants had left standing.

'The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth, the men of Cuth made Nergal, the men of Hamath made Ashima,'

'and the Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak; and the Sepharvites burned their children in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.'

Six gods named, and then a seventh sentence that stops the list dead.

The Sepharvites burned their children in the fire.

Verse 17 gave that as one of the reasons Israel was deported. It is being done in the same towns, within a few years, by the people brought in to replace them. The land has changed hands and the practice has not.

'They also feared the LORD and appointed from among themselves all sorts of people as priests of the high places, who sacrificed for them in the shrines of the high places.'

They add the LORD to the collection, and they staff his shrines exactly as Jeroboam did — with all sorts of people, anybody who volunteered.

'So they feared the LORD but also served their own gods, after the manner of the nations from among whom they had been carried away.'

There is the summary, and the writer will repeat it word for word in the last verse of the chapter so that it frames the whole section.

They feared the LORD but also served their own gods.

Now hear what that sentence is, because it is not a description of paganism. It is a description of the thing Elijah stood on a mountain and named. How long will you go limping between two different opinions? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him (1 Kgs. 18:21) — and the people said nothing, because there was nothing to say.

That was the sin of Israel, and it emptied the country. And the population brought in to replace them arrived from five different nations, with no history in the place at all, and settled into precisely the same arrangement inside a generation.

The LORD, and. It is the most natural religion in the world and it is available to anybody.

'To this day they do according to the former manner. They do not fear the LORD, and they do not follow the statutes or the rules or the law or the commandment that the LORD commanded the children of Jacob, whom he named Israel.'

Mark the apparent contradiction and do not smooth it over, because it is the point.

Verse 33 said they feared the LORD. Verse 34 says they do not fear the LORD. Both are true, and the writer means them both.

They did fear him, in the sense that they had him in the building, gave him a shrine, kept his festivals, and would have said so if asked. And they did not fear him at all, because a fear of God held alongside five other gods is not a smaller version of the real thing. It is a different thing entirely.

You cannot have the LORD also. That is the whole of what these two books have been arguing.

'The LORD made a covenant with them and commanded them, "You shall not fear other gods or bow yourselves to them or serve them or sacrifice to them,'

'but you shall fear the LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt with great power and with an outstretched arm. You shall bow yourselves to him, and to him you shall sacrifice.'

'And the statutes and the rules and the law and the commandment that he wrote for you, you shall always be careful to do. You shall not fear other gods,'

'and you shall not forget the covenant that I have made with you. You shall not fear other gods,'

'but you shall fear the LORD your God, and he will deliver you out of the hand of all your enemies."'

Count the repetition. You shall not fear other gods appears four times in five verses.

The writer is not padding. He is doing what a man does when he has explained something a great many times and it has not gone in — he says it again, in the same words, and then again. And the ground he gives is the same ground he gave in verse 7: not because I am powerful, but who brought you out of the land of Egypt with great power and with an outstretched arm.

The claim rests on the rescue, every time.

'However, they would not listen, but they did according to their former manner.'

And look at the verb, because it has been used before in this chapter about somebody else.

Of Israel, in verse 14: but they would not listen, but were stubborn. Of the nations brought in to replace Israel, in verse 40: however, they would not listen.

Two entirely different populations, one with six centuries of covenant history and one with none at all, taught by prophets in the first case and by a single deported priest in the second — and the writer files the identical verdict on both. The problem was never a shortage of information about God, and it was never peculiar to Israel.

'So these nations feared the LORD and also served their carved images. Their children did likewise, and their children's children—as their fathers did, so they do to this day.'

That is the last verse of the chapter, and it closes the frame: the same sentence as verse 33, with three generations added.

Their children did likewise, and their children's children. Whatever else is inherited, this is. A settled arrangement about God, arrived at by adults for practical reasons, becomes the ordinary assumption of a grandchild who never chose it and cannot remember a time when anything else was possible.

One more thing belongs here, because the reader of the New Testament will meet these people again.

The population described in this chapter — the mixed settlers of Samaria, worshipping the LORD and their own gods together — is the origin that the Jews of Jesus' day assigned to the Samaritans. It is why the woman at the well could say our fathers worshiped on this mountain and expect an argument, and why John explains in an aside that Jews have no dealings with Samaritans (John 4:9, 20). The Samaritans themselves told the story differently and traced their own descent otherwise, and historians are more careful about it than the first century was; but this chapter is what the men who would not eat with them had in mind.

That makes what the Lord Jesus did with them very deliberate indeed.

He went through Samaria when he did not have to, sat down at a well, and asked a woman of that people for a drink — and told her that salvation is from the Jews, without pretending the history away, and in the same breath that the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, on neither mountain (John 4:21-23). He made one of them the hero of his most famous story. Of ten lepers healed, the one who came back was a Samaritan.

After the resurrection, when the disciples asked what the plan was, Samaria was named in the second clause of it — Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (Acts 1:8). Philip went down to a city of Samaria and preached, and Luke's summary of what happened there is four words long: there was much joy in that city (Acts 8:8).

The last verse of 2 Kings 17 leaves a people fearing the LORD and serving carved images, and their children after them, and their children's children, to this day. It took seven hundred years, and a man sitting on the edge of a well at noon, to get past also.

17.theology:
The least bad king (v. 2). The end came under a man the writer grades above his predecessors — not under Ahab, not in the chapter with five kings and four murders. Judgment usually falls later than we expect and on somebody doing better than average, because it was never about him.

The one sermon in Kings (vv. 7-23). This writer records and lets the pattern argue; here he explains at length, and it is the longest continuous interpretation in either book. He begins the indictment not with the calves but with the exodus, because that is how every command God gave this people was framed — I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, and only then you shall have no other gods (Ex. 20:2-3). The claim was always the claim of a rescuer on the rescued.

Two hundred years of warning (v. 13). Every prophet and every seer — Ahijah, the man of God at Bethel, Jehu son of Hanani, Micaiah, Elijah, Elisha, Jonah, Amos, Hosea — with one message that never varied. The exile is not impatience; it is the end of two centuries of being told by men who were imprisoned and killed for saying it.

Became false (v. 15). The same Hebrew word twice — hevel, vapour, Ecclesiastes' word. They pursued emptiness and turned into it. Those who make them become like them (Ps. 115:8); they exchanged the glory of God for images and became futile in their thinking (Rom. 1:21-23). Worship is not an opinion held about an object but a process that shapes the worshipper into the likeness of the thing worshipped — which is also the hope, since beholding the glory of the Lord, we are being transformed into the same image (2 Cor. 3:18). The mechanism does not change; only the object does.

Judah also (v. 19). Twelve verses of airtight case against the north, and the sentence a Jerusalem reader is waiting for is but Judah. He gets Judah also, and then all the descendants of Israel in the next verse. This book was written for the south, and it will not let them read the fall of Samaria as news from abroad.

The god of the land (v. 26). The settlers are not irreligious; they are correctly diagnosing a problem in the terms everybody in that world used — every territory has a god with local procedures. What they have not grasped is that the God of that land is not the god of that land. And the expert sent to teach them is a priest of the calf cult, stationed at Bethel.

The LORD, and (vv. 33, 41). The framing sentence, said twice: they feared the LORD but also served their own gods. That is exactly what Elijah called limping between two opinions (1 Kgs. 18:21), now a settled national religion with its own clergy — arrived at within a generation by people who had no history in the place. And verse 34 flatly denies what verse 33 asserts, on purpose: a fear of God held alongside five other gods is not a smaller version of the real thing but a different thing altogether. You cannot have the LORD also, and that is what these two books have been arguing throughout.
17.examples:
Then: Five deported peoples were resettled in an emptied country, found lions in it, worked out that they did not know the local god's requirements, and asked the empire for a teacher — and were sent a priest of the golden calf to live at Bethel and instruct them how to fear the LORD.

Now: Three things. First, verse 15, which is the most personally useful sentence in the chapter. Nobody is left unchanged by what he gives himself to; chase what has no substance and you do not merely end up disappointed, you end up thinner. Take an honest look at what has had your attention for the last year and ask what it has been making you into. Second, verse 19. The chapter is constructed so that a reader settling comfortably into somebody else's indictment gets his own name in the middle of it, and the writer does not soften it or come back to it. Third, also. The sin that emptied a country was not the rejection of God; it was the addition of other things to him, held together, comfortably, for generations. It is still the most natural religion available, and the question to ask is not whether God is in your life but whether anything else is in there beside him on the same terms.

18.text: <sup>1</sup>In the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah the son of Ahaz, king of Judah, began to reign.<sup>2</sup>He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Abi the daughter of Zechariah.<sup>3</sup>And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that David his father had done.<sup>4</sup>He removed the high places and broke the pillars and cut down the Asherah. And he broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for until those days the people of Israel had made offerings to it (it was called Nehushtan).<sup>5</sup>He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel, so that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah after him, nor among those who were before him.<sup>6</sup>For he held fast to the LORD. He did not depart from following him, but kept the commandments that the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>7</sup>And the LORD was with him; wherever he went out, he prospered.
