18.overview:
The son of the man who burned a child and put a Syrian altar in the temple turns out to be the best king Judah ever had. He does what six good kings before him would not: he removes the high places. And he breaks up the bronze serpent — an object God himself had commanded Moses to make, through which God had genuinely healed people, and to which Israel had been burning incense for seven hundred years. He names it Nehushtan, a bit of bronze, and smashes it.

In his sixth year, ninety miles north, Samaria falls; he watched it happen. In his fourteenth, Sennacherib takes every fortified city in Judah, and the king of whom Scripture says there was none like him surrenders: I have done wrong... whatever you impose on me I will bear. He empties the temple treasury and peels the gold off doors he had gilded himself — which is exactly what his father did, for the same reason. And it does not work.

Then an army arrives anyway, and takes up position at the very spot where Isaiah had met Ahaz a generation before. The Rabshakeh's speech is a masterpiece: mostly true, aimed over the negotiators' heads at the men on the wall, and openly designed to stop them trusting God. He offers them their own vines and fig trees with deportation attached in a subordinate clause, and ends by putting the LORD in a list of gods who failed. Nobody answers him a word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — He Broke in Pieces the Bronze Serpent
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahaz's son does what is right according to all that David his father had done (v. 3) — and then does what no good king before him had done: he removed the high places and broke the pillars and cut down the Asherah. And he broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for until those days the people of Israel had made offerings to it (it was called Nehushtan) (v. 4). He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel, so that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah (v. 5); he rebels against Assyria and prospers (vv. 6-8). And in his sixth year, ninety miles north, Samaria falls (vv. 9-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The serpent was not a pagan object. God told Moses to make it, and Israelites bitten in the wilderness looked at it and lived (Num. 21:8-9). Seven hundred years later they were burning incense to it, and the most dangerous thing in the temple was the one piece of it that had genuinely come from God and had genuinely worked.
verseByVerse.examples: And the name he gives it as he breaks it is a shrug — Nehushtan, a bronze thing, a bit of metal. That is the reform in one gesture: not contempt for what God had once done through it, but a refusal to let a relic of real grace go on being treated as a source of it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah the son of Ahaz, king of Judah, began to reign. He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Abi the daughter of Zechariah. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that David his father had done. He removed the high places and broke the pillars and cut down the Asherah. And he broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for until those days the people of Israel had made offerings to it (it was called Nehushtan). He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel, so that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah after him, nor among those who were before him. For he held fast to the LORD. He did not depart from following him, but kept the commandments that the LORD commanded Moses. And the LORD was with him; wherever he went out, he prospered. He rebelled against the king of Assyria and would not serve him. He struck down the Philistines as far as Gaza and its territory, from watchtower to fortified city. In the fourth year of King Hezekiah, which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against Samaria and besieged it, and at the end of three years he took it. In the sixth year of Hezekiah, which was the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel, Samaria was taken. The king of Assyria carried the Israelites away to Assyria and put them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes, because they did not obey the voice of the LORD their God but transgressed his covenant, even all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded. They neither listened nor obeyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah the son of Ahaz, king of Judah, began to reign.'

'He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Abi the daughter of Zechariah.'

'And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that David his father had done.'

Only two kings in the whole of Judah's history get that sentence without qualification, and this is the first of them.

And remember whose son he is. He grew up in the palace of the man who burned one of his own children in a fire, who copied a Syrian altar and put it in the middle of the temple courtyard, and who cut up Solomon's bronze furniture for tribute. Nothing in the previous chapter would have led anybody to expect this.

'He removed the high places and broke the pillars and cut down the Asherah. And he broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for until those days the people of Israel had made offerings to it (it was called Nehushtan).'

Two things in one verse, and the first is remarkable on its own.

He removed the high places. Every good king in this book has been given the same footnote — Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joash, Amaziah, Azariah, Jotham, all of them right in the eyes of the LORD, nevertheless the high places were not taken away. Six times the writer has recorded the same failure. Hezekiah is the first man to do it, and it must have been enormously unpopular, because every village in the country lost the shrine on its own hill.

Then the serpent, which is the most interesting object in the chapter.

Go back seven hundred years. Israel is in the wilderness complaining about the food, and God sends serpents among them, and people are dying — and then he tells Moses to make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live (Num. 21:8-9). Moses makes it of bronze, and it works, exactly as promised.

So this is not a pagan idol smuggled in by a foreign queen. It is a genuine object, made on God's explicit instruction, through which God really did save lives.

And seven centuries later it is still in Jerusalem, and people are burning incense to it.

Hezekiah smashes it, and the name he gives it as he does is a dismissal. Nehushtan plays on the words for serpent and for bronze, and the sense is roughly: it is a bronze thing. A bit of metal.

Sit with that, because it is one of the most useful verses in the Old Testament for anybody who has been in a church for a long time.

The most dangerous objects are not the obviously pagan ones. Nobody in Jerusalem had to be persuaded that an Asherah pole was a problem. The hardest thing in that city to remove was the thing that had genuinely come from God, had genuinely worked, and had a real history of real grace attached to it — and had, over the centuries, quietly stopped being a signpost and started being a destination.

Every long-lived Christian institution collects these. The hymn book, the building, the translation, the shape of the service, the memory of a revival, the ministry God unmistakably used forty years ago. None of them were idols when they were given. They become idols by being kept past their moment and venerated for what they once carried.

And one more thing about this particular object, which is the reason it cuts both ways. The Lord Jesus picked it up: as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life (John 3:14-15).

So the thing Hezekiah broke was, all along, a picture of Christ. It was never wrong to value it. The trouble was that people had begun to look at it instead of through it, and a signpost that people stand and worship in front of has stopped doing the one job it was made for.

'He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel, so that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah after him, nor among those who were before him.'

The reason given for the verdict is one word: he trusted.

Not that he was the most competent, or the most successful, or even the most obedient. The thing that distinguishes him is where he rested his weight — which is precisely the subject the Rabshakeh is going to raise, seven times, from the bottom of the wall.

A reader who is paying attention will notice that almost the same thing is said of Josiah later: before him there was no king like him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart... nor did any like him arise after him (23:25). The honest answer is that the two men are being commended for different things — Hezekiah for trust, Josiah for turning to God with the whole heart according to the law of Moses — and that Hebrew praise of this kind is not a league table. Both statements are true in the terms in which they are made.

'For he held fast to the LORD. He did not depart from following him, but kept the commandments that the LORD commanded Moses.'

'And the LORD was with him; wherever he went out, he prospered. He rebelled against the king of Assyria and would not serve him.'

The verb in verse 6 is worth a moment. He held fast to the LORD is dabaq, to cling, to be glued to — the word used of a man who leaves his father and mother and holds fast to his wife (Gen. 2:24), and the word Moses used over and over for what Israel was to do with God. It is not the language of agreement. It is the language of gripping something and not letting go of it.

He tears up his father's arrangement.

Ahaz had written I am your servant and your son to Nineveh and made Judah a vassal state. Hezekiah stops paying, which is a declaration of independence from the largest empire the world had yet seen, and the writer files it as a good thing between two clauses about God being with him.

'He struck down the Philistines as far as Gaza and its territory, from watchtower to fortified city.'

And he goes on the offensive, which nobody in Judah has done for a long time. His father lost the port at Elath and had Philistine raiders taking towns in the lowlands; Hezekiah pushes the other way, all the way down to Gaza, and the writer uses the same phrase he used of Israel's shrines in the last chapter — from watchtower to fortified city, meaning the whole range of it.

'In the fourth year of King Hezekiah, which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against Samaria and besieged it,'

'and at the end of three years he took it. In the sixth year of Hezekiah, which was the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel, Samaria was taken.'

'The king of Assyria carried the Israelites away to Assyria and put them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes,'

'because they did not obey the voice of the LORD their God but transgressed his covenant, even all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded. They neither listened nor obeyed.'

The writer has told us all this in the previous chapter. He tells it again here, and the reason is the date.

In the sixth year of Hezekiah.

The destruction of the northern kingdom did not happen in some earlier age. It happened ninety miles from Jerusalem while this man was a young king in his twenties, six years into his reign, in the middle of his reform. He watched it. He will have known men who came south as refugees and could describe the three-year siege and what the city looked like at the end of it.

That is the context for everything that follows. When Sennacherib's army arrives outside his walls, Hezekiah is not facing an unknown. He knows exactly what these people do, because he saw them do it to his neighbours inside living memory.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In his fourteenth year Sennacherib takes all the fortified cities of Judah (v. 13), and Hezekiah sends to Lachish: I have done wrong; withdraw from me. Whatever you impose on me I will bear (v. 14). The price is three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold. He hands over everything in the temple treasury and the palace, and then stripped the gold from the doors of the temple of the LORD and from the doorposts that Hezekiah king of Judah had overlaid (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the part that gets left out. The king of whom it was said that there was none like him surrenders, admits fault, and pays — and pays by doing precisely what his father Ahaz did in the same building for the same reason. He even peels the gold off doors he had gilded himself as part of his own reform.
verseByVerse.examples: And it does not work. The tribute is paid in full and the next verse has an Assyrian army outside Jerusalem anyway. Faith is not a possession a man acquires and then owns; the man who will carry a letter up to that temple and spread it out before God in the next chapter is the same man who stripped its doors in this one.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them. And Hezekiah king of Judah sent to the king of Assyria at Lachish, saying, "I have done wrong; withdraw from me. Whatever you impose on me I will bear." And the king of Assyria required of Hezekiah king of Judah three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold. And Hezekiah gave him all the silver that was found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the king's house. At that time Hezekiah stripped the gold from the doors of the temple of the LORD and from the doorposts that Hezekiah king of Judah had overlaid and gave it to the king of Assyria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them.'

All of them.

This is one of the best-attested events in the Old Testament. Sennacherib left his own account of the campaign, and it claims forty-six walled cities of Judah taken, with two hundred thousand people counted as spoil, and Hezekiah himself shut up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage. The Assyrian palace at Nineveh had an entire room panelled with carved reliefs of the siege of Lachish — the ramp, the siege engines, the archers, the prisoners going out with bundles on their backs — and the panels are in the British Museum.

Judah has been reduced to one city.

'And Hezekiah king of Judah sent to the king of Assyria at Lachish, saying, "I have done wrong; withdraw from me. Whatever you impose on me I will bear." And the king of Assyria required of Hezekiah king of Judah three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold.'

Here is the sentence that most accounts of Hezekiah leave out.

I have done wrong; withdraw from me. Whatever you impose on me I will bear.

The king of whom this book says there was none like him among all the kings of Judah capitulates. He apologises to an idolatrous emperor for having stopped paying him, and offers a blank cheque, and asks him to go away.

Nobody should soften that or explain it away. The writer put it in, three verses after the greatest commendation given to any king in these books, and he did it on purpose.

'And Hezekiah gave him all the silver that was found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the king's house.'

'At that time Hezekiah stripped the gold from the doors of the temple of the LORD and from the doorposts that Hezekiah king of Judah had overlaid and gave it to the king of Assyria.'

Read the last clause again, because the writer has gone out of his way to name him twice in one sentence.

The doorposts that Hezekiah king of Judah had overlaid.

He gilded those doors himself. It was part of the reform — the high places came down, the pillars were broken, the Asherah was cut, the serpent was smashed, and the doors of the house of the LORD were overlaid with gold by a young king who meant it.

Now he is on a ladder with a chisel, peeling his own gold off his own doors to send to Nineveh.

His father did exactly this, in exactly this building, for exactly this reason, and the writer used the same vocabulary for it. There is no difference at all between what Ahaz did in chapter 16 and what Hezekiah does here, except that Hezekiah had more to undo.

Two things should be said about it, and the first is uncomfortable.

Faith is not a possession. It is not a quality a man acquires at twenty-five and then owns for the rest of his life, so that everything he does afterwards can be assumed to flow from it. The man in this paragraph and the man in the next chapter who carries a threatening letter up to that same temple and spreads it out before God are the same man, in the same year, in the same crisis. He did the wrong thing first.

The second is that it did not work. He paid what was asked, in full, immediately — and the very next verse has an Assyrian army standing outside Jerusalem. Sennacherib took the silver and sent the Rabshakeh anyway.

That is the ordinary return on buying off a threat, and Hezekiah had a family precedent for it he might have consulted. His father bought Assyria's help once and spent the rest of his reign rearranging the temple to suit them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–37 — On What Do You Rest This Trust of Yours?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three Assyrian officers arrive with an army and take up position by the conduit of the upper pool, which is on the highway to the Washer's Field (v. 17), and the Rabshakeh begins: on what do you rest this trust of yours? (v. 19). Egypt is a broken reed (v. 21); the reform has offended the LORD by pulling down his high places (v. 22); Judah could not find riders for two thousand free horses (v. 23); and is it without the LORD that I have come up against this place to destroy it? (v. 25). Asked to switch to Aramaic, he refuses and shouts louder in Hebrew (vv. 26-28), telling the men on the wall not to let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD, offering them their own vines and fig trees and then deportation in the same breath (vv. 30-32), and finishing with a list of gods who failed — including the one whose people fell at Samaria (vv. 33-35). But the people were silent and answered him not a word (v. 36).
verseByVerse.theology: Count the word. Trust appears seven times in his mouth, and he is asking exactly the right question — on what do you rest this trust of yours? is what any honest man should be able to answer. What he cannot conceive is that there might be an answer other than Egypt, or horses, or nothing.
verseByVerse.examples: And he stands to say it at the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field, which is the precise spot where Isaiah met Ahaz in this boy's father's reign and told him not to be afraid of two smouldering stumps (Isa. 7:3). Ahaz stood on that ground and sent for Assyria. One generation later Assyria is standing on it, shouting at his son.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king of Assyria sent the Tartan, the Rab-saris, and the Rabshakeh with a great army from Lachish to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem. And they went up and came to Jerusalem. When they arrived, they came and stood by the conduit of the upper pool, which is on the highway to the Washer's Field. And when they called for the king, there came out to them Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebnah the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder. And the Rabshakeh said to them, "Say to Hezekiah, 'Thus says the great king, the king of Assyria: On what do you rest this trust of yours? Do you think that mere words are strategy and power for war? In whom do you now trust, that you have rebelled against me? Behold, you are trusting now in Egypt, that broken reed of a staff, which will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it. Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him. But if you say to me, "We trust in the LORD our God," is it not he whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, saying to Judah and to Jerusalem, "You shall worship before this altar in Jerusalem"? Come now, make a wager with my master the king of Assyria: I will give you two thousand horses, if you are able on your part to set riders on them. How then can you repulse a single captain among the least of my master's servants, when you trust in Egypt for chariots and for horsemen? Moreover, is it without the LORD that I have come up against this place to destroy it? The LORD said to me, "Go up against this land and destroy it."'" Then Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, and Shebnah, and Joah, said to the Rabshakeh, "Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, for we understand it. Do not speak to us in the language of Judah within the hearing of the people who are on the wall." But the Rabshakeh said to them, "Has my master sent me to speak these words to your master and to you, and not to the men sitting on the wall, who are doomed with you to eat their own dung and to drink their own urine?" Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out in a loud voice in the language of Judah: "Hear the word of the great king, the king of Assyria! Thus says the king: 'Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you out of my hand. Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD by saying, The LORD will surely deliver us, and this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.' Do not listen to Hezekiah, for thus says the king of Assyria: 'Make your peace with me and come out to me. Then each one of you will eat of his own vine, and each one of his own fig tree, and each one of you will drink the water of his own cistern, until I come and take you away to a land like your own land, a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive trees and honey, that you may live, and not die. And do not listen to Hezekiah when he misleads you by saying, "The LORD will deliver us." Has any of the gods of the nations ever delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria? Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand? Who among all the gods of the lands have delivered their lands out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?'" But the people were silent and answered him not a word, for the king's command was, "Do not answer him." Then Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder, came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and told him the words of the Rabshakeh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the king of Assyria sent the Tartan, the Rab-saris, and the Rabshakeh with a great army from Lachish to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem. And they went up and came to Jerusalem. When they arrived, they came and stood by the conduit of the upper pool, which is on the highway to the Washer's Field.'

Those three words are titles rather than names — the commander-in-chief, the chief officer, and the chief cupbearer, who in the Assyrian system was a senior official and evidently the one who did the talking.

Now look at where they choose to stand, because a reader of Isaiah will sit up.

By the conduit of the upper pool, which is on the highway to the Washer's Field.

That is the exact spot, named in exactly those words, where God sent Isaiah to meet this man's father a generation earlier. Go out to meet Ahaz, you and Shear-jashub your son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, on the highway to the Washer's Field (Isa. 7:3).

Ahaz was standing on that patch of ground, inspecting the water supply while two kings marched on him, when a prophet told him not to be afraid and offered him any sign he liked. He refused it, and wrote to Assyria instead.

Now Assyria is standing on the same patch of ground, shouting at his son.

The writer says nothing about it. He simply gives the location in the same words Isaiah used, and leaves it there for anybody who has been reading both.

'And when they called for the king, there came out to them Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebnah the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder.'

Hezekiah does not come out. He sends his three most senior officials, and one of them is Eliakim son of Hilkiah, of whom Isaiah had prophesied that God would take the office off Shebna and give it to him, and lay the key of the house of David on his shoulder (Isa. 22:20-22) — a verse the risen Christ takes for himself in Revelation 3:7.

'And the Rabshakeh said to them, "Say to Hezekiah, 'Thus says the great king, the king of Assyria: On what do you rest this trust of yours?'

He opens with the right question.

On what do you rest this trust of yours? That is a fair challenge and an honest man ought to be able to answer it. And it is the word the whole chapter turns on: trust occurs seven times in this speech and the one that follows.

The Rabshakeh is not a fool and he is not merely abusive. He has done his homework on Judah's politics, its religion, its manpower and its recent history, and every argument he makes is constructed out of something true.

'Do you think that mere words are strategy and power for war? In whom do you now trust, that you have rebelled against me?'

And note the sneer in verse 20, because the chapter is going to answer it. Do you think that mere words are strategy and power for war? The Hebrew is something like a word of the lips — talk, breath, the cheapest thing there is.

He is a professional soldier and he is contemptuous of speech, and he is standing at the bottom of a wall conducting the entire operation by speech, because the one weapon he actually has today is his mouth. He has no siege train with him. He is trying to talk a city open.

And what will settle it, in the next chapter, is a word — carried by a prophet, about a rumour, into an army that never fires an arrow at that wall.

'Behold, you are trusting now in Egypt, that broken reed of a staff, which will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it. Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him.'

He is right about Egypt.

The image is exact and rather good: a reed looks like a walking staff and will take your weight until the moment you actually need it, and then it splinters and goes through your palm. Isaiah had been saying the same thing to Judah's court for years in almost the same words — woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses (Isa. 31:1).

An enemy at the wall is telling them what their own prophet had told them, and he is telling them the truth.

'But if you say to me, "We trust in the LORD our God," is it not he whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, saying to Judah and to Jerusalem, "You shall worship before this altar in Jerusalem"?'

This is the cleverest thing he says, and it is aimed with precision at the men on the wall rather than at the king.

The argument is: your own God must be furious with Hezekiah. He has spent his reign pulling down shrines — your local shrine, the one on your hill, where your family has always gone — and forcing everybody to worship at one altar in the capital. How can you expect help from a God whose places of worship your king has been demolishing?

To anybody who did not understand the reform, that is a strong argument, and the people it is aimed at are exactly the people who lost something in it. Every man on that wall from a country village had watched the high place near his home come down on royal orders.

It is also the standing tactic against every genuine reform: to accuse it of being irreligious. The man who removes what God did not ask for is always open to the charge of removing religion itself.

'Come now, make a wager with my master the king of Assyria: I will give you two thousand horses, if you are able on your part to set riders on them.'

A soldier's insult, and an accurate one. He is offering to donate two thousand cavalry horses on the condition that Judah can produce two thousand men able to ride them, and he knows perfectly well that they cannot.

'How then can you repulse a single captain among the least of my master's servants, when you trust in Egypt for chariots and for horsemen?'

'Moreover, is it without the LORD that I have come up against this place to destroy it? The LORD said to me, "Go up against this land and destroy it."'"'

Now he claims a commission from Judah's own God, and this is where the passage becomes genuinely uncomfortable, because he is not simply lying.

Isaiah, in these very years, was saying this: Ah, Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury! Against a godless nation I send him, and against the people of my wrath I command him (Isa. 10:5-6).

Assyria really was being used. The Rabshakeh has got hold of a true doctrine — that the God of Israel governs the movements of empires — and is using it at the foot of a wall to break the nerve of the people on top of it.

The reader of this book has seen that done before. Jehu stood at a gate in front of two heaps of heads and preached accurate theology about the word of the LORD not falling to the ground. Truth in the mouth of a man who does not submit to it is a weapon like any other.

And Isaiah answers the claim in the next breath of the same passage. Assyria is the axe, and shall the axe boast over him who hews with it? — and when the Lord has finished his work on Mount Zion, he will punish the speech of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria (Isa. 10:12-15). Being an instrument in God's hand is not a licence to make speeches about it, and the instrument is answerable for the boasting.

'Then Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, and Shebnah, and Joah, said to the Rabshakeh, "Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, for we understand it. Do not speak to us in the language of Judah within the hearing of the people who are on the wall."'

Aramaic was the diplomatic language of the region, and the officials speak it. What they are asking is that this be conducted between professionals, out of earshot.

That tells us what they have realised: he is not negotiating at all. He is fluent in Hebrew, and he has chosen it.

'But the Rabshakeh said to them, "Has my master sent me to speak these words to your master and to you, and not to the men sitting on the wall, who are doomed with you to eat their own dung and to drink their own urine?"'

He tells them exactly what he is doing and then describes a siege in the plainest terms available, deliberately, at volume, to the men who will be living it.

Anybody who thinks that is exaggeration should re-read the chapter about the siege of Samaria, where a donkey's head cost eighty shekels and two women made an agreement about their sons.

'Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out in a loud voice in the language of Judah: "Hear the word of the great king, the king of Assyria!'

Note the phrase, because it is a parody. Hear the word of the great king is built on hear the word of the LORD, which is how every prophet in this book has opened his mouth. He is offering the people an alternative revelation, from an alternative great king.

'Thus says the king: 'Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you out of my hand.'

'Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD by saying, The LORD will surely deliver us, and this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.'

There is the real objective, stated openly. Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD.

He has stopped arguing about Egypt and horses. The thing he has come to destroy is the confidence of ordinary people in God, and he says so.

'Do not listen to Hezekiah, for thus says the king of Assyria: 'Make your peace with me and come out to me. Then each one of you will eat of his own vine, and each one of his own fig tree, and each one of you will drink the water of his own cistern,'

Now listen to what he offers them, because it is the most skilful thing in the speech.

Each one of you will eat of his own vine, and each one of his own fig tree.

That is not Assyrian language. It is Israel's own picture of peace, the settled promise of the covenant — Judah and Israel lived in safety, every man under his vine and under his fig tree (1 Kgs. 4:25) — and it is what Micah, prophesying in Jerusalem at this very moment, was describing as the future God would give (Mic. 4:4).

He has taken the exact words of their hope and put them in his own offer.

'until I come and take you away to a land like your own land, a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive trees and honey, that you may live, and not die. And do not listen to Hezekiah when he misleads you by saying, "The LORD will deliver us."'

There is the clause where the whole thing turns, buried in the middle of a sentence about vines and honey: until I come and take you away.

It is deportation. It is precisely what happened to the ten tribes eight years ago, described in the warmest possible terms — a land like your own, grain and wine, olive trees and honey — and attached to the offer as a subordinate clause after the good part.

That is how every serious temptation is constructed. It is not a lie about what you want; the description of the good is usually accurate, and often borrowed word for word from something God has genuinely promised. The terms are in the subordinate clause, and the whole art of it is that the listener will hear his own vine and his own fig tree and stop listening before take you away.

'Has any of the gods of the nations ever delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria?'

'Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand?'

Here is his closing argument, and the last five words of it are the cruellest thing said in this chapter.

Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand?

He runs through a list of conquered cities and the gods who did not save them, and then, at the end, he names Samaria — which was not a foreign city with a foreign god. Those were Israelites. They had the same God, the same law, the same father Abraham, and eight years ago they were carried off five hundred miles and they are not coming back.

It is factually true, and everybody on that wall knew it, and some of them had relatives in it.

'Who among all the gods of the lands have delivered their lands out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?'"'

There is his mistake, in the last line, after a speech in which almost everything was accurate.

He puts the LORD in the list.

He has surveyed the evidence competently — no god anywhere in the region has stopped the Assyrian army, including the God of Samaria — and drawn the obvious conclusion, which is that the God of Jerusalem is one more item in a category he has already exhausted.

Everything the next chapter does is an answer to that sentence.

'But the people were silent and answered him not a word, for the king's command was, "Do not answer him."'

Nobody says anything.

The reader of these books has met a silent crowd before. Elijah stood on Carmel and asked a nation how long it would go limping between two opinions, and the people did not answer him a word (1 Kgs. 18:21) — and that silence was the silence of people with no defence.

This one is the opposite. These people are silent under orders, and it is discipline. Not one man on that wall shouts back, argues, negotiates, or takes the offer, and the writer notes that they were told not to and did not.

Some arguments are answered by not answering them. Everything the Rabshakeh said was designed to be engaged with, and the only reply that did not hand him something was the one they gave.

'Then Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder, came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and told him the words of the Rabshakeh.'

Three senior men walk back into the palace with their robes ripped, and repeat every word.

Tearing the clothes was the standard sign of grief or horror, and it is the last thing the chapter records. These are the head of the household, the secretary and the recorder — the three most composed men in the government, whose whole training is to bring information to a king without colouring it — and they arrive in pieces.

They also do the one useful thing available to them: they tell him all of it. Not a summary, not the gist, not the parts a king might bear to hear. They told him the words of the Rabshakeh. That is why the next chapter can begin the way it does.

18.theology:
Nehushtan (v. 4). Not a pagan object: God told Moses to make it and people bitten in the wilderness looked at it and lived (Num. 21:8-9). Seven centuries later the most dangerous thing in Jerusalem was the one relic with a real history of real grace attached to it. Every long-lived Christian institution collects these — a building, a translation, a hymn book, the memory of a revival, the ministry God unmistakably used forty years ago. None were idols when given; they become idols by being kept past their moment. And the sharpest edge of it: the Lord Jesus made that very serpent a picture of himself (John 3:14-15). It was never wrong to value it. It was fatal to look at it instead of through it.

He trusted (v. 5). The reason given for the highest verdict in the book is not competence or success but where he rested his weight — which is exactly what the Rabshakeh will attack seven times over. On the apparent clash with Josiah (23:25): the two are commended for different things, and Hebrew praise of this kind is not a league table.

The part that gets left out (vv. 14-16). I have done wrong... whatever you impose on me I will bear. He apologises to an idolatrous emperor, empties the temple, and strips gold from doorposts that Hezekiah king of Judah had overlaid — the writer names him twice in one sentence so nobody misses that he is undoing his own reform. It is precisely what Ahaz did. Faith is not a possession acquired once and thereafter owned; the man who spreads a letter before God in the next chapter is the man on the ladder with a chisel in this one. And the payment bought nothing — Sennacherib took the silver and sent the army.

The same patch of ground (v. 17). The conduit of the upper pool, on the highway to the Washer's Field is where Isaiah met Ahaz and offered him any sign he liked (Isa. 7:3). Ahaz stood there and sent for Assyria. A generation later Assyria stands there shouting at his son. The writer gives the location in Isaiah's own words and says nothing else about it.

Mostly true (vv. 19-25). Egypt really is a broken reed, and Isaiah had said so (Isa. 31:1). The accusation about the high places is the standing charge against every real reform — that removing what God did not ask for is irreligion. And the claim of divine commission is not a straight lie: Ah, Assyria, the rod of my anger (Isa. 10:5-6). A true doctrine in the mouth of a man who does not submit to it is a weapon, as it was for Jehu at the gate. Isaiah answers it in the next breath: shall the axe boast over him who swings it? God will punish the boasting (Isa. 10:12-15).

The offer (vv. 31-32). Each one of you will eat of his own vine, and each one of his own fig tree is not Assyrian language. It is Israel's own picture of covenant peace (1 Kgs. 4:25), and Micah was preaching it in that city at that moment (Mic. 4:4). The terms are in the subordinate clause — until I come and take you away — and that is how every serious temptation is built. The description of the good is accurate and often borrowed from something God has actually promised; the whole art is that you stop listening before the clause that carries the price.

One item too many (vv. 34-35). His survey is competent and his last example is unanswerable — Samaria's God did not save Samaria, and men on that wall had relatives in it. His error is in the final line, where he puts the LORD in the list. The whole of the next chapter is the answer to that sentence.
18.examples:
Then: A king climbed a ladder at the door of the temple and chiselled off the gold he had put there himself in the first years of his reform, to pay a bill to an emperor who took the money and sent the army anyway.

Now: Three things. First, Nehushtan. The hardest idol to break is never the obviously pagan one; it is the object, method or memory that really did come from God and really did work, and has quietly stopped being a signpost. Ask what in your church or your own history is being venerated for what it once carried. Second, verses 14-16, which are in the Bible on purpose. The best king Judah ever had did the cowardly thing first and the faithful thing second, in the same crisis, in the same year — so a bad first response to a threat does not settle what kind of person you are. Third, the Rabshakeh's offer. Almost everything he said was true, and the sentence that mattered was the subordinate clause in the middle of the pleasant one. When something is offered to you in the exact words of what you have always wanted, the terms will be in the part of the sentence you are least likely to still be listening to.
