And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.
19.overview:
The same king who two months earlier sent an apology and three hundred talents of silver to Lachish now tears his clothes and goes into the house of the LORD. His father had stood at that same conduit facing two kings and written to Assyria; his son goes up the hill.

What he asks Isaiah to pray about is not the army. It is the words: the Rabshakeh was sent to mock the living God, and Hezekiah appeals on the ground of the insult rather than on Judah's deserving. Isaiah answers with three predictions in one verse — a rumour, a return, and a sword at home — and the rumour arrives within seven verses.

Sennacherib's follow-up letter attacks God directly, and Hezekiah does not reply to it. He carries it up to the temple and spreads it flat on the floor, and prays a prayer that begins with who God is, concedes every fact in the enemy's argument, adds the one distinction the argument had no room for — they were not gods, but the work of men's hands — and asks for rescue so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you, O LORD, are God alone. God answers in poetry, addressed to Sennacherib, and the city is promised that not one arrow will be shot into it. That night a hundred and eighty-five thousand men die in the camp, and twenty years later the emperor is murdered at prayer in his own god's temple by his own sons.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Sent to Mock the Living God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hezekiah tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and went into the house of the LORD (v. 1), and sends to Isaiah with an image of complete exhaustion: children have come to the point of birth, and there is no strength to bring them forth (v. 3). And he reframes the whole crisis — the Rabshakeh was sent to mock the living God, so let God answer the words he has heard (v. 4). Isaiah's reply is three sentences long and predicts three things: I will put a spirit in him, so that he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land (v. 7). The rumour arrives at once (v. 9) — and with it a second and harder message, attacking not the king but God: do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you (vv. 10-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 1 is the same man in the same year as 18:14, where he sent an apology and three hundred talents of silver to Lachish. It is also his father's exact position — Ahaz stood at that same conduit facing two kings and wrote to Assyria. Hezekiah goes into the temple, and the difference between the two chapters is the difference between the two kings.
verseByVerse.examples: And the ground he takes is not that Judah deserves rescue or even that Judah is God's people. It is that God has been insulted in public by a man who put him in a list with wood and stone. He asks for a hearing on the strength of the offence, and asks Isaiah to pray for the remnant that is left — which is all Judah now is.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as King Hezekiah heard it, he tore his clothes and covered himself with sackcloth and went into the house of the LORD. And he sent Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and the senior priests, covered with sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz. They said to him, "Thus says Hezekiah, This day is a day of distress, of rebuke, and of disgrace; children have come to the point of birth, and there is no strength to bring them forth. It may be that the LORD your God heard all the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria has sent to mock the living God, and will rebuke the words that the LORD your God has heard; therefore lift up your prayer for the remnant that is left." When the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah, Isaiah said to them, "Say to your master, 'Thus says the LORD: Do not be afraid because of the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have reviled me. Behold, I will put a spirit in him, so that he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land.'" The Rabshakeh returned, and found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah, for he heard that the king had left Lachish. Now the king heard concerning Tirhakah king of Cush, "Behold, he has set out to fight against you." So he sent messengers again to Hezekiah, saying, "Thus shall you speak to Hezekiah king of Judah: 'Do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you by promising that Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria. Behold, you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands, devoting them to destruction. And shall you be delivered? Have the gods of the nations delivered them, the nations that my fathers destroyed, Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden who were in Telassar? Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, the king of Hena, or the king of Ivvah?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As soon as King Hezekiah heard it, he tore his clothes and covered himself with sackcloth and went into the house of the LORD.'

Read the last clause against the last chapter, because the whole difference between the two is here.

In chapter 18 this same man, in this same year, facing this same emperor, sent a message to Lachish saying I have done wrong; withdraw from me. Whatever you impose on me I will bear, and paid for it by stripping gold off the doors of the house of the LORD.

Now he goes in through those doors.

It is his father's exact position, too. Ahaz was standing at that very conduit with two kings marching on him when Isaiah came out to meet him with an offer of any sign he liked, and Ahaz declined it and wrote to Assyria. His son, at the same spot, with a worse army outside, goes up the hill.

'And he sent Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and the senior priests, covered with sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz.'

Note who goes. The head of the household and the secretary — the two most senior men in the government, the same two who stood at the wall — and with them the senior priests, and all of them in sackcloth.

A state delegation in mourning dress, walking through the streets of a besieged city to a prophet's house. Everybody watching them knew what it meant, which was presumably the point.

Isaiah has been standing behind this entire book without being named in it. He prophesied to Ahaz, he has been preaching in Jerusalem for something like forty years, and this is the first time the writer of Kings puts him on the page.

'They said to him, "Thus says Hezekiah, This day is a day of distress, of rebuke, and of disgrace; children have come to the point of birth, and there is no strength to bring them forth.'

The image is one of the best in the Old Testament and it is horribly exact.

A woman at full term, in labour, at the moment the child should come — and no strength left to push. Everything has arrived at the point of crisis and the one thing needed is the one thing that is gone.

He is not describing fear of what might happen. He is describing a situation that has already reached its decisive hour with nothing left in the room to meet it.

'It may be that the LORD your God heard all the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria has sent to mock the living God, and will rebuke the words that the LORD your God has heard; therefore lift up your prayer for the remnant that is left."'

And here is the turn on which everything else depends.

Hezekiah reframes the crisis. It is not, in the first place, a military problem. A man has been sent to mock the living God, and what Hezekiah asks God to deal with is the words.

Look at the ground he takes. He does not argue that Judah deserves rescue; his own conduct four verses into the last chapter rules that out and he knows it. He does not even argue that Judah is God's people and therefore entitled. He says: your name has been dragged through the dirt in public by a man who put you in a list with carved wood, and I am asking you to answer that.

The living God is the phrase that will run through the rest of the chapter — set against the gods of the nations, which were burned because they were only ever furniture.

The remnant that is left. Forty-six fortified cities are gone and two hundred thousand people have been counted as spoil. Judah is now one city and whoever got inside its walls, and the king's own word for his kingdom is a remnant.

'When the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah,'

'Isaiah said to them, "Say to your master, 'Thus says the LORD: Do not be afraid because of the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have reviled me.'

God takes the words personally, exactly as Hezekiah asked him to. With which the servants of the king of Assyria have reviled me.

'Behold, I will put a spirit in him, so that he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land.'"'

One verse, three predictions: a rumour, a return, a sword at home. Mark them, because the chapter records the fulfilment of all three — the first in seven verses, the second in twenty-nine, and the third twenty years later.

Note the means. The greatest military power on earth is going to be moved off Judah's territory by a piece of news.

The reader of this book has seen God do that before. An entire Syrian army abandoned its camp outside Samaria and ran twenty-five miles throwing its equipment away, because it heard the sound of chariots that did not exist (7:6-7). He does not need a battle. He can do it with a noise, or with something somebody says in a corridor.

'The Rabshakeh returned, and found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah, for he heard that the king had left Lachish.'

'Now the king heard concerning Tirhakah king of Cush, "Behold, he has set out to fight against you." So he sent messengers again to Hezekiah, saying,'

There is the rumour, arriving on schedule. An Egyptian force under a Cushite commander is reported to be moving, and Sennacherib now has a problem on a second front.

His response is to try to finish Jerusalem by post before he has to turn round.

'"Thus shall you speak to Hezekiah king of Judah: 'Do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you by promising that Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.'

The letter is shorter than the speech and it is worse.

At the wall the Rabshakeh spent most of his time on Egypt, horses, and Hezekiah's reforms, and only reached God at the end. Here he starts there and stays there. Do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you.

The accusation is now against God directly, and the charge is fraud — that he has made a promise he cannot keep, and that trusting him is being taken in.

'Behold, you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands, devoting them to destruction. And shall you be delivered?'

And there is a word in verse 11 that a reader of the Old Testament should catch: devoting them to destruction.

That is Israel's own vocabulary. It renders the root behind herem, the ban — the thing God laid on Jericho, the thing Achan died for touching, the thing Saul lost his kingdom over when he spared Agag, and the charge on which Ahab was sentenced for letting Ben-hadad go. It is a holy word. It means something set apart under God's sentence and removed from every human use.

The emperor of Assyria uses it of his own campaigns, as a boast, about cities he burned for plunder.

Whether he knew what he was borrowing hardly matters. Men who conquer things have always reached for religious language to describe it, and the sacred word for God's judgment is exactly the word an empire wants for its own violence.

'Have the gods of the nations delivered them, the nations that my fathers destroyed, Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden who were in Telassar?'

'Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, the king of Hena, or the king of Ivvah?'"'

The list is longer this time — nine places, some of them famous, some of them ancient, all of them gone.

Gozan is on the list. That is one of the places the Israelites of the northern kingdom were deported to eight years earlier (17:6). He is naming, to the king of Judah, a town full of Judah's relatives.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–19 — He Spread It Before the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers and read it; and Hezekiah went up to the house of the LORD and spread it before the LORD (v. 14). The prayer that follows begins with who God is — enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth; you have made the heavens and the earth (v. 15) — asks him to read the letter himself (v. 16), concedes every fact in it (v. 17), and adds the one thing the Assyrians left out: for they were not gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone. Therefore they were destroyed (v. 18). And the request rests on a ground nobody could improve: save us, please, from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you, O LORD, are God alone (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: He does not answer the letter. He does not convene the council, draft a reply, or send for Egypt. He carries the paper up the hill and opens it out flat on the floor in front of God, the way a man lays a document on a table and says: read that.
verseByVerse.examples: And notice the shape of the prayer, because it is a model and it is the opposite of how most of us pray under pressure. It opens with God's identity, not the emergency. It grants the enemy's evidence in full rather than disputing it. And it asks for rescue on the ground of God's own reputation among the nations, which is the highest ground anything can be asked on.

verseByVerse.quote: Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers and read it; and Hezekiah went up to the house of the LORD and spread it before the LORD. And Hezekiah prayed before the LORD and said: "O LORD, the God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth; you have made the heavens and the earth. Incline your ear, O LORD, and hear; open your eyes, O LORD, and see; and hear the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to mock the living God. Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste the nations and their lands and have cast their gods into the fire, for they were not gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone. Therefore they were destroyed. So now, O LORD our God, save us, please, from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you, O LORD, are God alone."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers and read it; and Hezekiah went up to the house of the LORD and spread it before the LORD.'

This is the most famous thing this king ever did, and it deserves to be.

Consider what he does not do. He does not draft a reply, and he had officials capable of drafting one. He does not convene the council. He does not send to Egypt, which is what everybody expected and what the Rabshakeh assumed he had already done. He does not conceal the letter, or read out an edited version to steady the city, or burn it.

He carries it up the hill, walks into the temple, and opens it out flat on the floor.

The verb is exactly that: he spread it out, the way a man lays a document on a table in front of somebody and steps back. Here is the letter. Read it.

Set it against what he did with the last Assyrian demand, in the same building, a few months earlier. Then he had gone into the treasury and up a ladder and sent the contents to Lachish. Now he goes into the same building with a piece of paper and no plan.

Anybody with something in writing that frightens them — a diagnosis, a letter from a solicitor, a message they have read eleven times — has been given a model here, and it is not a metaphor. He physically took the thing that was terrifying him into the presence of God and put it down where God could see it.

'And Hezekiah prayed before the LORD and said: "O LORD, the God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth; you have made the heavens and the earth.'

Watch the order of this prayer, because it is a model and it runs opposite to the way most of us pray when we are frightened.

It begins with who God is, and the emergency is not mentioned in the first sentence at all.

Enthroned above the cherubim — the ark was in that building with two golden cherubim over it, and the space above them, empty to the eye, was where God was understood to sit. He is standing a few yards from it.

You are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth — which is a direct answer to the letter on the floor. The Rabshakeh had produced a list of national gods and put the LORD at the end of it. Hezekiah says: you are not the God of Judah among others, you are the God of all the kingdoms, including his.

You have made the heavens and the earth. The empire that has taken forty-six cities did not make anything.

'Incline your ear, O LORD, and hear; open your eyes, O LORD, and see; and hear the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to mock the living God.'

He asks God to read it himself.

The gods on the letter's list had ears that did not hear and eyes that did not see, which is exactly what the psalms say about idols. Hezekiah asks the living God to do the two things carved gods cannot do, over a document written by a man who could not tell the difference.

'Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste the nations and their lands'

'and have cast their gods into the fire, for they were not gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone. Therefore they were destroyed.'

Here is the thing that makes this prayer honest, and it is the part most people skip.

Truly. He concedes it. Every fact in the Assyrian argument is granted without qualification: yes, they have laid waste the nations; yes, they burned the gods; yes, none of them stopped it. He does not dispute one word of the evidence.

And then he adds the single distinction the Rabshakeh's survey had no category for. For they were not gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone. Therefore they were destroyed.

Of course they burned. Wood burns. The Assyrians had been collecting statues and putting them in fires and drawing the conclusion that no god anywhere can resist them, and the conclusion was correct about every item in the sample and worthless about the one case it was being applied to.

There is a way of praying that has to deny the facts in order to keep going, and it is exhausting and it does not last. This is the other kind. He grants the whole case and then names the one thing that was never in it.

'So now, O LORD our God, save us, please, from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you, O LORD, are God alone."'

Now the request, at the very end, in half a verse — with the ground it rests on taking up more room than the request itself.

That all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you, O LORD, are God alone.

Not: because we are your people. Not: because we do not deserve this. Not even: because the city is full of children. He asks for the deliverance of a nation on the ground of what it will demonstrate about God to everybody else.

That is the highest ground anything can be asked on, and the great prayers of the Old Testament keep finding it. Moses, when God offered to destroy Israel and start again with him, argued that the Egyptians would say God brought them out to kill them in the mountains (Ex. 32:12). Elijah on Carmel asked for fire that this people may know that you, O LORD, are God (1 Kgs. 18:37).

It is also the safest ground, because it is the one request God has already committed himself to answering. The prayer the Lord Jesus taught begins there too, before it mentions bread: hallowed be your name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–37 — I Will Put My Hook in Your Nose
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers Sennacherib directly, and in poetry. Zion wags her head behind him (v. 21); whom have you mocked and reviled?... Against the Holy One of Israel! (v. 22); his boasts about cedars and wells and drying up the streams of Egypt are quoted back at him (vv. 23-24). Then the sentence that dismantles him: have you not heard that I determined it long ago? I planned from days of old what now I bring to pass (v. 25) — and I will put my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth, and I will turn you back on the way by which you came (v. 28). Judah is promised three years of recovery and a remnant taking root downward (vv. 29-31), and the city is promised that not one arrow will be shot into it for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David (vv. 32-34). That night the angel of the LORD strikes down a hundred and eighty-five thousand (v. 35). And twenty years later, worshipping in his own god's temple, Sennacherib is murdered by his sons (v. 37).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 25 is the answer to the entire campaign. Everything the man has boasted about was assigned to him long before he was born: I planned from days of old what now I bring to pass, that you should turn fortified cities into heaps of ruins. He is an instrument congratulating himself on being swung — which is exactly how Isaiah put it: shall the axe boast over him who hews with it? (Isa. 10:15).
verseByVerse.examples: And the picture in verse 28 is taken from Assyria's own art. Their palace reliefs show captives led away by cords fastened through the nose or lip, which is what an Assyrian meant by a defeated man. God tells the emperor he will go home by his own road, handled the way his own sculptors depict prisoners.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent to Hezekiah, saying, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Your prayer to me about Sennacherib king of Assyria I have heard. This is the word that the LORD has spoken concerning him: "She despises you, she scorns you— the virgin daughter of Zion; she wags her head behind you— the daughter of Jerusalem. "Whom have you mocked and reviled? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes to the heights? Against the Holy One of Israel! By your messengers you have mocked the Lord, and you have said, 'With my many chariots I have gone up the heights of the mountains, to the far recesses of Lebanon; I felled its tallest cedars, its choicest cypresses; I entered its farthest lodging place, its most fruitful forest. I dug wells and drank foreign waters, and I dried up with the sole of my foot all the streams of Egypt.' "Have you not heard that I determined it long ago? I planned from days of old what now I bring to pass, that you should turn fortified cities into heaps of ruins, while their inhabitants, shorn of strength, are dismayed and confounded, and have become like plants of the field and like tender grass, like grass on the housetops, blighted before it is grown. "But I know your sitting down and your going out and coming in, and your raging against me. Because you have raged against me and your complacency has come into my ears, I will put my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth, and I will turn you back on the way by which you came. "And this shall be the sign for you: this year eat what grows of itself, and in the second year what springs of the same. Then in the third year sow and reap and plant vineyards, and eat their fruit. And the surviving remnant of the house of Judah shall again take root downward and bear fruit upward. For out of Jerusalem shall go a remnant, and out of Mount Zion a band of survivors. The zeal of the LORD will do this. "Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the king of Assyria: He shall not come into this city or shoot an arrow there, or come before it with a shield or cast up a siege mound against it. By the way that he came, by the same he shall return, and he shall not come into this city, declares the LORD. For I will defend this city to save it, for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David." And that night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians. And when people arose early in the morning, behold, these were all dead bodies. Then Sennacherib king of Assyria departed and went home and lived at Nineveh. And as he was worshiping in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him down with the sword and escaped into the land of Ararat. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent to Hezekiah, saying, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Your prayer to me about Sennacherib king of Assyria I have heard.'

The answer opens by acknowledging receipt. Your prayer to me... I have heard. He asked God to hear the words of Sennacherib; God tells him he has heard his.

'This is the word that the LORD has spoken concerning him: "She despises you, she scorns you— the virgin daughter of Zion; she wags her head behind you— the daughter of Jerusalem.'

What follows is a poem, and God does not address Hezekiah in it at all. He turns and speaks to Sennacherib.

The first thing he says is that the city is laughing at him.

The virgin daughter of Zion — untouched, unentered, which is precisely what she is about to remain. She is pictured standing on her wall watching him go, shaking her head at his back like somebody watching a man storm out of an argument he has lost.

'"Whom have you mocked and reviled? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes to the heights? Against the Holy One of Israel!'

The question is about identification. He thought he was addressing a provincial deity of the sort he had burned a dozen of. He was raising his voice at the Holy One of Israel, and did not know what was in the room.

'By your messengers you have mocked the Lord, and you have said, "With my many chariots I have gone up the heights of the mountains, to the far recesses of Lebanon; I felled its tallest cedars, its choicest cypresses; I entered its farthest lodging place, its most fruitful forest.'

A small note on the printing, for readers who compare versions. Where your Bible prints LORD in small capitals it is rendering the covenant name; where it prints Lord in ordinary letters it is rendering adonai, the Master. There are exactly two of the latter in this book — one at 7:6, and this one.

Do not build too much on it. But the title chosen at the precise point where the insult is named is the one that means owner and sovereign, rather than the covenant name a foreign king could plead ignorance of. What Sennacherib mocked was the Master of the world, whether he knew whose name it was or not.

Then his own words are quoted back at him, and they are magnificent bombast. Cedars of Lebanon, the tallest and the choicest, felled by a man who went up the mountains himself with his chariots. Assyrian royal inscriptions read exactly like this; the boasting is not a caricature.

'I dug wells and drank foreign waters, and I dried up with the sole of my foot all the streams of Egypt."'

That is the high point of it: he claims to have dried up the Nile with his foot.

He means that his armies march wherever they like and drink whatever they find. But God has quoted him at the point where the boast becomes a claim to do the things only God does, and left it standing without comment.

'"Have you not heard that I determined it long ago? I planned from days of old what now I bring to pass, that you should turn fortified cities into heaps of ruins,'

Here is the answer to the whole campaign, and it is one sentence.

Have you not heard that I determined it long ago?

Every conquest Sennacherib has just listed was assigned. The forty-six cities of Judah, the fall of Hamath and Arpad, the emptying of Samaria — the whole record he has been reciting as evidence of his own irresistibility was planned from days of old and given to him to carry out.

He is an instrument congratulating himself on being swung, and Isaiah had already put it exactly that way: shall the axe boast over him who hews with it, or the saw magnify itself against him who wields it? (Isa. 10:15).

There is something almost pitying in the question. Have you not heard? The man does not know what he is. He thinks he is the subject of the sentence.

'while their inhabitants, shorn of strength, are dismayed and confounded, and have become like plants of the field and like tender grass, like grass on the housetops, blighted before it is grown.'

Grass on a housetop is the picture. Seed blows onto the thin layer of earth on a flat mud roof, comes up green after the rain, has no depth of soil, and is dead within days of the sun getting to it.

That is what the conquered nations were: not opponents overcome by a great general, but roof grass. It is not flattering to Assyria at all.

'"But I know your sitting down and your going out and coming in, and your raging against me.'

The language is the language of the psalms about ordinary people — you know when I sit down and when I rise up... you search out my path and my lying down (Ps. 139:2-3) — applied to the emperor of the world.

His movements, his campaigns, his temper. All of it observed, all along, by the God he had catalogued as a local option.

'Because you have raged against me and your complacency has come into my ears, I will put my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth, and I will turn you back on the way by which you came.'

The image is borrowed from Assyria's own picture of itself.

Their palace walls were carved with scenes of prisoners being led away with cords run through the nose or the lip, and the practice is recorded in their own inscriptions. It was their visual shorthand for a defeated man: something that used to be a king, walking where it is pulled.

God tells Sennacherib that he will go home on a hook and a bit, by the same road he came in on, handled precisely the way his own sculptors depict the people he has beaten.

'"And this shall be the sign for you: this year eat what grows of itself, and in the second year what springs of the same. Then in the third year sow and reap and plant vineyards, and eat their fruit.'

The sign is agricultural and it is entirely practical.

An invasion has meant that nothing was sown this year and nothing will be sown next year either; the countryside has been occupied and the population is inside the walls. So for two years they will live on whatever comes up by itself in unworked fields, which is thin but real. And in the third year they will plough and sow and plant vines and eat what they grow — which is a promise that there will be a third year, and that they will be on their own land in it, and that it will be safe to plant something that takes years to fruit.

'And the surviving remnant of the house of Judah shall again take root downward and bear fruit upward.'

'For out of Jerusalem shall go a remnant, and out of Mount Zion a band of survivors. The zeal of the LORD will do this.'

Root downward and fruit upward. The order matters and it is the way anything grows: what happens underground and out of sight comes first, and the fruit is the last stage and not the first.

And then the guarantee, and it is not Judah's resolve or Hezekiah's reform: the zeal of the LORD will do this. Zeal is the word for a jealous, burning commitment to something one regards as one's own.

'"Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the king of Assyria: He shall not come into this city or shoot an arrow there, or come before it with a shield or cast up a siege mound against it.'

Four denials, and they get smaller and smaller.

He will not enter the city. He will not shoot an arrow into it. He will not so much as come up in front of it with a shield. He will not throw up a single basket of earth for a siege ramp.

Not one arrow. After forty-six cities, a hundred and eighty-five thousand men in the camp and a Rabshakeh at the wall, the promise is that nothing at all will be launched at those walls.

'By the way that he came, by the same he shall return, and he shall not come into this city, declares the LORD.'

And by the way that he came, by the same he shall return is a small humiliation of its own. He will not even get a different road. Everything he passed on the way down — the towns he took, the ramps he built, the ground his army camped on — he will pass again going the other way with nothing to show for it.

'For I will defend this city to save it, for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David.'

Two grounds, and neither of them is Hezekiah.

For my own sake — which is precisely what Hezekiah had asked on. He prayed that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you are God alone, and God answers using the same reasoning.

And for the sake of my servant David — who has been dead three hundred years.

The reader has met this before. Judah was not destroyed in Jehoram's day for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever (8:19), and Abijam kept his throne for the same reason (1 Kgs. 15:4). Now the best king in the line is defended on exactly the same footing as the worst were: not for what he is, but for a promise made to somebody else.

Hold on to that. Hezekiah had trusted, reformed, torn down the high places, broken the serpent, prayed the best prayer in the book — and when God gives his reasons for saving the city, Hezekiah's name is not among them.

'And that night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians. And when people arose early in the morning, behold, these were all dead bodies.'

No battle. Nobody on the wall did anything. The city was told that not one arrow would be shot into it, and not one was shot out of it either.

People got up in the morning and looked over the parapet at a camp that had not moved.

The event left marks outside the Bible. Sennacherib's own annals, which are extremely detailed about this campaign and boast of shutting Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage, never claim to have taken the city — which for an Assyrian record is a silence with a shape. And Herodotus preserved an Egyptian story of an Assyrian army disabled overnight by a plague of mice that ate their equipment, which may be a distant memory of the same night.

'Then Sennacherib king of Assyria departed and went home and lived at Nineveh.'

The second of the three predictions in verse 7, fulfilled in one flat sentence. He went home.

'And as he was worshiping in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him down with the sword and escaped into the land of Ararat. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.'

Twenty years later.

The writer has held on to that sentence for two decades of narrative time in order to put it here, at the end of the chapter, because Isaiah had said I will make him fall by the sword in his own land and the word was not finished until it happened.

Look where it happens. The man who wrote to Jerusalem asking whether any god had ever delivered his people from the king of Assyria was killed at prayer, in his own god's temple, by his own sons, and the god he was bowing to did nothing at all.

Everything he had said about the gods of the nations turned out to be true of his own.

The Babylonian records confirm the assassination and the succession of Esarhaddon, and even preserve the political convulsion that followed. Sennacherib died in the year the tablets call the twentieth of his reign, and the sons ran for Ararat, which is Armenia, and were never brought back.

Three sentences of prophecy in verse 7 — a rumour, a return, a sword — and all three landed, the last of them long after most people had stopped watching for it.

19.theology:
Two responses, one year (v. 1). The man who stripped gold off the temple doors in 18:16 walks in through them here. Nothing external has changed and the army is closer; what has changed is where he takes it. A bad first response to a threat does not settle what a man will do next.

The reframing (v. 4). He turns a military emergency into a question of blasphemy, and asks God to deal with the words. He does not claim Judah deserves rescue — his own conduct rules that out — nor even that Judah is entitled as God's people. He asks on the strength of the offence done to God's name in public.

Moved by a rumour (v. 7). Three predictions in one verse, fulfilled at vv. 9, 36 and 37. And the means is a piece of news — as an entire Syrian army once abandoned its camp because it heard chariots that did not exist (7:6). He does not require a battle; a noise will do, or something somebody says in a corridor.

He spread it before the LORD (v. 14). No reply drafted, no council convened, no embassy to Egypt, no edited version read out to steady the city. He carries the paper up the hill and opens it out on the floor, the way a man lays a document on a table and steps back. Anyone with something in writing that frightens them has been given a model, and it is not a metaphor.

The shape of the prayer (vv. 15-19). It opens with God's identity, not the emergency. It answers the enemy's list directly — you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth. It asks the living God to do the two things carved gods cannot, hear and see. It concedes every fact in the Assyrian case with the word truly and then adds the one distinction the case had no category for: wood burns. There is a kind of praying that must deny the facts to keep going; this is the other kind. And the request is put last, resting on God's reputation among the nations — the ground Moses took at the golden calf (Ex. 32:12), the ground Elijah took on Carmel (1 Kgs. 18:37), and the first petition the Lord taught us to pray.

I determined it long ago (v. 25). The whole record Sennacherib recites as proof of his irresistibility was assigned to him before he was born. He is an instrument congratulating itself on being swung: shall the axe boast over him who hews with it? (Isa. 10:15). And have you not heard? has something almost pitying in it — the man does not know what he is.

His own art turned on him (v. 28). Assyrian palace reliefs show prisoners led away by cords through the nose or lip; it was their shorthand for a beaten king. God tells the emperor he goes home on a hook and a bit, by his own road, handled the way his own sculptors depict the defeated.

Whose sake (v. 34). For my own sake and for the sake of my servant David — the first is exactly what Hezekiah asked on; the second is the lamp again (1 Kgs. 11:36; 15:4; 8:19). The best king in the line is defended on the same footing as the worst were, and when God gives his reasons for saving the city, Hezekiah's name is not among them.

The third prediction (v. 37). Twenty years later, and the writer waited to record it. The man who asked whether any god had ever delivered anyone from the king of Assyria was killed at worship, in his own god's house, by his own sons — and his god did nothing. Everything he had said about the gods of the nations turned out to be true of his own.
19.examples:
Then: A king read a letter designed to destroy his nerve, walked up the hill with it, went into the temple, and opened it out flat on the floor where God could see it — and then prayed a prayer in which he agreed with every factual claim the letter made.

Now: Three things. First, verse 14 is a practical instruction and not a figure of speech. Whatever the piece of paper is — the scan result, the letter from the solicitor, the message you have now read eleven times — the thing to do with it is to take it somewhere and put it down in front of God, unedited. Second, the honesty of verses 17-18. Hezekiah does not pray as though the frightening facts were untrue; he grants them in full and then names the one thing the frightening argument left out. Prayer that has to keep denying reality is exhausting and does not last. Third, verse 34. He had trusted, reformed, broken the serpent and prayed as well as anyone in these books prays, and when God stated his reasons for saving the city they were his own name and a promise made to a man three hundred years dead. That is not a slight. It is the only kind of security that does not depend on how you are doing this week.
